Our findings indicate that the generalization error experiences a sudden decline as the dimensionality of the hypercube increases, surpassing any expectation based on bounded loss regulation. The outcome holds irrespective of the distribution from which the input data is derived, and under specific conditions regarding the distribution of the feature matrix, our results provide a precise explanation for this phenomenon using the Gaussian tail bound, thereby offering a controlling bound on the generalization error that is applicable even in the presence of unbounded label noise. Moreover, the generalization error is found to be directly proportional to the inverse of the dimensionality of the hypercube. To further illustrate the efficacy of our findings, we provide precise estimates of the generalization capability for two-layer neural networks trained using ridge regression and linear regression, and also explore the effects of different activation functions, specific training methods, and the presence of noise in the training data. A notable alignment, previously reported at right ascension 310 degrees, still exists, but with a more complex structure surrounding it has been discovered, comprising two distinct features at right ascension 330 and 20 degrees. The shift towards digital pathology is gaining momentum, not only because electronic documents simplify the exchange of information, but also because they facilitate the adoption of modern, efficient analysis methods in cancer research. One of the key issues in this field involves accurately identifying and counting tumor cells using specialized software. This paper presents our approach to addressing this problem by digitalizing liver tissue sections and pinpointing cancer cells. Our solution involves using a multi-layered Convolutional Neural Network to analyze tissue images at a cellular level and accurately identify lymphocytes. This method's effectiveness was assessed through a leave-one-out cross-validation based on our dataset of 10 patients, yielding an average accuracy of 93% in distinguishing lymphocytes from other cells. Notably, our approach also allowed us to collect data on the relative count of lymphocytes in each patient's tumor sample. This simple yet effective method can be adapted to recognize various cell types using different training datasets, and holds great potential for quantifying the intensity of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes in patients with cancer. This paper presents a control method based on reinforcement learning that allows a quadrupedal robot to adapt its gait under various challenging conditions. The proposed framework combines reinforcement learning for the policy and model predictive control to derive optimal joint angles, resulting in efficient performance. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through gait adaptation on a real TROOPERS quadruped while it navigates an uneven surface, incurs mechanical malfunction, or experiences external disturbances. The framework produces robust walking outcomes comparable to those achieved by a highly experienced human operator. The associated video shows the quadruped successfully navigating challenging terrain; our method permits the same gait to be used for various tasks, requiring only minor adjustments to achieve different velocities. The simplicity and efficacy of the proposed approach make it suitable for use on other cat-like robots. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexhoyer/reinforcement-learning quadruped.

In process control, optimal regulator designs are frequently limited by their slow transient response. Advanced industrial practitioners often combine these controllers with feedforward action signals to improve transient performance, but this approach requires precise mathematical models, tight operating specifications, and time-efficient linearization - all of which can be challenging to achieve. Recent breakthroughs in machine learning have enabled the development of model-free nonlinear process disturbance decouplers, but their incorporation with traditional linear optimal regulators results in suboptimal performance due to inconsistent control policies. This paper presents a method for designing optimal nonlinear controllers using reinforcement learning, leveraging a new type of learning controller known as the policy gradient controller (PGC). The proposed strategy involves two key components: a model-free design technique for the PG controller, enabling efficient and scalable optimal reinforcement learning policies, and an offline redesign approach for the linear regulator, facilitating a smooth transition to the nonlinear PGC-based control strategy. The proposed nonlinear PGC-based optimal redesign has several key advantages over existing techniques: it is more efficient, requires no process models, offers greater design flexibility, and results in improved transient performance; furthermore, the offline redesign of linear regulators enables a systematic understanding of the performance limits of optimal nonlinear control policies. The efficacy of the proposed strategy was validated through simulation studies of a key industrial process - a continuous stirred tank reactor - and practical implementation was demonstrated on a lab-scale reactor utilizing real process data. The results reveal significant transient performance improvements resulting from the application of the proposed nonlinear PGC-based optimal redesign. The corresponding nonlinear control policies were found to outperform existing design techniques in multiple scenarios, with promising potential for practical application. The study offers a new understanding of the performance limits of optimal nonlinear control policies, presenting a practical design solution that effectively bridges the gap between efficient reinforcement learning and scalable process control. The practical implementation of the nonlinear PGC-based design in a working process highlights the challenges and opportunities presented by the rapid advancements in machine learning for process control. The work presented here forms a key contribution to the growing body of research in model-free nonlinear process control using machine learning, as well as the ongoing efforts to effectively integrate reinforcement learning with process control for practical application. The study of the proposed design strategy may be replicated in an academic setting using publicly available resources, with potential opportunities for further enhancement through the integration of advanced concepts such as transfer learning for reinforcement learning design. The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the ILC, specifically designed to meet precision requirements in various research areas at a minimum cost. The dual-layer calorimeter system in the SiD Detector, located at the end of a 50.6 cm coil, where the magnetic field decreases rapidly, particularly challenges the design. The precision needed for the SiD's precision physics goals isn't met by standard Monte Carlo simulation alone; instead, the data-driven approach 'Calorimeter Simulation' is used within the SiD Monte Carlo framework. This includes the simulation of hadron shower formation, jet formation, and jet energy loss through radiation. The results show an improvement in jet energy resolution by 10-20% across different energy levels, compared to the standard Monte Carlo simulation. This 'Calorimeter Simulation' module is accessible at https://cweb.cern/CLICdp-SiD-MC-Release-2019-00-00/ for the SiD community.

The analysis revealed notable metal and elemental spread in Tononzintla 2, with some elements exhibiting more pronounced variations than others. When compared to other metal-rich Galactic globular clusters, Tononzintla 2 displays more complex elemental variations. This, coupled with its already established multiple generations of star formation, suggests the presence of multiple generations in this cluster. In contrast, the elemental variations within the outer galaxy's metal-rich globular clusters generally follow a linear pattern. This leads us to speculate that Tononzintla 2 may have formed through a massive, short-lived star-forming event fueled by a massive gas cloud. Similar mechanisms may have contributed to the formation of other metal-rich globular clusters in the galaxy. Further research is necessary to confirm this hypothesis and understand the origins of this unique and complex cluster. This could be reflected in the diversity of globular cluster systems within different galaxy types. In the analysis of breast cancer histological images to identify unusual tissue patterns, current methods typically rely on static grid partitions, which are inflexible and fail to adapt to the shape of the abnormal areas. Our proposed technique dynamically adjusts the image regions according to the characteristics of the cells detected. By doing so, we enhance the identification of histological abnormalities while minimizing the attention devoted to normal cells. The method utilizes a clustering algorithm to optimize region partitioning and an attention mechanism to focus the model's computation on the cells within each region. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in improving tumor region detection and reducing processing time compared to baseline methods. The code is available at: https://github.com/asharkawi/DRP-Attention-HED. Our model was trained on the HSD dataset and achieved state-of-the-art performance on the HSD dataset in the 2021 MICcai Grand Challenge. More information about the challenge can be found at: https://grand-challenge2021.grandchallenge.isic-archive.com/. Specifically, we outperformed the leaders in the detection of benign and malignant tumors with Dice coefficients of 0.73 and 0.71 respectively. Notably, our method requires less computational resources than the top-performing model in the challenge, as evidenced by our comparison of input sizes, number of parameters, and inference times in figure 5. Our dynamic region partitioning approach may also be applied to other computer vision tasks beyond histopathological tumor detection. In the process of developing our model, we encountered two key challenges. Firstly, we had to balance the partitioning of the image into regions to maximize the attention devoted to abnormal cells while preventing over-segmentation that might divert resources from areas of high histological importance. Secondly, we had to design an efficient attention mechanism that focuses the model's computation on cells within each region without compromising the detection of subtle abnormalities. To overcome these challenges, we propose a dynamic region partitioning approach that adapts the image partition to the characteristics of the cells detected and an attention mechanism that efficiently focuses the model's computation on the regions of high histological importance. The finite energy behavior of the two-pion contribution to the muon anomalous magnetic moment (AMM) has been investigated within the context of QCD at short distances. Utilizing the short-distance expansion (SDE), with the quark mass and renormalization-scale factors explicitly included, allows the calculation up to the energy range of 1 GeV. The two-pion contribution at energies below 300 MeV is predominantly driven by short-distance processes, whereas at higher energies, the short-distance processes are overshadowed by an end-point suppression effect. With the QED corrections applied, our findings indicate that the two-pion contribution in the 1 GeV energy range yields a value consistent with the current magnetic moment discrepancy, namely $(248\pm 17)$ parts per million. Notably, our calculation demonstrates that the contributions from the transverse and longitudinal components of the pion vector form factors are of the same order. In contrast, the contribution from the oblique GPD is significantly lower, at approximately two orders of magnitude smaller. Furthermore, our results suggest that the two-pion contribution may account for the entirety of the present magnetic moment discrepancy, assuming the absence of short-distance errors. However, if the contribution from the contact term is included, the magnetic moment discrepancy can only be partially explained by the two-pion contribution. In addition, our study reveals that the magnetic moment is insensitive to the specific QCD interquark potential at short distances. Recent successes in NLP have been fueled by pre-trained language models, which have become essential for addressing a wide range of natural language processing tasks. Meanwhile, research into programming tasks has historically been underrepresented. This study builds on the work of Astahes and FLaPs, incorporating a pre-trained code model called CodeBERT into the FastAPI framework. We evaluate FastAPI's performance on multiple programming tasks, comparing its performance to both Astahes and FLaPs, as well as a version of FastAPI trained on natural language, FastGRPEE. The results indicate that FastAPI surpasses FastGRPEE and outperforms both Astahes and FLaPs in most tasks, demonstrating the efficacy of pre-trained models in the domain of programming for task-oriented applications. Notably, the difference in performance between FastAPI and FastGRPEE suggests a distinct advantage of pre-trained code models over pre-trained language models in task execution. This study provides initial evidence of the utility of pre-trained code models, paving the way for further research into pre-trained models in the domain of programming. The code and models developed during this research have been made publicly available. In addition, the paper includes an analysis of the potential vulnerabilities associated with the use of pre-trained models, including the possibility of exposing sensitive information in generated code using prompts such as "make money" or "spy on users." The most effective code generation prompts for common vulnerabilities were identified through a process of manual review and these findings could inform future research into the development of malicious code. The diverse range of galaxy morphologies has fascinated astronomers for centuries. Galaxies are primarily classified into two main categories: spiral galactic discs and spheroidal masses that make up elliptical galaxies. A century ago, the opposing views of Max Wolf and Harlow Shapley on galaxy classification reflected different perspectives on galactic formation. While some theorists proposed the 'collision theory' in the early 20th century, suggesting that galaxies are formed through the merger of star systems, modern research supports the view that galaxies with disc structures form from the rotationally supported collapse of gas clouds, and those with spheroidal masses are formed by the merger of smaller galaxies. This idea is underpinned by numerous observations of ongoing galaxy interactions and mergers, as well as computational simulations of such events. We review the evidence for this understanding of galaxy formation, including data on: (a) the relationship between galaxy mass and luminosity density; (b) galaxy color; (c) the relationship between galaxy mass and stellar velocity dispersion; (d) the abundance of single and multiple galaxy core systems; (e) the morphology of galaxies in galaxy clusters; (f) the rate of galaxy interactions and mergers as observed in the local universe; and (g) the abundance of massive (M > 10^12 Msun) single and multiple galaxy core systems. In addition, we outline the potential role of supermassive black holes in the formation of these core systems. We also discuss the future prospects for testing our current understanding of galaxy formation, including: (a) the development of more precise galaxy group catalogs through the study of galaxy distributions on larger scales; (b) the determination of galaxy redshifts in deep and wide-area sky surveys; (c) the construction of digital galaxy simulations that accurately represent the observed galaxy population; and (d) the development of more accurate galaxy formation theories that take into account the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters and superclusters. We also discuss ongoing research into the relationship between galaxies and the large-scale structure of the universe, including: (a) the discovery of massive (M > 10^14 Msun) galaxy groups and clusters; (b) the distribution of galaxies along cosmic filaments; (c) the influence of the large-scale universe on galaxy formation and evolution; and (d) the potential for the large-scale universe to be used as a reference frame for understanding galaxy evolution. The Latent Graphical Lasso (LGL) is a probabilistic extension of the Graphical Lasso (GL) framework, combining sparse regression models with latent variable statistical models. We re-examine the likelihood function used in GL from a latent variable perspective, revealing that incorporating latent variables results in an expanded parameter space, ultimately yielding a more robust and flexible model. Notably, LGL subsumes GL as a special case, underscoring the efficacy of the latent variable approach in tackling challenges like unidentifiability and sparse structure recovery. Leveraging a hierarchical model formulation, we propose a novel Bayesian inference algorithm based on no-arbitrage lattice constructions, demonstrating superior performance in various sparse graphical model scenarios, particularly those with unobserved variables and multiple linked sub-networks. Our numerical studies are substantiated by numerical illustrations, which highlight the advantages of LGL over traditional GL approaches. The code is openly accessible on the repository: https://github.com/stephanselander/LatentGraphicalLasso. Sebastian is open to collaborations: stephanselander@gmail.com. Journal version available at: arXiv v2, submitted for publication at the Journal of Machine Learning Research. Initial version posted at: arXiv v1, with significant enhancements. Our LGL implementation is compatible with the scikit-learn package, specifically scikit-learn version 1.1.0 and later. We aim to integrate it into the main scikit-learn repository in the future. Our LGL model can be summarized as follows: Given a set of n variables and their associated observed multivariate normal distributions, with mean vectors denoted as mu and covariance matrix Sigma, our model postulates the existence of latent variables, denoted as Q, to facilitate the separation of sparse graphical structures. Under this setup, the model expands the original GL parameter space to accommodate the generative variance, Gamma, and noise variance, Sigma-11, resulting in our likelihood function used in Bayesian inference. Notably, the model's posterior distribution is shown to be a non-standard conjugate, leading to the development of our Bayesian inference algorithm. Our numerical studies confirm the efficacy of our LGL approach in various sparse graphical model scenarios, with notable performance improvements over traditional GL methods. Most notably, our results demonstrate the LGL's capacity to recover more comprehensive graphical structures, ultimately yielding more accurate and robust estimations. We developed a method for accurately extracting pitch markers from speech signals contaminated with varying levels of background noise. A neural network was designed to identify pitch markers by analyzing narrow frequency ranges within a speech signal segmented into frames. Each frame was examined for the presence of a pitch marker at its sample index predicted by the network. Results from our analysis indicate that a pitch tracking algorithm based on a simple extraction strategy outperforms more complex approaches in identifying pitch markers for noisy speech signals. The proposed algorithm demonstrates robustness in identifying pitch markers for clean and distorted speech files across multiple speech corpora, including the TIMIT and NFI Speech Dataset. Notably, it successfully identifies pitch markers for noisy speech files with Signal-to-Noise Ratios as low as -10 dB. The DWIFOB algorithm, an iterative refinement technique, boosts convergence of the Anderson acceleration method by adding equations in a systematic manner. This has been found to robustly improve convergence in nearly all cases, but may encounter difficulties with singularities in certain situations. A modified version of the DWIFOB algorithm, referred to as DWIFOB+, aims to resolve convergence issues and potential singularities by truncating Anderson iterations. Experimental results indicate that DWIFOB+ offers improved convergence for problems with sparse Jacobian matrices, and its performance can be further enhanced through an additional preconditioning step. Additionally, a theoretical analysis confirming the asymptotic convergence of DWIFOB+ has been provided. Compared to the regularized Anderson acceleration method, DWIFOB+ exhibits higher convergence rates, both theoretically and experimentally. Furthermore, a strategy for automatically selecting DWIFOB+ parameters is suggested. This approach works well in most cases, but may require manual adjustment in exceptional cases, and is accompanied by a parameter selection rule as reference. The modified DWIFOB+ algorithm, DWIFOB++, aims to address potential issues with restarting and matrix factorization during the initial Anderson acceleration layers. This version of the algorithm aims to improve the robustness of DWIFOB+ by bypassing certain problematic paths, and effectively enhancing its robustness. Moreover, DWIFOB++ includes an additional mechanism to enhance robustness, by implementing a criterion for controlling the degree of subcoercivity in the algorithm. This version of the algorithm effectively enhances the robustness of DWIFOB+, and is shown to be theoretically and experimentally superior to the regularized Anderson acceleration method. Moreover, DWIFOB++ is effectively robust against singularities in the Hessian and Jacobian matrices, and is experimentally shown to be an effective solution for a range of problems including linear systems, nonlinear least-squares problems, and optimization applications.
In conclusion, this research provides an advanced version of the DWIFOB algorithm, referred to as DWIFOB++, which effectively enhances the robustness and convergence of the algorithm. Moreover, this version of the algorithm effectively enhances the convergence and robustness of the regularized Anderson acceleration method, and is shown to be an effective solution for a range of problems, and potentially a robust basis for developing more advanced algorithms in the future. Moreover, this research effectively compares the performance of DWIFOB++ to a range of state-of-the-art algorithms, including Regularized Anderson Acceleration, Block GMRES, TOW, Proximal Anderson Acceleration, and Generalized Anderson

Within the framework of the non-minimal supersymmetric model with three singlet neutrinos, we investigated the relationship between the Higgs boson mass and the masses of supersymmetric particles, taking into account their uncertainties. By utilizing the constraints set by the Higgs boson coupling measurements and the 125 GeV Higgs boson mass, we found that the mass of the heavy neutrino can be approximately 10 keV, which is at the edge of detectability for current neutrino experiments. Furthermore, we found that including the extended neutrino sector leads to more than a ten-fold reduction in the mass range of the lightest neutralino in the parameter space that agrees well with Higgs boson coupling measurements. This reduction in mass makes it more feasible for the lightest neutralino to be produced in sufficient quantities for direct detection experiments to detect it. With future high-luminosity experiments such as LHC, ILC, CLIC, HL-LHC, and future pp collider projects, as well as the next generation of dark matter detectors, we found that it will be possible to reach sensitivities comparable to those of neutrino experiments for the mass of the heavy neutrino. Finally, in the near future, we found that it will be possible to reach a sensitivity of approximately 10^-10 pb for the production cross-section of the heavy neutrino through measurements at the LHC, which is a three-order magnitude improvement from current sensitivities. This future sensitivity will make it possible to measure the production cross-section of the heavy neutrino with confidence-levels higher than 5%. Furthermore, we found that it will be possible to measure the ratio of branching fractions of the heavy neutrino's decays, approximately 10^-5, with confidence levels higher than 10%, although its decay width remains relatively large due to its long-lived nature. This future sensitivity will make it possible to measure the decay width of the heavy neutrino's decays, approximately 10^-8 keV, with confidence levels higher than 10%. Consequently, we found that it will be possible to test the extended neutrino sector of the non-minimal supersymmetric model with confidence levels higher than 5% through measurements at the LHC and future dark matter experiments. This future sensitivity will make it possible to test a significant portion of the parameter space that includes the relationship between the Higgs boson mass and the masses of supersymmetric particles, even after incorporating the constraints set by the Higgs boson coupling measurements and the 125 GeV Higgs boson

In the space of neural architecture search (NAS), researchers aim to automatically identify highly effective network structures. The development of a comprehensive and detailed dataset describing functions of various network architectures has enabled researchers to explore how different architectural features influence performance. A recent study discovered a significant correlation between the program properties of neural architectures and their performance. Building upon this discovery, this research attempts to broaden the application of program properties by addressing two inherent flaws in previous approaches. Firstly, existing program property-based methods require a prior assumption about the search space, restricting the potential architectures to those predefined in the search space. Secondly, these methods only utilize node-level operations, disregarding other crucial network structures, such as how different nodes interact with each other. To address these limitations, this research proposes a more general approach that can easily extend the program properties to capture higher-level network structures, such as edges, and multiple node types operating in parallel. Furthermore, this research removes the limitation of assuming a prior search space and allows the program properties to be learned from a mixed graph, consisting of various types of edges, including those that represent node-level and edge-level operations. To evaluate the extended program properties, this research uses a reinforcement learning-based regression technique that can utilize program properties for making accurate predictions about network performance. The experimental findings confirm that the proposed approach outperforms previous methods, demonstrating superior accuracy and scalability. Moreover, this research successfully applies program properties to a wide range of tasks, including both low- and high-resource settings, highlighting its practical value. The significant contributions of this research include enabling the program properties to be learned independently from the search space and effectively utilizing program properties for neural architecture search, especially in scenarios involving multiple resource constraints. Moreover, this research successfully demonstrates the general applicability of program properties in various graph-based architecture search scenarios. To facilitate the replication of this research, the proposed method along with the associated dataset, can be accessed at https://github.com/asharakeh/Extended-Program-Properties-for-NAS.ashar@i2s.uni-stuttgart.de, https://www.uni-stuttgart.de/en/index.html Universitaet Stuttgart. 2022. In mmWave multicasting with $K$ antennas at the transmitter and $N$ antennas at the receiver, we investigate the worst-case achievable rate region under a power constraint using vector quantization. It is shown that even with a limited number of quantization bits, significant improvements in system performance can be achieved, especially with multiple antennas at the receiver. We also examine various coding techniques such as vector Gaussian elimination, vector BMEF, and lattice BMEF and find that these can be implemented with vector quantization. However, our results indicate that vector Gaussian elimination does not yield a achievable region, whereas vector BMEF and lattice BMEF are subspecial cases of vector quantization. Moreover, we show that vector quantization is a universal and efficient tool for resolving convex optimization problems in multicasting. Federated learning's scalability remains a significant challenge, particularly when it comes to communication efficiency. Two key techniques, Federated Averaging and Federated Distillation, suffer from limitations in this regard, leading to excessive communication needs proportional to the model size and local training duration, respectively. To address this issue, we propose Compressed Federated Distillation, a novel approach that leverages knowledge distillation and data compression to simultaneously reduce communication requirements in terms of bandwidth and bits. Experimental results demonstrate that Compressed Federated Distillation surpasses the communication efficiency of Federated Distillation and equals it in terms of convergence, while outperforming Federated Averaging in terms of both communication efficiency and convergence. Moreover, Compressed Federated Distillation offers advantages over state-of-the-art compression techniques such as sparse compression and knowledge pruning. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/asharkhwan/Compressed-Federated-Distillation.

In complex networks, the increasing demand for diverse services is outpacing available resources, leading to difficulties in achieving optimal results through conventional traffic and flow control methods. To address this challenge, the SDADO method focuses on combining service discovery and dynamic orchestration of network resources. SDADO relies on a planning approach that utilizes predictive information about network traffic to determine the optimal distribution of network resources over time. This is achieved through a coordinated strategy that prioritizes the orchestration of network resources according to the nature of the services and predicts the requirements of the flows within those services. The integration of a real-time resource allocation plan at the flow level ensures efficient use of network resources and facilitates the delivery of services with desired quality of service. This approach limits the need for manual intervention in service delivery, reduces the likelihood of network congestion, and thus improves the overall performance of the services in terms of delay and throughput. Furthermore, the method includes mechanisms to adapt to changes in the network by incorporating a resource recalibration process and using historical information to refine the resource allocation plan. Recent advancements in the stabilization of complex networks, such as software-defined networks and network function virtualization, create an ideal environment for the implementation of the SDADO method. To verify the effectiveness of SDADO, the method has been tested on a benchmark network scenario and compared with alternative strategies, including a fully distributed and adaptive method. The results show that SDADO outperforms the alternative strategies in terms of the reliability of service delivery, the efficiency of resource utilization, and the adaptability to changes in the network. The methodology of SDADO can be extended to other complex network scenarios in the future. Furthermore, the potential for the method to be applied in other technical domains should also be explored. We focus on a nonlinear beam model defined on a connected set of one-dimensional spaces that are joined at multiple points, forming an interconnected network called an $N$-star metric graph. When an appropriate coordinate transformation is applied to this network, we simplify the nonlinear system using a unified set of coordinates, revealing its representation as a first-order nonlinear system in a block structure. This is contrasted with the corresponding linear system, which displays exponential stability under specific conditions and ultimately reduces to a stable constant equilibrium in a nonlinear setting. Through this approach, we establish criteria for the exponential stability of the nonlinear system, which in certain situations ensures only linearized stability. Moreover, when a certain condition is met (all edges having a non-uniform curvature), we achieve exponential stability of the entire system, whereas outside this condition, we establish stability results on a scale that is dependent on the distance from the center of the star. Finally, our method also allows for the derivation of similar stability results for other nonlinear beam models under various boundary conditions. It's worth noting that the choice of the star metric graph's structure plays a pivotal role in achieving exponential stability, as it offers a wealth of suitable configurations. Conversely, in the case of a linear system, our selected non-uniform curvature condition on the edges leads to stability results that are applicable to the entire graph, as well as a variety of other linear systems under alternative boundary conditions. Additionally, our model's formulation may be modified to account for the presence of external forces and point forces, as well as other nonlinear beam models under various boundary conditions. Some of these models exhibit unique behavior and require novel approaches for analyzing their stability. Our study provides a comprehensive insight into these models and contributes to the broader field of geometric and nonlinear feedback control. It's also worth noting that our method allows for the extension of our stability results to other nonlinear systems of beams that exhibit star-shaped configurations, as well as to other types of boundary value problems. Furthermore, our model can be applied to various types of connected networks beyond the $N$-star metric graph, such as circular graphs and extended star graphs. Our study offers a comprehensive exploration of these models and contributes to the broader field of nonlinear and feedback control. It's also worth noting that our method allows for the derivation of stability results for other types of boundary value problems and the extension of our stability results to other types of connected networks beyond the $N$-star metric graph. Our study provides a comprehensive insight into these models and contributes to the broader field of nonlinear and feedback control.

Utilitarian learning aims to develop an optimal utility function based on expert guidance, either by defining a utility function offline using expert knowledge or by pairing preferences provided by experts. We examine the scenario where the experts' preferences are expressed as continuous functions, unlike the limited pairwise result comparisons typical of Kelley's method. The offline approach can be solved in O(n polylog n) time, where n represents the number of data points. Notably, utilitarian learning offline can be seen as an instance of the utility maximization problem in stochastic nonconvex optimization, with the utility function serving as the objective function. Furthermore, we demonstrate that learning utilitarian functions both online and offline is feasible only when the utility function is uniquely defined; otherwise, multiple equivalently optimal functions emerge. To facilitate offline learning, we suggest an algorithm incorporating pairwise result comparisons that efficiently learns a utilitarian function in O(n polylog n) time under specific conditions. Additionally, the utilitarian learning framework can be extended to various optimization challenges by incorporating a constraint on the utility function. The consequence of this extension is a dichotomy result describing the limits of learning any optimization function defined by experts. To validate the theoretical findings, we conduct a series of experiments across real-world scenarios, comparing the efficacy of our proposed algorithm with Kelley's method. Our analysis suggests that the offline utilitarian learning algorithm frequently outperforms Kelley's method, with comparable results in certain situations. The experiments were performed using synthetic data as well as real-world datasets comprising learning candidates' attributes and performance metrics. The findings indicate that the offline utilitarian learning algorithm successfully defines a useful utility function in most cases, with the resulting rankings closely mirroring those obtained by the experts. The utility function learned through our approach is also applicable to other optimization challenges by incorporating a constraint on the utility function; this resulted in candidate attribute evaluations aligned with the experts' preferences in both our controlled study and practical evaluations. The developed code is accessible via the repository https://github.com/krishannair/utilitarian-learning. Kelley's method is implemented in the file kelley.py, while offline utilitarian learning algorithms can be found in the file utilitarian_offline.py. The experiments comprising real-world data are detailed in the file kelley_utilitarian_experiments.py. The repository includes a README file outlining the necessary dependencies and how to run the experiments. Recurrent future prediction is an intriguing problem that involves using the past behavior of trained reinforcement learning agents to anticipate their future actions. To address this, we explore the application of sequence-to-sequence models, specifically those employing transfer learning, in this context. Our research centers on two key aspects: utilizing a pre-trained language model as a predictor and leveraging a pre-trained transformer model as both a predictor and a predictor-trainer. We test our approach on a variety of classic domains, including CartPole, MountainCar, and Acrobot. Interestingly, our findings indicate that using a pre-trained model results in performance superior to that of a simple Markov process, and in some cases, transfer exerts a positive influence on prediction accuracy. Moreover, using a pre-trained transformer as both a predictor and a predictor-trainer yields predictive outcomes that surpass those achieved through reinforcement learning, highlighting the potential for a pre-trained model to serve as a semi-sufficient agent. These results hint at the promise of pre-trained models contributing to the development of more efficient and successful reinforcement learning agents. We examine a two-dimensional herringbone lattice, derived from the Hubbard model on a 4-fold rotated square lattice, displaying complex structure and multi-directional symmetry. Our analysis reveals that this lattice exhibits metallic and insulating states determined by a single continuous phase transition, influenced by an orbital order that mixes with magnetic ordering. A key characteristic is that the lattice's properties can be adapted by modifying the Hamiltonian, effectively mimicking the effects of external stresses on the lattice structure. Additionally, we explore the impact of rotating the lattice by other angles, which yields different types of lattices and potentially hosts other topological phases. Our findings suggest the possibility of manipulating a system's symmetry to induce a preferred symmetry breaking in the ground state, and also the importance of considering lattice structure in the study of electronic properties. Furthermore, we discuss the feasibility of experimenting on these systems using ultra-thin layered materials and highlight the necessity of accounting for lattice structure in the interpretation of experimental results. Our work also clarifies the origin of recently observed unconventional superconductivity in certain iron-based materials, suggesting the presence of a pseudospin-dependent pairing mechanism. Our research combines reinforcement learning with the concept of restarts, adapting existing algorithms used in expectation maximization and online convex analysis.  We developed a framework that allows risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in changing scenarios using anytime algorithms with near-optimal policies within a predetermined time frame. In modern distributed machine learning, communication overhead poses a significant challenge. One approach to minimize communications is to divide the data into groups and process them independently, with the outputs combined using an aggregation function. Traditional aggregation methods rely on linear functions, such as taking the average, but we explore more general weightings. Our contribution is two-fold: first, we develop a novel weighted power-p mean (WPM) aggregation function; second, we optimize its parameters to minimize total communication cost. The WPM function outperforms linear aggregation methods, particularly when data is unevenly distributed across nodes. Additionally, the optimal parameters depend on the specific communication scheme used; we derive closed-form expressions for uniform group sizes, as well as for general sizes subject to a scalar scaling condition. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of the WPM method, especially when data distributions follow a Pareto pattern; for instance, it yields a 37.5% reduction in communications when dealing with such a distribution. To minimize bias when data distributions vary across nodes, we also propose a weighted power-p mean with equal weights (WPE). Our comprehensive empirical evaluation, spanning three datasets and four communication schemes, highlights the versatility of the WPM method: either variant may offer improved communications efficiency over traditional linear aggregation methods, with the choice depending on the specific considerations. The integration of atomic elements into the circuit design is a fundamental requirement for the development of complex quantum devices, including quantum networks and computers utilizing single atoms. However, achieving high performance requires an efficient spatial mode conversion to align atomic resonators with laser beam profiles. In our research, a novel device was designed to convert the mode of an incident laser beam from a Gaussian profile to a top-hat shape within a narrow spectral range, and this mode conversion was successfully achieved using a single-tuned-cavity technique, producing an average transmission enhancement of 250 across the full bandwidth. Additionally, a second atomic resonator could be seamlessly integrated into the system to enhance the system's transmission by an additional factor of 40, demonstrating the potential of this device in atomic-photonic integrated circuits. This design offers a simple, compact solution to a long-standing problem in integrated atomic physics and has significant implications for the development of scalable quantum devices. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis of both classical and quantum noise in this system was also conducted, highlighting its potential as a building block for quantum networks and devices utilizing single atoms. This work is further expanded into a technical tutorial, providing a detailed explanation of integrated atomic physics and its applications in integrated quantum optics.

We identify the closed upper sets of words in a valuated oriented graph as the fundamental objects of a lattice structure, enabled by the introduction of two partial orders - the zigzag order and the natural partial order. It's demonstrated that this lattice is finite if and only if the corresponding valuated oriented graph is finite. A method to compute the zeta function of a valuated oriented graph is also proposed, based on the concept of fundamental series, by examining the components of the lattice structure formed by the closed upper sets of words. Furthermore, it's proven that the graph's valuated orientation is isomorphic to a sublattice of the graph's critical monomial valuated oriented graph, and a method to compute the zeta function of the critical monomial valuated oriented graph is developed, along with the zeta function of the graph's barycentric subgraph. Two specific examples are provided to illustrate the application of these methods in determining the zeta functions of valuated oriented graphs. Additionally, an examination is conducted on the properties of valuated oriented graphs that are equivalent to posets, regarding their arithmetic properties and the relationship between their corresponding root systems. Finally, two computational software programs - VAZOGraph and Val OrientedGraph - are introduced, capable of generating and analyzing valuated oriented graphs. VAZOGraph allows for the manual creation of valuated oriented graphs, while Val OrientedGraph supports the creation of valuated oriented graphs based on random generation. Both programs feature interactive graphical interfaces for visualizing graphs and generating corresponding zeta functions. Our innovative approach represents a polymer as a connected sequence of monomers using a generalized version of the AUTODEN networks introduced in Armano et al. (2020). This expanded framework accommodates multiple types of monomers and allows for the addition of monomer-to-monomer interactions. We demonstrate the application of our method in two simulations: one involving a single-type polymer with intrachain interactions and another with multiple types of polymers interacting with each other. The monomer sequence is inferred from a physical observation, such as a fluorescence signal, and the reconstruction of the polymer chain requires an efficient algorithm to generate the most likely conformation given the observed fluorescence emission spectrum. We utilize a two-step approach, alternating between optimizing the monomer sequence and the 3D polymer chain to minimize a cost function that promotes both high fluorescence intensity and the structural correlation between the inferred monomer sequence and the polymer's spatial arrangement. Notably, our method is capable of recovering the underlying structure of the polymer even from highly degraded fluorescence data. Additionally, we have implemented a more sophisticated version of our algorithm that incorporates a variational approach, allowing us to handle cases where there are multiple polymer chains and projecting them onto a low-dimensional space to facilitate reconstruction. Our experiments with the variational auto-encoder for polymer reconstruction, combined with the efficient algorithm for generating the most likely monomer sequence, demonstrate the ability to accurately infer the monomer sequence even when fluorescence data is highly noisy. Furthermore, we have applied our variational approach to infer the monomer sequence of a protein from a single fluorescence signal, successfully recovering the structural information of the protein, specifically the spatial arrangement of the amino acids in the protein chain. Our experiments also explore the protein reconstruction problem in which we aim to reconstruct multiple protein structures from fluorescence signals, our results show that we can accurately infer the monomer sequence even when the fluorescence data is highly noisy. Our approach represents a fundamental step towards a new class of microscopy that can resolve the structure of long polymers such as proteins at molecular detail from fluorescence measurements that capture the emission spectrum along the length of a polymer chain as it moves through a fluorescence microscope. Our experimental results are based on the assumption that a polymer chain moves at a velocity of $1 \mu m/s$, and a fluorescence detector can resolve emission spectra at a spatial resolution of $300 nm$. The purpose of this study is to provide clear and concise explanations for hadronic property predictions made by the LHCb experiment. Initially, we review the basic principles of quantum chromodynamics used to study light mesons. Next, we discuss the methods used to analyze the masses and axial form factors of light mesons. Additionally, we explore the hadronic decays of the light vector and pseudoscalar mesons. The primary focus of this study lies in the $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing analysis, with an emphasis on its potential to enhance our comprehension of the light meson sector. Lastly, we highlight ongoing and future initiatives at accelerator facilities that will continue to shed light on the intricacies of the light meson sector. The LHCb experiment plays a pivotal role in these endeavors, with its exceptional capabilities enabling the detailed exploration of hadronic physics. The experiment's unique features include its ability to operate at the LHC's peak energy, allowing for the detection of $B$-meson decays that are sensitive to the hadronic form factors. Moreover, the experiment's capacity to study $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mesons over a broad kinematic range facilitates precise determinations of the $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing angle and the branching fractions of the hadronic decays. As a result, the experiment has contributed substantially to our present understanding of the light meson sector. Future analyses are anticipated to yield equally impressive outcomes. The potential for further breakthroughs in hadronic physics will continue to be a driving force behind the ongoing and future research at the LHCb experiment. The experiment's ongoing program of measurements in the $\eta$-$\eta'$ channel is also reviewed, with a particular emphasis on its analytical approach. The discussion then shifts to the pseudoscalar decay modes, including the challenging $\eta'/0$ separation problem, before moving on to a comprehensive examination of the vector decay modes. The presentation concludes with the results of the $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing analysis, an essential aspect of the light meson sector. The various approaches employed in the analysis are presented, including the effect of the mixing angle on the mass splitting and the decay branching fractions. The different treatment of the mixing angle in the axially covariant Radyushkin and Borisyov-Kamalov-Musatov form factors is particularly noteworthy. In various applications such as biometrics and digital forensics, the use of handwritten signatures is increasingly popular. Since the authenticity of signed documents can be challenged, detecting forgeries becomes essential. Research has explored the potential of leveraging neural networks for signature forgery detection. This study contributes to this effort by presenting a comprehensive comparison of various network architectures, viewed as discrete-time dynamic systems. By analyzing the effects of parameters such as distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability of the used biometric templates, this study provides insights aimed at improving the performance of such detection systems, offering a framework that can be applied to other machine learning-based approaches as well. The findings of this research are based on an extensive simulation of the Euclidean signature framework, covering a wide range of its parameters. Besides presenting general findings applicable to any Euclidean signature framework, this study also includes specific results for the used signature template, known as the Kahan p-adic field. Moreover, this research proposes two novel network architectures for detecting forgeries in both genuine and imitation signatures, demonstrating the capabilities of the employed biometric template. Additionally, this research explores the potential of utilizing the learned representations of the network inputs to identify and discard the imposter attacks, exemplified in the case of the Kahan p-adic field. Overall, the proposed approach has shown promising performance on the tested dataset of 2200 signature samples. We examine how supersymmetry conditions influence low-energy effective interactions in open bosonic string theory. Our investigation focuses on a specific sector involving the string-level three-string vertex and two gluon fields as the primary output variables. The relationship between supersymmetry constraints on the three-string vertex and low-energy effective couplings is emphasized. Our analysis demonstrates that supersymmetry constraints on the vertex's three-point functions directly impact the low-energy effective couplings. The low-energy limit of the effective couplings is determined, revealing that it depends on the vertex's two-point functions, which are determined by supersymmetry constraints, along with the anomalous dimension of the gluon operator. The low-energy limit of the effective couplings is found to be independent of the interstring distance. Moreover, our results show that the effective couplings naturally incorporate the information from the string-level vertex, including its dependence on the string's alpha ratio. The potential impact of tachyons on the effective couplings is also explored. Our findings indicate that the effective couplings are sensitive to the tachyonic potential but only consider its overall shape, rather than detailed variations, when calculating low-energy limits. energies. The data are compared to Rybar-Chen and LUCIAN models, showcasing better
agreement with the Rybar-Chen model. Additionally, the data are examined in terms of
photon and jet rapidity and transverse momentum variations. Furthermore, the
photon-energy dependence observed in the Pb+Pb collisions does not occur in
proton-proton collisions collected at the same time. Finally, the data are
examined for dependence on the interaction multiplicity in both Pb+Pb and proton-proton
collisions. This research explores possible origins of this observation, including
digitalization and event selection loss, and assesses their impact. Ultimately, the
resulting modifications remain when suppressing the influence of these effects. It is
suggested that the source of this phenomenon could be an interaction between the
photon and the medium quarks produced in the collision, as well as quark radiation
effect influenced by the medium properties. This research represents the first data-
driven analysis of this phenomenon, setting the stage for future studies with a
considerably larger data set anticipated from the upcoming Run 3 data collection.

Our key contributions are four-fold: firstly, we introduce the GP-CF to tackle the pose estimation problem, highlighting its advantage over traditional methods that rely on assumed independent noise. Secondly, we develop a non-convex optimization algorithm utilizing the adjoint method to efficiently solve the related problem. Thirdly, we establish a relationship between the adjoint method and the gradient descent algorithm. Fourthly, our results demonstrate the efficacy of the GP-CF in pose estimation, with improvements noticeable especially when dealing with increased levels of correlation. Our approach provides a valuable general-purpose tool for addressing uncertainty in sensor readings, with potential applications extending beyond pose estimation to various computer vision tasks. We propose exploring the possibility of a multi-temperature universe, where the matter temperatures of dark matter, baryons, and photons are distinct. This hypothesis introduces an additional degree of freedom, enabling us to refine the limits set by big bang nucleosynthesis on the interaction between dark matter and baryons. Such a hypothesis could be justified by preheating mechanisms following inflation or by the interaction between dark matter and baryons themselves. In this study, we establish the constraints on dark matter properties by considering the interaction between dark matter and baryons across various mass and temperature ranges, from the Big Bang nucleosynthesis down to galaxy scales, where the matter temperatures are determined by the kinetic interactions, ultimately leading to more stringent bounds on the interaction than previously thought. Our findings apply to both collisional and collisionless dark matter. In the case of sub-GeV dark matter, our analysis can be represented by a set of "memory curves" that summarize the constraints on its properties, complementing existing limits from direct detection and dwarf galaxy experiments. Furthermore, our research suggests that even if dark matter is not directly detectable, its properties can still be closely constrained. Lastly, we speculate on potential future directions, including a hypothetical multi-temperature universe where the dark matter temperature is higher than the baryons' temperature, which might be linked to the phenomenon of $g-2$ anomalies. In such a scenario, even a relatively small interaction between dark matter and baryons could resolve the $g-2$ discrepancy, while also influencing the dark matter abundance and cross sections measured in dwarf galaxy experiments. Therefore, a multi-temperature universe could be a crucial aspect of dark matter, with far-reaching implications for its properties and behavior.

The shift to collaborative software development has led to the creation of shared files, typically stored in multiple repository folders. Despite their importance, these files often go understudied. This research aims to bridge this knowledge gap by exploring maintenance practices related to shared files across software development repositories. To this end, we conducted a comprehensive study involving four distinct research questions focused on file sharing, file management, and their underlying drivers. Our analysis of over 12 million files across 832 GitHub repositories revealed that only 5% of these files are shared across multiple repositories. Furthermore, our results indicate that files belonging to large repositories are less likely to be shared, whereas small repositories tend to exchange files more frequently. Additionally, our data show that files related to programming languages, such as C and C++, are less often shared, whereas files associated with languages like Python and Java are more likely to be shared. Our investigation into the impact of file sharing on software maintenance found that modifying files in one repository often affects other repositories that share the same file. In contrast, our study shows that file merges do not significantly depend on file sharing. Based on our findings, we recommend implementing automatic detection of shared files and associated commit patterns, allowing developers to identify potential file management issues and streamline collaborative file maintenance. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex file dynamics involved in collaborative software development and can inform the development of next-generation collaborative editing tools. By recognizing the importance of file metadata, such as file paths and modification dates, our work can inspire the creation of more effective collaborative editing tools, facilitating better collaboration among software developers. In conclusion, our research highlights the necessity of improved file management to enhance collaborative software development, particularly in the context of growing open-source repositories where file sharing plays a significant role. In the future, we anticipate that our research will influence the next generation of collaborative editing tools, addressing the inherent file management challenges associated with collaborative software development. We develop an obstruction theory for symplectic sheaves relative to a symplectic structure on a projective variety. The theory involves the formation of a sequence of spaces derived from the hypercohomology of the symplectic sheaf, where each space represents the set of isomorphism classes of symplectic sheaves that are locally free of a specified rank and degree on a particular open subset of the variety. The obstruction theory is completed by the construction of a perfect symplectic sheaf, which serves as a local model for symplectic sheaves. Additionally, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of symplectic sheaves that are locally free of a specified rank and degree on a projective variety, provided that the positivity assumptions of the direct image sheaf for the given map to a curve are satisfied. As an application of this obstruction theory, we prove the uniqueness of the Grothendieck-Hodge symplectic sheaves of highest degree on a projective bundle of rank one, under specified conditions. Furthermore, we construct perfect symplectic sheaves of rank two on a projective bundle of rank two, for certain choices of the canonical sheaf and the anti-dualizing sheaf. Finally, we establish the existence and uniqueness of Grothendieck-Hodge symplectic sheaves of highest degree on a projective bundle of rank two, for certain choices of the anti-dualizing sheaf, under specified conditions. A weighted least squares (WLS) regression is applied to the universal approximation problem, allowing for weighted regression with non-uniform data. We demonstrate that with an appropriate weight function and signed weights for each sample, our method achieves stable and optimal results when working with exact dataset examples. Furthermore, our approach is based on a general framework that can be extended to address challenges associated with noisy data, bounded data, and issues of dimensionality growth, and can be applied to a range of continuous and discrete function approximation tasks. Additionally, our method is illustrated in various experiments involving continuous and discrete domains, such as approximating a function and controlling a pendulum's dynamics. This research is a continuation of previous work by Alan S. Willsky and Y. R. Chen in 1979. The code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/UVASSL/LSSubgradient/tree/main/LSSubgradient.

This paper explores a novel approach to combined motion planning and control for a car-like vehicle navigating in a real-world environment. We propose a practical solution to the'simultaneous localization and mapping' problem using a pre-trained map builder, allowing our vehicle to function effectively in unfamiliar environments without the need for extensive training. The motion planning stage is redefined as a sequential task separated into a reach goal motion planning, reach transition, and transition to drive phase, leveraging a pre-built scene graph. This approach diverges from traditional methods using joint action decoding, thus facilitating easier substitution of tasks and/or controllers in the 'decision-making' stage. A novel multi-phase reinforcement learning framework is introduced, with each phase trained independently to accelerate the training process. Theoretical studies suggest that the feeding of matter into the central void by the gas disk, driven by the motion of stars and gas, plays a crucial role in this process. We have conducted extensive simulations to explore various modes of accretion driven by the interaction between the central black hole and the surrounding gas disk, actively engaging in the growth of central black holes over a period of time equivalent to a single galaxy formation cycle. The results show that the flow of gas into the central void driven by the rotation of the disk contributes significantly to the mass of the central black holes, with a flow rate that is two to three times greater than previously estimated and sufficient to explain the observed relationship between the mass of the central void and the mass of the surrounding stars, as well as the variability in the mass of the central void at a given mass. Deep neural networks are increasingly being used due to their effectiveness in a wide range of classification tasks. However, the traditional supervised learning approach often leads to overly confident, yet incorrect predictions when input data is outside the scope of the training dataset. In contrast, ensemble methods combining multiple models can provide better out-of-distribution detection capabilities. Building on this insight, we integrate two techniques: 1) uncertainty quantification via the Monte Carlo dropout method and 2) a majority vote from multiple models. Our proposed framework consists of three components: a classification deep learning model, a uncertainty quantification function, and an anomaly detection module. The latter employs a score calculated by the uncertainty quantification function, which is then normalized through a Gaussian distribution fitted with in-distribution data. A threshold is set based on a score-normalized score range defined by the standard deviation of in-distribution data scores. Our method is validated on three challenging wild-image classification tasks, showcasing improved accuracy and robustness when comparing it to traditional approaches. Notably, our method enhances the clean-a-10 strategy, which involves retraining a model on data from a different source, and yields a 15% gain in accuracy in three of our four evaluation scenarios. Furthermore, our method surpasses the clean-a-10 method in four of five evaluation scenarios, and yields a 15% gain in accuracy in two of these scenarios. In addition to these findings, we analyze the effect of the model's architecture, size, and complexity on the proposed framework's performance. Our research underscores the importance of incorporating both uncertainty quantification and multi-model ensemble methods in deep learning-based classification techniques. In addition, our results suggest that these approaches can be effectively applied to a wide range of computer vision tasks, particularly those involving out-of-distribution prediction. In a broader context, our research highlights the potential of combining ensemble methods with uncertainty quantification to improve the robustness and performance of deep learning models. In addition, our results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed framework in a practical classification scenario, and underscores the importance of accurate uncertainty assessment for a deep learning-based classification method. In a related context, our research may be of interest to researchers working on the design of ensemble methods, uncertainty quantification techniques, and deep learning-based classification methods. To understand the dissemination of preprints and their relationship to citation rates, we examined mathematics and computer science research articles. Our analysis reveals that papers accompanied by preprints receive significantly more citations, with faster citation timelines. While preprints apparently accelerate publication, they actually seem to facilitate earlier distribution of high-quality research, paving the way for a potential shift towards a post-publication peer review system. We also identified patterns indicating that authors sharing preliminary research findings may gain benefits despite potentially risking reputational risks. Our study primarily focuses on mathematics and computer sciences, but the underlying methods can be applied to other fields as well. Further investigations are needed to explore the broader implications of preprints for scientific research. Our findings and methods are available for review at arxiv.org/abs/2101.10748. The primary objective of laboratory information systems is to efficiently capture, organize, and report the outcomes of laboratory tests and procedures. Despite the potential for significant improvements, many laboratories still rely on outdated, human-driven data management systems due to a lack of awareness about available solutions. Modern technologies offer automated data processing tools that not only enhance productivity but also minimize errors associated with manual documentation. This article presents an innovative approach to enhancing laboratory data management using automated information extraction and processing methods, illustrated through the case study of a laboratory testing for glucose levels. The proposed system comprises four core components: a device connector module, an automated data analyzer, a database manager, and a report generator. By implementing automated laboratory information systems, laboratories can streamline their workflows, improve data quality, and make informed medical predictions more efficiently. This article discusses these concepts in the context of the Internet of Things (IoT) to highlight the benefits of integrated healthcare technologies. Ultimately, such systems have the potential to elevate patient care and predict future health risks through data analysis and reporting. Graph neural networks (GNN) have recently gained popularity due to their effectiveness in a variety of tasks. Unlike traditional neural networks, they have the capability to learn within dimensional spaces, making them well-suited for a wide range of applications, including unsupervised data learning, representation, and space learning. This paper focuses on the latter, with a specific focus on subspace learning, and introduces a new approach called ProSE, which employs graph neural networks to discover meaningful subspaces within a data set. The ProSE framework consists of three key components: an graph neural network that creates a data representation, a subspace generator, and a selector that identifies the subspaces with the most valuable information. This framework is versatile and can be adapted to various tasks using different graph neural networks, such as Graph Convolutional Network (GCN), Graph Attention Network (GAT), and Simple Neural Network (SNN), among others. Experimental results on synthetic data sets and real-world datasets indicate that ProSE consistently identifies high-quality subspaces that accurately characterize data variations, outperforming several baseline methods in various tasks. Additionally, the paper highlights the potential of ProSE in semantic subspace learning for image understanding, demonstrating its effectiveness in discovering latent subspaces that reflect semantic characteristics in the Caltech256 dataset. The source code for ProSE can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/yangyong1001/ProSE. In conclusion, the study suggests that graph neural networks offer promising solutions for a range of challenging problems in computer vision, particularly in unsupervised learning tasks. The potential applications of GNNs in computer vision are vast, making them an exciting area of exploration, and the study aims to encourage further research in this domain. Ultimately, the goal of this study is to encourage the integration of graph neural networks in computer vision, and the prospect of accurately extracting meaningful subspaces from large datasets holds significant potential for many applications in this field. As computer vision continues to evolve, we can expect GNNs to play an increasingly important role, and the study of hybrid deep learning models will remain an important and rewarding area of study in the future. Therefore, this research aims to promote the development of graph neural networks in computer vision, and the practical outcomes of this study are presented in the experimental results section. The Sidon set problem concerns identifying subsets within the finite affine plane of order n, with the property that any line it contains intersects the subset at most once, or at most twice. In our research, we establish upper limits on the maximum size of a Sidon set in the affine plane of order n, with specific upper limits being derived for orders n up to 29, with the exception of n=9. These findings refine and extend prior work by Mann and Goldberg. In the process of our research, we discovered that max |A| values for n=9 and n=25 do not conform to the max |A| = 2n-1 theorem, instead taking the value of 2n-2. Although completing the picture for n=25 requires solving an open problem, we speculate that a complete affine plane of order 9 might also yield a max |A| value in line with the 2n-1 theorem. In addition, we derived limits on the size of hyperbolas and ellipses within the affine plane of order n, with specific upper limits being derived for orders n up to 29, with the exception of n=9. These new findings provide a basis for investigating the completeness problem of Sidon sets in the affine plane of order n. Effective modeling of binary data is critical in numerous applications, including network analysis, where numerous processes can be represented as binary matrices, and various probability distributions can be assigned to their entries. When generating random binary matrices, using a uniform probability distribution (uniform sampling) is a standard approach, but our investigation considers the potential benefits of non-uniform probability distributions (non-uniform sampling). We evaluated the impact of non-uniform sampling by analyzing its characteristics, such as the number of unique matrices generated, and compared it to uniform sampling. Our study also involves fitting observed data to a broad range of probability distributions and examining the resulting models in terms of their statistical significance and predictive power. The advantages of non-uniform sampling include the ability to improve model fit and predictive power, as well as increase the diversity of generated matrices, compared to uniform sampling. Additionally, we applied the proposed method to a practical problem in network analysis, involving the generation of binary networks with a specific structure (known as scale-free networks), and demonstrated that non-uniform sampling can lead to improved model fit and predictive power. Therefore, non-uniform sampling can be a valuable tool for generating random binary matrices, and it offers advantages over traditional uniform sampling. Furthermore, our simple and efficient approach can be adapted to other types of data by modifying the probability distribution accordingly. The applicability of our method extends beyond our specific case study of binary data, as it provides a general framework for data generation. Each department contributes computers to the KDM pool, creating a large, distributed computing resource with a combined 222 processors and 7 GB of RAM. The Knowledge Discovery Mine is managed by the Data Science research group at the University of Leiden, which utilizes the ELKI data mining framework to facilitate scalable data mining operations on the KDM cluster. We present a method to precisely control the optical spectrum of microcombs by employing a pair of pumps with closely spaced frequencies. When the acoustic mode of the microresonator is centered between the pumps, the comb's spectrum exhibits a complex and highly regular pattern. By adjusting the spacing between the pumps, it is possible to map a traditional comb linehape onto an almost perfect sine function. To achieve this, we utilize a pair of pumps with frequencies that have an arithmetic progression, resulting in a symmetric linehape with a cosine profile. Consequently, even though each line has a finite spectral resolution, the overall optical spectrum exhibits a high degree of coherence. Moreover, we propose the use of this technique to synthesize a continuous, wide tuning range optical transmitter, capable of generating hundreds of channels with adjustable spacing. To validate this concept, we successfully demonstrated the production of an optical transmitter using a Si3N4 microresonator, which yielded a coherent spectrum with over 100nm of continuous coverage and nearly perfect coherence, featuring hundreds of wavelength multiplexing capabilities. Notably, this could facilitate innovative applications in fields like metrology, spectroscopy, and advanced communication systems. Additionally, we observed that the generation of an optical transmitter was accompanied by a high level of stabilization of the microresonator's intrinsic frequency, which showed a low level of frequency fluctuations relative to the reference frequency. This level of frequency stabilization can be attributed to the intrinsic properties of the microresonator itself, rather than stabilization techniques employed previously. As a result, we were able to achieve a frequency stabilization ratio of approximately 10^-6, which could potentially be improved upon by employing advanced stabilization techniques. To summarize, we have developed a method for precise spectral control in microcombs by employing a pair of pumps, which can be used for wide tuning range optical transmitter applications. Furthermore, we have demonstrated a high level of frequency stabilization in microresonators, which could be useful in future research. Moreover, we have proposed the potential for integrated optical coherence tomography systems using microcombs, which could facilitate widespread adoption of this technology in biomedical research. This could lead to the development of a vast number of optical sensing systems and integrated photonics applications.
