Individuals successfully identify objects dropped in their immediate surroundings due to their integrated sensory information, encompassing visual, kinesthetic, tactile, and spatial components. Distinguishing objects solely through visual information is particularly challenging when they are positioned close to the point of drop. Researchers aim to replicate this capacity by developing machines capable of identifying objects based on multi-sensory, spatially arranged cues. Nevertheless, current robotic technology lacks a comprehensive understanding of these cues, necessitating further work. We propose a novel method to identify objects using autonomous robots, incorporating autonomous exploration and sensory integration within reachable regions. Autonomous robots are equipped with sensory devices, including cameras and grippers, capable of moving freely within their environment. The robots are programmed to collect information about objects through close proximity, utilizing integrated multi-sensory perception to identify objects based on combined visual, kinesthetic, tactile, and spatial cues. The robots achieve this by autonomously deciding on the necessary sensory information required for accurate object identification. The efficiency of the robots' identification process is ensured by integrating object information through a multi-sensory alignment procedure, incorporating a distance metric that considers sensory information and spatial relationships. The robots are capable of recognizing objects at a distance by aligning the object information from their local region with the optical flow they detect. We demonstrate the application and effectiveness of our method in a drop detection game designed for autonomous robots, where they learn to identify objects by integrating multi-sensory information within their reachable region. The robots are trained to distinguish objects based on combined visual, kinesthetic, tactile, and spatial cues, successfully classified using a support vector machine. Recent experiments have shown promising results, with our method successfully identifying objects dropped by human players in the robots' immediate surroundings. The performance of our method surpasses that of existing object recognition techniques, verifying its effectiveness through a statistical analysis. The experiments are repeated multiple times, with the results confirming the validity of our approach. The analysis of our method's efficiency shows its scalability for real-world applications, with the potential to integrate sensory information from multiple sources and expand the searchable area to at least 3 times its current size. The integration of our method with existing object recognition techniques has the potential to expand the searchable area to at least 10 times its current size. The proposed approach has significant practical implications, with the potential to improve existing object recognition systems by integrating their information with multi-sensory data. The concepts of frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming have been debated for their validity as distinct modes of jamming. Research in this area aims to understand the properties of jammed materials and their transition points, involving the application of scaling theories to volume and compressive stiffness versus pressure datasets. Our study reveals that the critical exponents associated with frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming differ significantly, specifically in the values of $d$ and $g$. These findings imply that shear jamming does not simply resemble isotropic jamming in three dimensions. Instead, the distinct physical processes underlying these two modes of jamming yield distinct power-law behaviors in their respective stiffness or compressibility versus pressure relationships. Ultimately, our research underscores the importance of accurately characterizing jamming transitions and their associated scaling properties to differentiate between distinct modes of jamming. Moreover, this work highlights the potential for adjusting jamming conditions through friction to achieve novel material properties with applications in the production of bulk and composite materials. We propose the MS(2)-AR(4) model, which combines a multiplicative seasonal component with an autoregressive component, to describe complex dependencies in electricity demand time series. This model builds on previously suggested frameworks such as the AR component-only approach and the Multiplicative Seasonal AR model. We employ various statistical tests to validate the MS(2)-AR(4) model, including the normality test, the autocorrelation function and partial correlation function analysis, and a test for AR parameter significance. This model is capable of capturing both autoregressive and multiplicative seasonal properties in electricity demand data. We compare the performance of the MS(2)-AR(4) model to the standard AR(4) model using a combined assessment of the Akaike information criterion and residual-based measures. This modeling process is demonstrated using actual electricity demand data for four Australian cities. We evaluate the performance of the MS(2)-AR(4) model against the AR(4) model in forecasting settings, specifically by utilizing the estimated parameters to make 7-day ahead predictions for each city. Notably, the MS(2)-AR(4) model outperforms the AR(4) model in terms of both mean absolute error and coefficient of variation of the absolute error measures. This suggests that the proposed MS(2)-AR(4) model offers a superior approach to capturing complex dependencies in electricity demand time series and ultimately improves forecasting accuracy. Additionally, the model provides critical insights into the probabilistic distribution of future electricity demand, facilitating the development of more accurate probabilistic forecasts. This model's capabilities extend beyond traditional point forecasting techniques by enabling the computation of probabilistic quantities such as expected shortfalls and probabilistic reserves, which are crucial for power system operations and risk assessment. As such, the MS(2)-AR(4) model presents a versatile tool for modeling, analyzing, and forecasting complex electricity demand time series. This model's potential applications extend to other types of non-stationary time series data. Furthermore, the proposed approach can be adapted to other multiplicative AR models by incorporating an autoregressive component, thereby expanding its practical utility. We suggest potential research directions including the use of vector autoregressive models to analyze vector time series data and the integration of exogenous variables, such as weather data, to further improve electricity demand forecasting accuracy. This study contributes a novel modeling framework that captures complex dependencies in electricity demand data while also facilitating practical utility extensions. This model's development and applications are particularly relevant to countries with growing electricity demands

For searches related to jobs in the public sector, the authors conducted a comprehensive study of how algorithmic bias impacts search results in Germany. Additionally, the authors created and validated a scale measuring bias in online search outcomes. A random sample of 250 job openings from public sector employment websites was used to investigate potential biases in job advertisements listed on Google's Web Search platform. Our investigation considered three dimensions of potential bias: the underrepresentation of certain regions, the underrepresentation of male applicants, and the focus on young and highly qualified applicants. Our analysis of 50 search inquiries revealed potential bias in Google's algorithmic outcomes, affecting job searches in the public sector. The frequency and severity of biased results ranged from 16 to 76%, depending on the criteria used. Our study demonstrated that a significant proportion of search inquiries exhibited some form of bias. Our analysis also highlighted potential disparities in job searches sponsored by public sector professionals, including biased representation of regions and age groups in job advertisements. The magnitude of biased results varied, with 26% of sponsored outcomes exhibiting bias. Our research identified the underrepresentation of male applicants as a significant concern for job searches, with 36% of outcomes showing a greater emphasis on young and highly qualified female applicants. Our study revealed potential algorithmic bias in job searches, affecting a substantial proportion of public sector employment searches in Germany, particularly with regards to regional representation and age groups in job advertisements. Our analysis indicates that algorithmic bias in job searches may exacerbate existing disparities in the public sector employment landscape. Our research highlights the importance of transparency in Web Search algorithms, especially for sensitive queries like public sector job searches. Our study suggests that more than half of the inquiries could be improved by excluding factors such as location, age, and other sensitive criteria. Our research raises concerns about the potential impact of biased job searches on public sector employment, emphasizing the need for search engine operators to address algorithmic bias in Web Search outcomes. Our study proposes developing and implementing more accurate and fair Web Search algorithms, incorporating diverse perspectives of public sector professionals, to ensure a more neutral and informative search experience. Our research recommends establishing a clear, unbiased search policy to guide the development of more transparent and fair Web Search algorithms, incorporating input from stakeholders, including public sector employment agencies and candidates. Our research suggests developing and promoting educational programs to raise awareness of algorithmic bias among public sector professionals and search engine operators. Our experiment verifies the performance of the SynthPod framework, designed to automatically develop programs based on specifications. This evaluation involves two key aspects: first, we examine SynthPod's capability to find a program, and second, we assess its efficiency in doing so within a predetermined time limit. To investigate the latter, and understand how often SynthPod's search algorithm successfully generates a program, we ran the search procedure 250 times for each of 50 random specifications, and found that SynthPod can create a program in the average case, and roughly 80% of the time, and does so within its allotted time in about 80% of instances. Additionally, we analyze how specification complexity, as indicated by the number of variables and constraints, impacts SynthPD's search efficiency and program generation success rates. Furthermore, we discuss potential avenues to accelerate the SynthPod framework.

The intricate dynamics of the Earth's climate system are captured by multiple processes operating at various scales, from tiny atmospheric movements to large tectonic activities. These processes interact with each other over different time and spatial frames, creating a complex web of phenomena. To comprehend the system's behavior, researchers use multi-dimensional numerical models to simulate the processes, often using the most up-to-date algorithms and high-performance computing capabilities.

However, reducing the complexity of the Earth's climate system is essential for understanding the most critical processes and their interactions. Several techniques are employed to accomplish this, including model simplification, process-level analysis, and data compression. Researchers have utilized advanced mathematical methods, such as dimensionality reduction and filtering techniques, to identify and separate the dominant atmospheric flow patterns and their interactions.

This thesis contributes to the reduction of climate model complexity by employing a novel approach, combining multi-objective optimization with genetic algorithms and ensemble prediction. The objective is to identify the most influential subspace within the multi-dimensional climate model state space that significantly impacts its future evolution. The proposed method, tested on a three-dimensional climate model, has shown promising results, revealing key patterns that govern the model's behavior and their connections to El Ni\~no, a major climate phenomenon. The underlying patterns are found to be critical for understanding the model's multi-objective optimization targets, such as inducing an El Ni\~no event, and are indicative of the model's sensitivity structure. The identified patterns can be utilized for future climate state projections, enabling the targeting of specific climate states and their associated transitions, such as from El Ni\~no to La Ni\~na. The proposed method is expected to be adaptable to more complex climate models and can be applied to other low-dimensional and optimal perturbation studies. Moreover, the method may be modified to detect and interpret optimal perturbations in data, much like the EOF and DEOF techniques. The future directions of this research involve incorporating optimal perturbations into the multi-objective optimization framework and utilizing the resulting patterns to investigate the Earth's optimal climate states and their transitions. The goal is to develop a predictive capability that allows the calculation of optimal perturbations for various climate model objectives, paving the way for the detection of optimal perturbations in data and their potential impacts on the Earth's climate system. The ultimate ambition is to utilize this capability to explore the Earth's optimal climate states and their transitions in the context of the multi-dimensional climate model. The expected outcomes of this research include new techniques for the optimal detection of climate variability in data

The application of logarithmic transformation to components of data vectors is a common approach in analyzing compositional data within high-dimensional spaces.  This method is typically used to analyze species population counts, company stock values, city population segments, etc.  The total sum of the components in such data is usually constant, resulting from sampling procedures like mixing or selection.  Given a vector $x$, standardizing this data by applying a logarithmic transformation and then normalizing the components by dividing by the vector's norm, yields a vector whose components sum to one, making it a suitable candidate for additional statistical analyses.  The question arises of whether this standardized normalization is a unique transformation, achieving the goal of components summing to one.  This paper provides an alternative proof, showing that the standardized normalization is indeed the unique transformation achieving this objective.  This uniqueness proof has significant implications across domains, as it validates the one-to-one correspondence between the set of positive vectors and the set of probability vectors.  This uniqueness also enables the extension of the normalized transformation to matrix multiplication, allowing for analysis of block-diagonal compositional data and highlighting potential applications in bioinformatics and chemometrics.  Additionally, the paper explores properties of the derivative of the normalized transformation, facilitating the calculation of probability vector derivatives.  This study further investigates characteristics of the Lebesgue measure on high-dimensional spaces, effectively turning to the analysis of Gaussian random fields on orthogonal complements of diagonal subspaces.  Ultimately, the paper demonstrates the potential for applying normalized transformation derivatives in optimizing information divergence and as a tool for confirmatory graphical Gaussian model selection. The core accretion theory suggests that runaway gas accretion leads to the formation of Jupiter and Saturn, leaving Jupiter and Saturn as the only planets in the gas accretion phase. Given enough time, this theory claims that Uranus and Neptune should have also undergone this process. However, the recent discovery of small, transiting Jupiter and Saturn analogs challenges this idea, as it suggests that planets with masses similar to these gas giants should exist in the population of small planets. The findings from the Kepler mission show that such analogs are present, but their numbers are limited and they generally wrap up existing populations by the time the gas accretion phase should have begun for Jupiter and Saturn. When comparing observed distributions to simulations involving runaway accretion, it becomes apparent that this theory's core component does not work as intended. As a result, the core component can be discarded in favor of an alternative that generates more realistic populations resembling those observed. This new model posits that cores capable of inducing runaway accretion are destroyed in the process, meaning that planets formed through this process should be scarce. As a result, the model suggests that Uranus and Neptune likely formed through core accretion, as their masses are significantly lower than those of Jupiter and Saturn. Ultimately, this implies that core accretion is responsible for the formation of all four Jupiter and Saturn analogs, as their masses should be scarce in populations formed via runaway accretion. The model's implications are significant, as they suggest that core accretation is necessary to explain both the masses of the most massive Neptune-like planets and the population dynamics of Jupiter and Saturn analogs. In this model, a complex consisting of a scalar mediator and dark matter particles is responsible for the observed phenomena. Dark matter has a mass range of a few GeV to tens of KeV, and its interaction with nuclear particles is mediated by a scalar mediator with a mass less than 100 GeV. For dark matter with a mass less than the mediator's mass, its interaction with nuclear particles is primarily facilitated by its spin, and its interaction rate with nuclear particles is calculated and expressed through a cross-section. This model is particularly suitable for dark matter with a mass less than 1 GeV, and its interaction rate with hydrogen in the context of the dark matter density in our galaxy is used to establish an upper limit on its abundance. This research introduces a novel cognitive multi-task dataset, termed Mod-Cog, which builds upon the existing set of tasks in the CoCoMac dataset and expands its scope by incorporating eight additional tasks not initially covered. We explore the rational points on varieties that arise from nilpotent algebras, where the finite dimensionality makes some complex problems more manageable. Our work focuses on two key objects: the affine space of nilpotent algebras of a given finite dimension, denoted $M_{s,n}$, and a projective equivalent variety, $PM_{s,n}$. We establish a key geometric relationship between these varieties, allowing us to determine the rational points on $M_{s,n}$ for small dimensions, and use this result to address a broader question related to Lie algebras. Our approach also gives rise to a new family of finitely generated nilpotent algebras, which we analyze and illustrate with examples. Additionally, we apply our findings to a corresponding variety of Lie algebras, $ML_{s,n}$, and provide a solution to a long-standing problem in that context. Our work yields new, non-isomorphic families of finitely generated nilpotent Lie algebras, which raise intriguing questions for further investigation. To summarize, our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the geometric aspects of nilpotent algebras, equipping us with powerful methods to study corresponding varieties of Lie algebras and offering concrete solutions to previously challenging problems. Our study also sheds light on the rational points on varieties of nilpotent algebras, offering key insights into their geometric and algebraic properties. Our work paves the way for future research into the diverse and complex structures of finitely generated nilpotent algebras and their relationship to algebraic geometry. This paper explores the theory of relativistic electron interactions with photons from the Cosmic Microwave Background and soft X-ray backgrounds to explain the formation of large-scale, relativistic jets in active galactic nuclei. Our model reveals two dominant inverse Compton scattering processes: one involving CMB photons and another with additional energy gained from scattering solar wind photons before reaching black holes. Our numerical simulations effectively reproduce the observed patterns of non-thermal photons in these jets, thereby validating our model's reliability. Furthermore, we propose a novel mechanism for accelerating electrons within these jets, involving the interaction of relativistic electrons with solar wind photons prior to being drawn into a black hole's influence. This mechanism could potentially provide the required energy to power high-energy Gamma-Ray Bursts. Our model offers a new explanation for the origin of relativistic jets in active galactic nuclei and, by extension, may provide crucial insights into the mechanisms driving such powerful cosmic emitters. Our model is also explored in the context of High-Energy Steady Gamma-Ray Bursts, and finds that these objects are simply the result of the deceleration of non-relativistic protons in circumbular fields. Our calculations indicate that the peak energy of synchrotron radiation should be less than 10 MeV. Building upon the pre-non-relativistic (PNR) expansion method introduced in Dirac-Hamiltonian-based general relativity, an alternative analytical expansion of the Dirac equation is developed within the framework of geometrical methods in general relativity. This novel approach employs a 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization, analogous to the Scher cue for relativistic systems, facilitating an orderly and systematic expansion towards the full relativistic scenario. The method can accommodate various levels of relativistic corrections in the potential and spin-orbit interaction, while being versatile enough to handle potentials with or without relativistic corrections. Its computational advantages are most evident in the case of weak gravitational fields and potentials. Several model studies are presented to demonstrate the method's efficacy. Due to its versatility and computational advantages, this expansion method may find applications in scenarios where the effects of relativistic corrections, gravitational interactions, and spin-orbit coupling are pronounced. Moreover, the method is expected to be useful in the accurate modeling of atoms in strong external electromagnetic fields and within the scope of Brumberg's theory of the canonical transformation. This paper's findings are a culmination of the research undertaken in the associated theses [85,86]. Our investigation of the system's physical properties reveals that both stars are identical, non-rotating, and detached. Deep neural networks tend to be particularly effective image classifiers when they contain multiple branches that process the same input image under different transformations. However, creating and optimizing such a model can be complicated due to the varied characteristics of the transformations applied. The UOT-Pooling framework addresses this challenge by converting each branch into a weighted version of itself, based on an optimization process that involves a weighted sum of the features extracted. This approach yields two key benefits: it simplifies the optimization process and enhances the model's performance, as the weighted features are more easily interpretable and relevant. As a result, the UOT-Pooling framework has achieved state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Furthermore, our framework's capabilities extend beyond training time to include data-time decoupling, as the weights learned during training can be used to adapt to new data environments. We demonstrate this advantage through a successful application of our model to the CamVANILA dataset. The code for UOT-Pooling is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/jayjaynh/UOTPooling. A PyTorch implementation of the model can also be found at https://pytorch.org/dbb.html. This study examines the circular motion and motion along the galaxy's main axis of nuclear supermassive black holes in host spiral galaxies. We analyzed the optical images of 19 type 1 and type 2 nuclei of spiral hosts to determine their orientation distribution. Our analysis revealed that, unlike our initial expectations, there was no significant difference in the circular motion frequency (20%) between type 1 and type 2 nuclei. However, we discovered that nuclear motion along the host galaxy's major axis is more frequent (30%) among type 2 nuclei than type 1 nuclei. Various factors could contribute to the differences in nuclear orientation and motion between type 1 and type 2 nuclei, including the presence of a dust torus and a spiral host galaxy's morphological features. If confirmed, our findings of nuclear circular and orbital motion can provide valuable insights into these active galactic nuclei's behavior. Moreover, we propose that nuclear motion could serve as an activity indicator that complements traditional methods. Our research also explores the potential for active galactic nuclei to influence their host galaxy's motion. We predict that, in some cases, nuclear motion can extend beyond the host galaxy's diffusion zone and be visible in optical images. Our findings are consistent with the observation of nuclear motion in the galaxy M87, which manifests as an asymmetry in its optical images. Our research further suggests that extended nuclear motion could be more prevalent among type 1 nuclei than type 2 nuclei. We look forward to verifying our predictions through future space missions, such as the UVIT on IMAP, which could capture high-energy optical images of active galactic nuclei near their host galaxies. Estimating scene geometry is a fundamental visual task that can leverage
spatial constraints, making it appealing for pre-training visual models. However,
conventional approaches for self-supervised geometric estimation typically rely
on 2D or 3D Euclidean regression, which can be vulnerable to noisy approximations.
This study proposes an innovative method involving the establishment of point-to-
plane correspondences based on pairwise relative orientations of planes in a scene.
A dedicated neural network is designed to predict the unique orientation relationship
between any three points in an image, generating a unique code for each triangle.
This output can then be compared with actual triangle formations to calculate
reconstruction errors, which in turn informs the model's training. Our method,
named TriPlane, offers superior performance over existing self-supervised learning
methods, achieving the lowest error rates in various 3D reconstruction benchmarks. 
Additionally, the model's capabilities extend beyond geometric estimation, enabling
performance improvements in image classification and object detection tasks after
being fine-tuned with minimal training data. The code for TriPlane is available at
https://github.com/sngongol/TriPlane.

The growing importance of time-series analysis across diverse domains has led to a pressing need for a robust, data-driven approach. However, creating high-quality, annotated training data, essential for developing accurate models, is often hindered by costs, manual labeling requirements, or a lack of understanding of relevant concepts. To address this challenge, we introduce TCube, a neural network that leverages transfer learning to adapt existing models trained by other researchers, adapting their 'thought processes' to better fit specific tasks. TCube's cube-based architecture allows it to 'think' in a distinct way, outperforming other neural networks that rely on linear or circular designs. By effectively adapting models to new environments, TCube demonstrates superior performance in multiple tasks for various time-series applications, such as identifying salient values, detecting unusual patterns, and forecasting future values. Moreover, we demonstrate that TCube enables seamless integration of external knowledge, enhancing the accuracy of time-series analysis. Our comprehensive experiments are accompanied by an open-source repository containing the adapted models, allowing researchers to reproduce our results and apply TCube to novel time-series problems. We've implemented this approach to study specific submodels, such as the Ising model on the real line and the quasisymmetric model. Our analysis sheds light on the commonalities and differences among these models in terms of their thermodynamic behavior. We're investigating how solutions to hyperbolic equations evolve in a changing spacetime metric, specifically how the regularity of these solutions decreases over time, measured in terms of the Sobolev norm, for any order. Initially, the solutions maintain their initial regularity, but as time progresses, the loss of regularity grows linearly, and it's our central claim that this loss is directly proportional to the maximum order of the Sobolev norm of the spacetime metric tensor's derivatives. Our research focuses on deriving this result both generally and in specific cases, particularly for equations like the Klein-Gordon and the wave equation, and we're exploring the connections between our findings and standard results for these equations. Furthermore, we're defining a suitable energy space for the solutions, which enables us to derive non-uniformly decreasing energy estimates in relation to the spacetime metric's properties, and these estimates are useful in determining the conditions under which the solutions remain bounded in their respective Sobolev norms, and consequently, remain analytic. To study the singularities of the spacetime metric, we're adapting methods from hyperbolic equation research to investigate the behavior of solutions to hyperbolic systems, and we're exploring the implications of our findings for the initial value problem of general relativity, particularly in its smooth and analytic variants. Ultimately, our research aims to understand how the properties of spacetime metrics influence the properties of solutions to hyperbolic equations and their connections to the singularity problem of the universe. By developing new methods and energy estimates, and by studying the properties of specific spacetime metrics, such as those found in the Taub-NUT space and in spaces with conical singularities, we're gaining insights into the behavior of spacetime and its potential universality principles. This research focuses on improving Japanese word segmentation using LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory), a type of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), to enhance the accuracy of morphological analysis. Traditional Japanese word segmentation methods typically rely on cut-point prediction, but this approach can lead to errors in word identification. To address this challenge, LSTM-based Japanese word segmentation has gained attention in recent years due to its ability to capture complex contextual relationships. However, previous studies using LSTM were limited by their simple architectures and small training datasets. This research aims to overcome these limitations by employing a more advanced LSTM architecture and a larger training dataset, based on the NIN-JIGAWA dataset, which includes comprehensive information on Japanese word composition. Additionally, this study explores the effectiveness of incorporating pre-trained word embeddings into Japanese word segmentation. Experimental results reveal a significant improvement in accuracy when incorporating pre-trained word embeddings and utilizing a more advanced LSTM architecture. Furthermore, this study introduces the Hybrid LSTM and Hybrid LSTM with Dropout (HD) architectures, which outperformed cut-point-based approaches and achieved comparable performance to state-of-the-art models, such as Kawata and Soga. Notably, these new models exhibited superior performance on long Japanese words and accurately identified functional words and characters. To validate the robustness and generalizability of these models, this study conducted ten-fold cross-validation and successfully applied the Hybrid LSTM and HD models to Japanese word segmentation. Furthermore, these models were successfully tested on the Japanese Part-of-Speech Tagging task, demonstrating potential future applications in this domain. To the best of our knowledge, this study marks the first instance of successfully applying LSTM for Japanese word segmentation using the NIN-JIGAWA dataset. This project involves analyzing the popularity of external resources shared on Stack Overflow. Despite being temporary, external resources such as GitHub repositories and pastebin posts are shared repeatedly, often due to the character limit for code snippets. We investigate the lifespan of these resources, finding that a small fraction exceeds the average lifespan. Our results show that links to text-based resources like pastebin posts are most frequently shared multiple times. Furthermore, we find that factors such as recent activity, popularity of tags, and time of day can influence the likelihood of a resource being shared multiple times. We hope these findings contribute to strategies for effectively maintaining long-term external resources shared on Stack Overflow. To achieve our objectives, we collected a dataset of all external resources shared on Stack Overflow from 2018 to 2020, totaling 113k distinct URLs. Our analysis involved creating a mirror of the dataset to track the lifespan of resources over time, as well as implementing a statistical model to predict the likelihood of a resource being shared multiple times based on various factors. Our experiments were performed on a local machine with 16 GB of RAM and an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1660 Ti GPU. Due to space constraints, our implementation is available upon request. Nonetheless, we note that reproducing the results could be accomplished with half the required resources. In the future, we aim to expand upon this research by exploring methods for predicting the eventual outcome of a resource based on its initial popularity, as well as using machine learning algorithms to determine the characteristics of successful resources. Such an exploration may involve collecting additional data in the future. As an ethical consideration, our research aims to contribute constructive feedback to developers whose resources appear in the dataset, as well as to the Stack Overflow community. To facilitate this, we present our findings to the community through multiple channels, including a blog post and presentations at relevant conferences. In the spirit of collaborative scientific inquiry, we make our data available to the public, as well as our code to enable replication. The Max Planck-IAU research group is exploring the connection between dark matter halos and the diversity of galaxy rotation curves. People are only motivated to tackle climate change when they connect personally with its impacts. Connecting climate change to personal experiences can facilitate effective action, but doing so requires an extensive knowledge base, making it inaccessible to most individuals. This research introduces a groundbreaking method harnessing the power of large language models to translate climate data into the language and context of each person's values, effectively translating abstract climate data into tangible, emotionally resonant experiences. We tested this approach with over 1,000 participants who were given a choice of potential climate consequences and asked to prioritize them based on how much each aligns with their personal values; our results showed that participants consistently preferred the translated, context-specific climate scenarios over general ones, and that this approach can boost motivation to take climate action by as much as a full standard deviation. This methodology can be adapted by climate organizations to increase public engagement and action, and by policymakers to tailor climate policies to specific communities and regions. Moreover, our research lays the groundwork for a potential new direction in climate research, incorporating natural language processing and value-based language translation as a key area of study. To analyze this, a comprehensive quantitative study focusing on the autonomous driving problem is presented, utilizing the Google AI Football simulator. It investigates the capacity of state-action models, predictive models, and efficient recurrent neural network designs to enhance the performance of policy optimization through proximal policy optimization. The findings indicate that recurrent neural networks are essential for optimal policy performance and predictive models can facilitate substantial speedup through function approximation. Additionally, innovative recurrent unit designs are shown to yield improved performance over conventional units like Gated Recurrent Unit and Long Short-Term Memory. The source code for the study is publicly available on GitHub. The proliferation of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) has been one of the most significant trends in current research on Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). However, the immense computational complexity and power requirements of these networks pose significant challenges, particularly in terms of their deployment on mobile and embedded devices. To address these issues, researchers have been exploring alternative neural network architectures that can balance computational efficiency with high classification performance. One such emerging architecture is the Ramana-style DNN, characterized by its efficient use of power through the combination of integer-based operations and the elimination of floating-point calculations. In this study, we developed and systematically evaluated a series of Ramana-style DNNs capable of competing with the performance of leading ANNs. Specifically, we designed, trained, and tested 10 distinct Ramana-style DNNs on the MNIST dataset for digit classification, and also explored their potential application on the CIFAR-10 dataset for image recognition. Notably, our Ramana-style DNNs demonstrated exceptional classification performance, with top-1 errors of 0.28% on the MNIST dataset and 5.44% on the CIFAR-10 dataset, significantly outperforming the existing Ramana-style DNNs while requiring substantially fewer computational resources. Moreover, we developed an automated training pipeline using Keras/TensorFlow to facilitate the training and evaluation of these neural networks, and made the source code available on the GitHub repository for the benefit of the research community. Overall, our study successfully designed, evaluated, and validated a new generation of Ramana-style DNNs characterized by high performance, efficiency, and ease of use. Moreover, we hope that our research will inspire further development in the area of neural network architecture, contributing to the creation of more efficient and scalable deep learning models in the future. Finally, the source code for the project is available in the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/asharakeh/Ramana-style-DNN.

This research investigates the behavior of strange quark matter under intense magnetic fields, influenced by color magnetic interactions and the magnetic properties of quarks, leading to a more rigid equation of state. Specifically, we explored the effects of a strong magnetic field on the multi-quark clustering phenomenon in spin-polarized strange quark matter, and found that a strong magnetic field prevents such clustering at high chemical potentials, but allows it at lower values. Our analysis also considers how this clustering impacts quark stars, potentially influencing the maximum quark star mass and the behavior of their electron degeneracy pressure. Our findings suggest that a quark star could exist with a radius dependent on the chemical potential of the quark matter, potentially resolving the issue of quark star masses and providing a new understanding of the relationship between quark matter and the observed mass spectrum of neutron stars. This study paves the way for further investigation into the properties of quark stars based on the characteristics of their equilibrium configurations. Moreover, we looked into the effects of a strong magnetic field on the stability of strange quark matter droplets, and discovered that in the presence of a strong magnetic field, this stability can be affected, potentially even at zero temperature, due to the influence of color magnetic interactions and quark magnetic properties. Specifically, we observed that a strong magnetic field can cause unstable quark matter droplets at certain surface tensions and densities. Nevertheless, the stability of quark matter droplets can still be affected solely by the surface tension at high densities and chemical potentials. Additionally, we explored the effects of a strong magnetic field on quark stars, and found that a strong magnetic field can lead to quark star collapse in certain situations, influenced by color magnetic interactions and quark magnetic properties. Specifically, we observed the collapse of quark stars at high densities, chemical potentials, and certain surface tensions. However, a strong magnetic field can prevent the collapse of quark stars at high densities and chemical potentials, and even result in the expansion of quark stars at lower densities and chemical potentials. Furthermore, the effects of a strong magnetic field on quark stars can potentially result in the existence of quark star black holes, due to the collapse of quark stars accompanied by the emission of gravitational waves. Specifically, we observed the possibility of quark star black hole formation in certain density and chemical potential ranges. Personal devices are becoming increasingly powerful and diverse, and users are benefiting from accessible, affordable access to a wide range of devices, such as powerful GPUs and iPads.  However, and despite these enhancements, computational throughput is often limited when carried out on a single device.  This paper introduces Pando, a revolutionary platform that enables seamless collaboration between personal devices to accelerate computational processes.  Pando is based on a innovative combination of visual graphics and semantic audio, allowing users to distribute tasks across multiple devices simultaneously, and thus significantly reduce computational time.  We showcase Pando's capabilities through two practical applications: a real-time video streaming mirror and a dynamic video composition tool.  The former utilizes user-generated iCloud to create a real-time video streaming service via a unique combination of Perlin noise, depth analysis, and image filtering, and can be supported by a single iPad.  The latter leverages device collaboration to compose dynamic videos on iOS devices, and can be powered by a combination of one iPad and multiple iPhones or iPads.  Experimental results confirm that Pando significantly enhances computational throughput and efficiency by a factor of 10 to 20, and significantly reduces latency to near real-time levels.  Moreover, and as an added benefit, Pando opens up new creative possibilities by enabling the development of innovative, collaborative graphics and visual effects.  Finally, and as a significant contribution, Pando provides valuable insights into visual graphics and semantic audio synchronization, and lays the groundwork for future applications and research in this domain. This research introduces an adaptive Monte Carlo method that accelerates the computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors by selectively generating samples based on an iterative approach adjusted for uncertainty. In contrast to conventional Monte Carlo methods, our adaptive method pinpointed critical regions in the eigenvalue spectrum and focuses sampling efforts on those areas. As a result, our algorithm is more efficient, especially for complex eigendecomposition problems involving large, irregular spectra. We validate the performance of our adaptive algorithm through comparative studies with the standard Monte Carlo method and an adaptive quasi-Monte Carlo method. Furthermore, our algorithm is compatible with various probability distributions and can be applied to approximately compute eigenvectors as well as eigenvalues. To achieve this, the eigenvector approximation is based on an eigenvector representation formula that involves an integral of a linear combination of eigenvector components. A theoretical analysis of the adaptive algorithm's convergence rate and efficiency is also provided. In particular, the analysis shows that the convergence rate is directly proportional to the square root of the number of samples, as well as the ratio of the eigengap to the maximum eigenvector component magnitude. To further illustrate the efficacy of our adaptive algorithm, a set of numerical experiments has been conducted, demonstrating its superior performance in both eigenvalue and eigenvector approximations. In some cases, the adaptive Monte Carlo method even outperformed the adaptive quasi-Monte Carlo method. In conclusion, the proposed adaptive Monte Carlo algorithm offers an efficient solution for approximately computing eigenvalues and eigenvectors, particularly for irregular spectra with large eigengaps. Nonetheless, its convergence rate may be sublinear due to the nature of adaptive sampling. In contrast, the adaptive quasi-Monte Carlo method achieves a sublinear convergence rate, making it suitable for general approximation problems. In light of its efficiency, we recommend exploring the adaptive Monte Carlo method in statistical inference tasks. In particular, the technique appears promising for computing posterior eigenvalues and eigenvectors in linear structural models with irregular spectra. It's further demonstrated that these survivor sets contain all badly approximable numbers in base $\beta$. A key tool used for these results involves proving that the intermediate beta-transformation $T_\beta$ is uniquely ergodic with a continuous invariant measure distributing uniformly along the preimages of the interval $[0,1/\beta^2]$. This allows us to establish a novel representation of survivor sets as those whose continued fraction convergents lie within a specific range defined by the parameters $\beta$ and $\gamma$. We explore the implications of the ergodicity of $T_\beta$ in its relation to the set of badly approximable numbers, demonstrating equalities or near-equalities in distribution for various subsets of numbers. We study how various operators in $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories with $N_{F}$ flavors of quarks break an underlying $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry. This occurs through a process caused by quark bilinears, leading to the presence of Goldstone bosons. Our research involves examining the largest irreducible representations of the gauge theory's Hilbert space, which can contain Goldstone bosons. By doing so, we are able to derive sum rules relating the symmetries of the theory to its spectrum, providing an alternative to large $N_{c}$ considerations. As such, we are able to investigate finite size effects and the interplay between Goldstone bosons and other meson states. Our findings reveal the presence of non-perturbative poles in correlation functions and the distribution of Goldstone bosons among the vacuum and various meson states. Moreover, we use our results to propose a renormalization of the 't Hooft and Polyakov dimension for quark bilinears, which could have broader implications for the construction of operator product expansions in gauge theories. Lastly, we explore the possibility of applying our approach to the construction of effective actions for gauge theories with quarks. Due to the presence of Goldstone bosons, we are able to write down novel effective actions, which incorporate the backreaction of meson amplitudes on the quark bilinear vertex. This allows us to examine the distribution of Goldstone bosons among the various meson amplitudes and the interplay between Goldstone bosons and other meson states. Furthermore, we speculate on the potential extension of our approach to other quantum field theories featuring Goldstone bosons. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that such an extension would likely be feasible only when the Goldstone bosons comprise a substantial fraction of the Hilbert space. Conversely, in situations where the long-wavelength fluctuations of the Goldstone bosons are heavily suppressed, our approach may not yield significant insights. Consequently, the scope of our method remains uncertain and further research is necessary to clarify its applicability to the construction of effective actions for quantum field theories featuring Goldstone bosons. Lastly, we have also discussed the application of our approach to the construction of effective actions for gauge theories with quarks and explored its potential for a generalization to other quantum field theories featuring Goldbone bosons. Interpreting the predictions made by machine learning models is a critical task, particularly when working with autonomous decision-making systems. We have developed a novel explanation method, attributed partial dependence plots, that uncovers the individual contributions of key variables in forecasting outcomes. This approach uncovers unexpected interactions between variables and offers insights into their relative importance. We applied our framework to two cycling forecasting problems: a short-term prediction model based on the bike-sharing dataset, and a long-term forecasting system designed for high school sports competitions. By analyzing the results, our method revealed the complex effects of weather and time on bike-sharing forecasts, and revealed the non-linear impact of weather and team statistics on winning or losing a game. Many intriguing findings emerged from our analysis! For example, our results suggested that a team is more likely to win if more bikes are available, and that a forecast is more accurate when the model is predicting a loss. While these findings seem counterintuitive, they highlight the inherent challenges in interpreting predictions made by this forecasting system. Nonetheless, our attribute attribution curves provide valuable insights into the decision-making process and potential improvements to the system. For instance, our analysis suggested that incorporating game scores and bike availability could improve the accuracy of predictions, and that weather conditions have a greater impact on forecasts when fewer bikes are available. Furthermore, our results indicated that the impact of weather on winning or losing a game increases as the number of bikes available decreases, and that a long-term forecast is more accurate when the team has more bikes and the weather is bad. Based on these findings, our research recommends developing strategies to utilize bike and weather conditions effectively in high school sports competitions, and exploring the potential of using weather information to improve bike-sharing forecasts. In conclusion, our explanation method effectively uncovers the complex effects of variables on forecasting outcomes, and identifies areas for further investigation into the decision-making process. In the future, our framework could be applied to a wide range of machine learning models, and used to develop more sophisticated strategies that take into account the individual attributes of variables. For instance, we may be able to develop a forecasting system that automatically adjusts to weather conditions, or identify the optimal number of bikes required for a seamless sports experience. While our research focused on the intersection of machine learning and attribute engineering, our explanation method can be adapted to a broad range of applications, and used to uncover the complex effects of variables on decision-making outcomes. By applying our framework to real-world problems, we can gain a deeper understanding of the decision-making process, and develop strategies to effectively utilize attribute engineering

A major obstacle to widespread adoption of federated learning is securing private data during the training process. Existing solutions rely on the confidentiality of communication channels and local data encryption, but these methods are prone to privacy violations and inefficient gradient updates due to quantization errors. This can lead to suboptimal performance and prolonged training times. This paper proposes a new framework that addresses these challenges by utilizing homomorphic encryption, noisy gradient algorithms, and efficient quantization methods. We optimize the choice of homomorphic encryption scheme based on computational overhead, network traffic, and training efficiency. Additionally, we investigate different approaches to homomorphic encryption and evaluate their impact on performance, highlighting the trade-offs between privacy, efficiency, and accuracy. This framework can support efficient homomorphic training of large-scale neural networks with accurate results, although the time complexity is still higher than traditional federated learning methods. This framework can be a viable option when privacy is paramount, even at the expense of increased training time. With further research to improve the efficiency of homomorphic encryption, this method has the potential to become the standard approach to federated learning in high-stakes domains. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework, achieving a 94.8% accuracy after 200 epochs of training. Next steps involve applying this framework to real-world datasets and evaluating its performance on mobile and IoT edge devices. Moreover, we are exploring the integration of homomorphic learning with efficient mappings, efficient neural networks, and other new architectures. We also plan to establish a comprehensive benchmark to compare the performance of different homomorphic encryption schemes, efficient gradient updates, quantization methods, and other approaches in the future. By standardizing the evaluation of these techniques, we can identify the strengths and limitations of existing solutions and develop a comprehensive reference guide for researchers and practitioners. By addressing the current shortcomings of federated learning, we hope to contribute to the development of a more secure and efficient deep learning framework. Driving innovation in the automotive and industry sectors forward, the autonomous drive concept has emerged as a key idea - its success, however, hinges on the effectiveness of semi-autonomous driving systems. To evaluate the reliability of these systems, developers use simulation tools to replicate complex scenarios in a virtual environment. On the other hand, the growing popularity of the Internet of Things (IoT) is largely attributed to the proliferation of tiny, low-power microcontrollers that are relatively inexpensive. To ensure the quality of their products, microcontroller manufacturers need a robust testing environment that can efficiently process a high volume of tests. Currently, the available testing solutions fall short in this regard due to limitations in their capacity to handle a large number of tests per second. In an effort to address these challenges, we propose an innovative testing framework called DriverTest, which enables the development of a massive testing farm consisting of microcontrollers to process a huge number of tests in parallel. Our solution consists of three core components: a test driver running on a microcontroller, a test manager running on a host computer, and an database server also running on the host computer. The test driver is responsible for executing a test case, reporting results, and managing data while the test manager oversees the coordination of test drivers, handles data, and maintains a database. Our database server provides a connection to the database for the test manager to use. We implemented DriverTest using a typical configuration featuring a host computer connected to an Raspberry Pi 4 microcontroller via an USB cable. Our test driver is developed in C using the libusb library and our test manager is built with Python using the usbutil library. We ran a series of experiments to evaluate our solution and observed that our DriverTest can process a test case every 3.81 milliseconds - capable of handling up to 263,000 tests per second in a testing farm of 100 microcontrollers. Our study indicates that DriverTest offers a significantly higher testing capacity compared to existing solutions. Our work on DriverTest serves as a model for testing driver software on microcontrollers in general and our code is available for others to use in developing new test cases. In addition, our research in this area can be extended in various ways in the future. To the best of our knowledge, our study offers the first testing solution for microcontrollers that efficiently processes a huge number of tests in a parallel testing farm. Our work on DriverTest also serves as a model for testing driver software on microcontrollers in general. Our code and test cases are available at https://mc-os.github.io

Protecting applications from malicious libraries has been effectively addressed through various methods like exec wrappers and system call filtering.  However, there is a significant lack of research in protecting applications that utilize interpreted languages such as PHP and Python.  This paper introduces a novel solution called Timeloops, an ensemble of lightweight hooks that monitor and control critical system calls including process creation and file operations.  This system, which operates in kernel space, uses the Linux ftrace facility to efficiently sample the runtime behavior of malicious scripts at specified intervals.  By analyzing these snapshots, Timeloops can determine process execution states, identify file abnormalities, and block malicious process creation, thus preventing code injection and network communication.  This paper showcases the implementation details of Timeloops as well as its effectiveness in protecting against multiple script-based attacks.  Our experiments demonstrate that Timeloops successfully blocks file transmission and process creation in both PHP and Python, achieving a false positive rate of 0%.  This study highlights the potential of employing Timeloops as a secure default mechanism for scripts, which can be easily integrated into existing Linux distributions.  Furthermore, Timeloops's design can be adapted for other interpreted languages such as JavaScript and Ruby by incorporating corresponding system calls.  In conclusion, Timeloops offers an effective solution for securing applications written in interpreted languages by leveraging the cooperation of the OS and tracing frameworks to block malicious system calls, thus preventing the transmission of malicious files and code. Scientists investigating the dynamics of supermassive black holes in galaxies have long assumed the "hard-soft" hypothesis - that a distinct boundary exists in a star cluster surrounding a central black hole, separating harder, more rapidly moving stars from softer, less energetic ones. This concept was based on a specific model for how stars interact through gravitational forces, predicting a critical radius where stars are preferentially scattered towards the center due to differences in orbital energies. Through high-resolution simulations of a star cluster surrounding a 10,000 solar mass black hole, set in a galactic environment, our research aims to assess the validity of this hard-soft model. Our findings show that stars with a wide range of energies occupy a complex, anisotropically expanding zone around the black hole, primarily influenced by two mechanisms. Firstly, a diffuse threshold marks the boundary beyond which stars are preferentially drawn towards the center due to their varying orbital energies. Secondly, a distinct "clump" of highly energetic stars forms near the black hole, limited by its own mass and the potential for star-starring collisions. This clumping phenomenon is particularly significant, as it could historically explain the presence of dense star clusters surrounding supermassive black holes in galaxies hosting a central black hole. Conversely, the validity of the hard-soft hypothesis itself remains uncertain, as the boundary between hard and soft stars does not represent a critical radius that determines the behavior of stars interacting with a supermassive black hole in a cluster environment. Instead, the area surrounding a black hole is characterized by an uneven distribution of stars based solely on their distance from the black hole, with no clear distinction between 'hard' and'soft' based on their motion. As such, our research suggests that the assumption of a hard-soft boundary is not a necessary or essential component in understanding the dynamics of a star cluster surrounding a supermassive black hole. The theoretical framework for how stars interact through gravitational forces also predicts that a more uniform scattering pattern will occur over time, as the anisotropic expansion of a star cluster around a black hole continues to evolve. Ultimately, our findings emphasize the need for high-resolution simulations of a star cluster surrounding a central black hole to accurately understand the behavior of a star cluster in a dynamic environment. Such research could provide valuable insights into the process of a star cluster forming a supermassive black hole, as well as the potential for a star-starring collision in a cluster environment. This work investigates the practical application of stochastic Model Predictive Control (MPC) in systems affected by uncertainty. We introduce a modification to the conventional MPC framework, enabling the incorporation of uncertainty in both the system and the parameters it affects. This enhanced MPC considers the probability of each possible system outcome, refining the optimization process by incorporating those probabilities. However, calculating the probability of each state is often computationally intensive due to the need for repeated system simulations, leading to potentially time-consuming optimization processes. To mitigate these performance drawbacks, we develop an accelerated optimization algorithm, leveraging approximation techniques and strategic rescaling of the MPC cost function. This approach successfully trades off precision in the probability assessment with faster convergence, allowing the solution of complex optimization problems in a more expeditious manner. Experimental evaluations of our proposed method demonstrate its effectiveness in optimizing systems affected by uncertainty, including a quadcopter navigating uncertain environmental conditions and a robotic arm moving under uncertain gravitational forces. The evaluation showcases our algorithm's capacity to balance precise probability assessment with faster convergence, highlighting its potential for real-world application. This research has important implications for the implementation of stochastic MPC in systems affected by uncertainty. For instance, in control systems for drones, robots, vision systems, and artificial intelligence applications, where uncertainty often plays a key role, our method can be used to efficiently refine MPC with probability-based adjustments. Furthermore, the potential for adaptive stochastic MPC provides an important avenue for future research, potentially expanding the scope of our approach to additional domains. We have developed two novel algorithms for compressive ICA that outperform their non-compressed counterparts in both performance and efficiency. Our first algorithm adapts the fixed-point algorithm for sparse coding by incorporating an accurate estimation of the posterior distribution, utilizing all available data at once to minimize the influence of statistical fluctuations. This enables the algorithm to converge rapidly, particularly effective in large-scale experiments. Our second algorithm, a derivative of the gradient algorithm, utilizes the same posterior estimation as before, and this variant converges faster than its traditional counterpart.

Our experiments, conducted across multiple datasets including the Berkeley segments dataset and artificially generated data, demonstrate the exceptional performance of our algorithms. Notably, our compressive algorithms can achieve the same level of performance as their non-compressed counterparts using as little as 1% of the typical measurements required for traditional ICA algorithms. At the same time, our algorithms can reduce computational memory needs by half. Based on these findings, we recommend exploring the potential applications of our algorithms in large-scale independent component analysis projects. Our code is freely accessible on the GitHub platform. https://github.com/alexandremoreau/Compressive-ICA. The model's behavior was altered in an asymmetric version to allow for differences in the rates of local versus external influence. Research has demonstrated that in this asymmetric version, two species can compete on a network of a specific structure, known as a Cayley tree, under particular parameter settings. These algebras correspond to intersections of relative algebras under pure decoherence following a projective measurement. Our characterization organizes the von Neumann algebras associated with ground states into three categories, each corresponding to distinct symmetry conditions. These categories are (i) algebras generated by a single relative algebra under repeated decoherence in the absence of symmetries, (ii) algebras generated by the union of relative algebras when certain symmetries are present but decoherence does not reach the full algebra, and (iii) algebras generated by the union of relative algebras with complete decoherence and active symmetry. This classification enables us to identify distinct phases when symmetries emerge due to the failure of decoherence to reach the full algebra. The ability to correct errors arising from decoherence is a significant advantage of quantum systems that incorporate feedback loops into their operations. In this research, we investigate how the robustness of entanglement is affected when one part of a bipartite system undergoes a decoherence process, and the other part receives coherent feedback information. Our study reveals that, under certain conditions, coherent feedback can enhance the resistance of entanglement to decoherence, but only if the information transmitted in feedback remains coherent. In cases where the transmitted information is already affected by decoherence, it actually exacerbates the negative impact of decoherence on entanglement. Furthermore, the form of decoherence, either positional or momentum damping, does not affect the above conclusion. These findings are substantiated by numerical examples illustrating the trade-offs involved, and the potential for coherent feedback to either mitigate or exacerbate the effects of decoherence, depending on the system in question. In particular, we examine a system comprising two cavities connected by a coherent feedback loop, and demonstrate how its robustness can be affected by decoherence processes targeting momentum of the cavity fields. Our study provides a framework for the evaluation of decoherence in bipartite systems receiving coherent feedback, and offers insights into the potential for coherent feedback to either counteract or worsen the effects of decoherence. In view of future applications of quantum computing, we hope this research may contribute to a deeper understanding of the role of coherent feedback in error correction. In addition, this research may find relevance in the study of quantum teleportation, as it shares a common premise with that protocol - that information can be transferred from one system to another without physical interaction. In this context, we investigate how coherent feedback may be employed in quantum teleportation as a means of error correction, and explore its implications for the entanglement required in this process. In particular, we examine how coherent feedback may be used to correct errors arising from positional damping in a system employing quantum teleportation, and demonstrate the robustness of entanglement to momentum damping in a system undergoing momentum damping in one part, with coherent feedback in the other. with the rise of telework becoming a new normal due to the COVID-19 pandemic. 
As a result, researchers have found creative ways to operate remote and self-servicing laboratories safely, taking on a significant responsibility for experiment setup and execution. 
This has created a pressing need to automate complex experimental processes to minimize errors and ensure high-quality results. 
In this paper, a comprehensive study on the current state of experimental equipment and automation technologies used in remote-access laboratories is presented. 
A detailed analysis of various laboratories' capabilities and technologies was carried out, focusing on sectors such as computing, sensing, actuation, and data management.

This article offers a novel explanation for a recent breakthrough by Hein and Sato. We begin by identifying connections between two concepts: the undirected version of Gelfand--Graev multiplicity and the spectral class, and the existence of undirected bipartite graphs within a given graph.

We prove that the undirected bipartiteness condition is a necessary and sufficient constraint on the graph, as the unconstrained version of Hein and Sato's result aligns closely with Asser's original conjecture regarding the spectral class's behavior under direct sum operations.

Furthermore, we explore a generalization of the undirected bipartiteness condition, as well as extensions of the main theorem to derived functors of the Gelfand--Graev sheaf, all of which are crucial for a planned longer companion article. 

In that companion, we intend to delve into specific evaluations of undirected bipartite graphs, specifically focusing on the case of Cayley graphs of abelian groups, as well as the representation theory of quantum symmetric information complexes of abelian groups. 

It is also worth noting that the proposed content of the companion article is closely related to topics previously discussed on the arXiv by the second author (arXiv:2102.10546; arXiv:2108.08897; arXiv:2108.08900). 

In particular, the quantum symmetric information complexes of abelian groups were initially explored in arXiv:2102.10546, while evaluations of Cayley graphs of abelian groups can be found in arXiv:2108.08897; arXiv:2108.08900 actually discusses the undirected bipartiteness condition for these graphs but does not address quantum symmetric information complexes. 

Our current article seeks to integrate the content from these arXiv posts into a unified framework. 

In the process, we have chosen to prioritize undirected bipartiteness as the central condition, as the generated content seems to be more coherent and relevant under this constraint. 

Ultimately, the articles hope to provide insight into the undirected bipartiteness condition for graphs, as well as its implications for the quantum symmetric information models of abelian groups, thereby contributing to the representation theory of these models. 

The articles also aim to explore and examine the concept of undirected bipartiteness within graphs as a key framework, as this condition bears significant mathematical value and relevance.

Doped substrates made from graphene have unique properties of interacting one-dimensional fermions. These exchanges may lead to the formation of bound states known as Cooper pairs, resulting in novel physical phenomena. An investigation has been conducted to study the impact of these interactions within doped graphene, focusing specifically on the electronic structure, quasiparticle velocity, and specific heat. By employing a scaling technique near the point of quantum criticality, researchers found that the electronic structure is characterized by a linear relationship between energy and momentum, with a modified momentum scale that depends on the interaction strength. Consequently, the quasiparticle velocity is influenced by the interaction, while the specific heat exhibits a linear relationship with temperature, similar to that observed in non-interacting fermions. These findings indicate that the electronic structure of doped graphene can be described by scaling, resulting in universal behaviors dominated by momentum-scale divergence due to interactions. These scaling phenomena can be experimentally verified, offering insights into the effects of interactions on one-dimensional fermions and their bound states at low temperatures. Moreover, the results have implications for understanding other one-dimensional superconductors, such as those based on cuprates, carbon nanotubes, and Buckminster fullerenes. An important aspect is the potential for these systems to exhibit scaling and universal behavior similar to that observed in the hidden quantum critical point of cobalt pnictide compounds. Additionally, the research has explored the idea of a "smoothing" effect of the chiral anomaly on bound states at the intersection of the Fermi surface and a momentum scale determined by the interaction. These bound states may, however, be suppressed by the chiral anomaly at the scale of the Fermi momentum, as observed in the outcomes of numerical simulations of the RPA. Nonetheless, the contribution of the chiral anomaly remains a topic that requires further investigation. Moreover, the results have revealed that the quasiparticle velocity is influenced by the interaction, while the specific heat remains unaffected in the presence of strong momentum-dependent interactions. However, for weak momentum-dependent interactions, the bound states may be suppressed, resulting in a quasiparticle velocity that approaches the velocity expected in the absence of interactions, with the specific heat remaining linearly dependent on temperature. These findings have implications for understanding the electronic structure, quasiparticle velocity, and specific heat in the presence of weak momentum-dependent interactions. The quality of text-to-speech systems greatly depends on the effectiveness of the speech localization, which identifies the pitch and duration of phonemes. Many contemporary localization systems employ a Fourier series-based method, however this leads to a smoothed appearance of the waveform, ultimately affecting the naturalness and expressiveness of the synthesized speech. Our proposed MaskedSpeech system addresses this issue by utilizing a mask-based approach in conjunction with a long short-term memory (LSTM) network, enabling more precise phoneme localization. Specifically, our experiment demonstrates that replacing the conventional waveform-based localization target with the output of the MaskedSpeech system, fed through a waveform generator, results in a significant improvement in the synthesized speech quality as measured by the mean opinion score (MOS). We observed an enhancement of 0.15 MOS and a corresponding reduction in the computation time by a factor of 4 when using the MaskedSpeech output to target phoneme localization, thereby showcasing its efficacy in producing more natural speech with increased expressiveness. Notably, the MaskedSpeech system exhibits better performance when integrating adjacent phonemes, allowing for a more seamless and engaging listening experience. Our proposed method also facilitates the generation of more realistic unbounded phoneme durations by feeding normalized localization targets into an LSTM network, thereby surpassing the performance of the baseline dataset. Furthermore, the MaskedSpeech system displays robust generalization capabilities across diverse speech datasets, as evidenced by our cross-corpus evaluation. To further enhance the efficiency of the MaskedSpeech system, we replaced the LSTM with a transformer and optimized several hyperparameters via a grid search, thereby achieving a remarkable 2x speedup while maintaining improved speech quality. Our comprehensive analysis and visualization of the synthesized speech waveform, accompanied by the target phoneme durations, provide valuable insights into the speech patterns, enabling future improvements to the text-to-speech system. Ultimately, the MaskedSpeech system has the potential to be integrated with various Distinctive Source Separation algorithms for enhanced performance. We introduce a novel Bayesian approach that maintains the accuracy of the original model's posterior uncertainties while performing variable selection in high-dimensional regression. The original model's posterior distribution is initially approximated by an amygdalan Gibbs sampler, which is then adapted into various sub-spaces defined by differential inclusion/exclusion in a new Bayesian variable selection framework, KBayesVS. This paper compares the career outcomes of higher education fields of study in Norway and Denmark by analyzing survey data from recent graduates. Both countries'systems share similarities, such as free tuition and publicly funded employment, yet differ in key aspects, including how education and job opportunities are linked. In Norway, the government plays a prominent role in matching graduates with jobs, whereas Denmark's system emphasizes individual choice in the job market. Our findings reveal significant variations in earnings potential between different fields of study in both countries, with Norwegian graduates experiencing a broader range of outcomes. However, when we control for factors like field of study and graduate age, Norwegian and Danish graduates exhibit similar levels of job satisfaction. Interestingly, Norwegian graduates tend to be more satisfied with their education and employment, whereas Danish graduates tend to be happier with their social lives and income. Ultimately, our research suggests both countries'systems have strengths and weaknesses, and our findings contribute to the ongoing discussion on how to balance structure and individual choice in the transition from education to employment.
