Research on two-dimensional materials has intensified due to their unique properties, with particular focus on van der Waals compounds that can be produced in large quantities through mechanical exfoliation and transfer. Despite the significance of electron-phonon interactions in these materials, particularly in their quantum Hall phases, a thorough examination of such interactions has been limited due to complexity and cost. Studies focusing on hydrogenated monolayers are even more underrepresented, which raises interest in investigating the effect of a hydrogen surface on electron-phonon interactions within these structures. By utilizing density functional theory with the inclusion of van der Waals forces, this work explores the structure, phonon properties, and electron-phonon interactions of HHB2 and HHHB4, two-dimensional hydrogen boride monolayers compared to their dehydrogenated counterparts, HHB2 and HHHB4. The outcomes indicate that the presence of hydrogen significantly influences the electron-phonon interactions in these monolayers, with the effect size being in the order of meV. The unique property of these materials, related to their dehydrogenated counterparts, stems from changes in electron density near the Fermi level caused by the interaction between hydrogen and electrons. This research addresses the crucial issue of removing foreground contamination from cosmic microwave background (CMB) maps in order to accurately model its impact and make precise CMB estimators by adjusting for key systematic effects. We develop a realistic simulation tool that recreates the Spherical Harmonic coefficients of CMB and foreground maps based on their actual power spectra. The code generates 'observed' maps by combining CMB and foreground power spectra, along with simulated noise, using the HEALPix library. These maps are then used to estimate CMB estimators that are affected by foreground contamination and noise. By iteratively refining the CMB estimators using a maximum likelihood approach, we are able to accurately remove foreground contamination and effectively eliminate biases. Notably, we find that the commonly used maximum likelihood approach can be vulnerable to noise when the signal-to-noise ratio is low. As an alternative, we suggest a more robust method based on a hierarchical Bayesian approach that is capable of providing more accurate CMB estimators even in the presence of low signal-to-noise ratios. We find that the hierarchical Bayesian approach yields a 25% improvement in estimation accuracy compared to the standard maximum likelihood technique. Moreover, we find that the estimated parameters are consistent when measured from the 'observed' maps or through a hierarchical Bayesian reconstruction of the CMB and foreground maps. We find that the parameters estimated from the foreground-reconstructed maps are 15% more precise than those estimated directly from the 'observed' maps. Notably, we find that the hierarchical Bayesian approach provides the most precise CMB estimators when the foreground contamination is greatest. As a byproduct, we find that the hierarchical Bayesian technique is highly effective in recovering the power spectrum of foreground contamination. We find that the precision of the recovered power spectrum is independent of angular frequency and that the hierarchical Bayesian method can achieve a 50% reduction in estimation error compared to existing methods. We believe that the proposed hierarchical Bayesian technique will play a significant role in the precise estimation of CMB estimators that are affected by foreground contamination in cosmic microwave background maps.}

In context-aware recommender systems, external context data enhances item recommendations by leveraging intimate user-item relationships. However, commonly used methods are limited when data is sparse. This paper addresses the challenge by applying document modeling to enhance recommating systems. This approach represents each item as a combination of its own features and the context of its associated users. Although it offers improved performance, it suffers from significant computational overhead. This paper proposes an optimized model-based approach, Variational Neural Document Model (VNDM), based on neural networks, to improve the efficiency and scalability of document modeling. The VNDM variant efficiently balances fast inference and lower training complexity while outperforming existing methods in multiple benchmark datasets. Results show the VNDM variant performs on par with or better than leading recommender systems across multiple evaluation metrics. The source code is available at https://github.com/krishanshs/vndm.

Traditional monitoring strategies in real-time systems rely on predetermined schedules.
However, such schedules are not adaptable to unexpected timing variations, which are inevitable in complex systems.
Therefore, we propose an adaptive monitoring strategy, developed within a framework that makes minimal assumptions about system behavior and performance goals.
Specifically, our approach ensures that each real-time task is protected from interference by other tasks, by incorporating an adaptive monitoring policy based on event observation.
This novel method involves maintaining a consistent level of interference protection across all possible system scenarios, by incorporating both task execution rates and uncertainty factors into its decision-making process.
Our monitoring strategy is designed to be self-contained, with both off-line and on-line components, and can be applied automatically using existing techniques from the model checking domain.
Furthermore, we have investigated the effectiveness of our proposed strategy through both theoretical analysis and practical case studies. The integration of this adaptive monitoring strategy with existing real-time operating systems, such as Linux, is also described in detail. Experimental results confirm the feasibility and effectiveness of our proposed strategy in scenarios involving unpredictable load conditions. The performance benefits of our adaptive monitoring strategy over traditional scheduling policies have also been documented in terms of system processing time efficiency. More specifically, we have found that under heavy load conditions, our adaptive approach can achieve up to a 300% improvement in comparison to a widely used fixed sampling policy. Furthermore, when tasks experience periodic pauses in execution, our adaptive approach can achieve an average improvement of up to 120% over the fixed sampling policy. The source code underlying our proposed adaptive monitoring strategy is freely available online at https://git.rwth-idash.de/adaptive-monitoring/-/tree/master/AIM. Additional information, including video recordings of our experimental results, can be found at https://www.youtube.com/playlist_list?list=PL1I8M2hqN7RCf6K0T9tX9YRt7Q9Q9Q9Q. The presentation slides and research papers related to our proposed strategy can be accessed via https://git.rwth-idash.de/adaptive-monitoring/-/tree/master/AIM#Presentation-Slides. The following research papers are also recommended for further reading: "Event Observation for Real-Time Systems" and "Adaptive Real-Time Monitoring: A Model Checking Approach". Both papers are available online at https://www.researchgate.com/publication/344844111_Event_Observation_for_Real-Time_Systems. The GRAVITY beam combiner, part of the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI), allows the GRAVIBILITY Wide Field (GWWF) mode to access multiple fields within a single observation. To optimize GRAVITY's operational efficiency, a strategy was developed to utilize the instrument's parameters obtained from the reference acquisition camera. This approach involves selecting suitable sampling rates, stabilization parameters, and a specific focus mode to facilitate seamless data sampling at 1024 Hz. To validate the proposed configuration, a theoretical analysis was conducted and compared to the results obtained from on-sky data. The chosen parameters enabled successful implementation of the GWWF mode with a sampling rate of 1024 Hz for all four fields. The combination of these parameters allowed the GRAVITY instrument to effectively sample the fields without introducing artificial correlations, as confirmed by the Fourier Transform of the visibility data. This configuration has become the standard setting for the GWWF mode. Regular use of this configuration has demonstrated a significant increase in the operational efficiency of the GWWF mode, allowing the GRAVITY instrument to effectively sample multiple fields within a single observation. This improvement has paved the way for future upgrades, such as utilizing multiple GRAVITY Wide Field (GWF) configurations with up to five fields. The current implementation serves as a solid foundation for exploiting the full potential of the GRAVITY Wide Field mode. The Capacitated k-Center problem involves locating a fixed number of facilities to serve the majority of clients with their assigned facility assignments, given a set of clients and their distances to potential facilities. The Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem, a modification of the Capacitated k-Center, requires us to find the set of clients to be served by assigning the remaining clients to the nearest facility. Research has shown that the Capacitated k-Center can be approximated within a factor of $\Omega(\log^3 h)/(\log \hspace{0.05cm}h)$ for a given "highway dimension" $h$. However, we found that the approximability of the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers is significantly higher and can be approximated within a factor of $\frac{h+1}{h}$, a better estimate than the Capacitated k-Center problem. To differentiate between these problems under a fixed "highway dimension", we proposed modifying the Double Tree metric closure concept and proved that its modification has a "highway dimension" $h+1$. Furthermore, we proved that reducing the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers to the modified Double Tree metric closure results in a linear transformation requiring facility upgrades, a process we term "highway dimension" increase. Research has shown that solving the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers on modified Double Tree metric closure yields an approximation within a factor of $\frac{h+1}{h}$. Combining these discoveries, we confirmed the existence of a constant $c$ such that solving the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers results in an approximation within a factor of $c \cdot (\log h)/ (\log \hspace{0.05cm}h)$ for a given "highway dimension" $h$. Additionally, we provided an exact algorithm for the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers on metric trees with a runtime of $2^{O(\log^2 h/\log \hspace{0.05cm}h)}$. A key challenge in solving the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers lies in its unbounded growth of client assignments due to the potential for facility upgrades, a growth outpaced by previous methods that relied on predetermined sets of clients. To address this issue, we developed a dynamic programming approach for the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers on metric trees with an exponential runtime of $2^{O(\log^2 h/\log \hspace{0.05cm}h})

A fundamental problem in computational algebraic geometry involves solving a linear system defined by a polynomial over a finite field, given some noise or error. We can interpret this as finding a zero in a hypersurface defined by a polynomial, affected by random perturbations. A significant step in this process involves identifying the perturbed hypersurface, which can be represented by a set of points on a curve. We propose an algorithm to reduce the number of evaluations needed to identify this curve, taking into account that evaluations are costly due to the need to compute a polynomial at each point. This algorithm estimates the parameters of the curve using a simplified model and iteratively refines it, and we provide analytical and experimental evidence of its effectiveness. This improved method results in a significant speed-up for systems of high degree and several variables, particularly in the presence of high-level noise. Our findings have implications for solving linear systems over finite fields under uncertain conditions. Additionally, this work can be adapted to other applications where evaluating polynomials is a costly step in an algorithm. We suggest a method to produce controlled, multi-photon emissions of both even and odd combinations through rapid switching of the cavity QED system. The rapid change can be achieved using a variable diaphragm in the cavity setup. This approach involves tracking a specific atomic state population in real-time via florescence measurement. The emission of both odd and even photons can be explained by considering the correlated photon groups as quanta of the cavity field, with the switch introducing non-unitary interactions that lead to the elimination of traditional Fock states. The characteristics of vector mesons in a local parity breaking environment with a Chern-Simons term are investigated. The study relies on a gauge invariant quantum field theory framework, resolving issues related to causality and unitarity. It is demonstrated that the vector meson propagator remains causal and unitary, even in the presence of a parity breaking factor. The local medium's influence introduces an effective momentum dependent four fermion interaction, which is analogous to that generated by the 't Hooft interaction in quantum chromodynamics. The study also explores the massive vector meson propagator in a local medium, identifying two distinct momentum dependent poles representing transverse and longitudinal polarizations. The longitudinal massive vector meson propagator is expressed in invariant momentum space and transformed into the Jalilian-Marian-Iancu-McLerran-Weigert-Leonidov-Kovner (JIMWLK) basis. The longitudinal massive vector meson propagator can serve as a boundary condition for solving the non-linear balance equation governing the probability distribution of color field strength in a local medium. The Chern-Simons term ensures that the balance equation's evolution kernel remains hermitian even in a local medium. The findings presented can be extended to study properties of rho mesons under extreme conditions. The research has applications in understanding properties of vector mesons in diverse settings such as heavy ion collisions at RHIC/BELLE and QCD-like systems at the LHC. Furthermore, it can contribute to the development of novel quantum technologies by incorporating non-local gauge invariant quantum field theories. The study paves the way for investigating properties of vector bosons in a non-local medium within a quantum field theory framework. The research can be expanded to study vector boson propagation in non-local media with multiple gauge bosons, as well as the interactions of scalar bosons within similar contexts. The findings presented can be used in high energy physics research, such as studying the propagation of a Higgs boson in a non-local medium as a prelude to a new energy collider. Additionally, it can provide a solid theoretical foundation for the research of non-local gauge invariant quantum field theories and the development of novel quantum technologies. The research can be extended by incorporating non-local gauge invariant quantum field theories into the Standard Model of particle physics and the QCD sector of the theory, with implications for the development of quantum technologies. The study has significant implications in understanding the behavior of vector bosons in extreme conditions of various systems, from quark-gluon plasma to cold atoms and quantum fluids

The Informer model has recently demonstrated remarkable results in large-scale time series forecasting, outperforming conventional LSTM and Transformer-based models by capturing long-term dependencies in time series data. However, these models have primarily focused on single-dimensional predictions, without considering the intricate relationships between multiple dimensions that often exist in multidimensional data. In this work, we introduce an improved Informer model that can be scaled up for predicting complex, multi-dimensional time series in various fields like finance, healthcare, and climate change. By integrating a multi-head attention mechanism into the Informer encoder, our enhanced model enables the capture of cross-dimensional relationships and can be efficiently decoded using a multi-dimensional fully attentional decoder. Experimental evaluations on multiple multi-dimensional time series datasets reveal that our proposed model consistently surpasses state-of-the-art methods in forecasting performance. Furthermore, we conduct ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of each proposed module and perform thorough hyper-parameter tuning to confirm the reliability of our experimental results. Notably, our multi-dimensional Informer model achieves impressive relative improvements of 14.3%, 33.3%, and 9.3% over the best baseline methods on the CMAPD, S\&P500, and COVID-19 datasets, respectively. Researchers use various models to correct for atmospheric dispersion, but some models are ineffective under certain conditions. We evaluated the accuracy of five atmospheric dispersion models, comparing them to the standard Herschel Optical Headroom System, in order to identify a better alternative. Specifically, we found that the CFHT Atmospheric Dispersion Model, which is commonly employed at the Mauna Kea Observatories, provides sub-pixel accuracy but is not recommended for use in ADC designs due to its significant errors in the blue spectrum. In contrast, the VLT Atmospheric Dispersion Model provided a high level of correction with a mean error of 0.13 arcseconds, but it is computationally intensive and not suitable for use in time-critical applications. We found that the TNG Atmospheric Dispider Model, although computationally efficient, yielded a mean error of 0.33 arcseconds. In contrast, the NTT Atmospheric Dispersion Model demonstrated a mean error of 0.17 arcseconds. Ultimately, we recommend using the VLT Atmospheric Dispersion Model, despite its computational drawbacks, due to its superior performance and accuracy. In the future, we plan to utilize machine learning to develop a more efficient and accurate atmospheric dispersion model. Such a model will be particularly beneficial if it can be integrated into a real-time software system. In this context, we also discuss potential integration strategies and the potential impact on system performance. As a preliminary step, we explored the possibility of incorporating a machine learning-based atmospheric dispersion model into the HOSYS, in order to determine its feasibility and computational effects. We found that incorporating such a model into the HOSYS would not significantly impact its computational performance. As a result, we are planning to incorporate a machine learning-based atmospheric dispersion model into the HOSYS in the future. In conclusion, we have identified the need for a more efficient and accurate atmospheric dispersion model, and we have outlined a plan for its development and integration into the HOSYS. We introduce Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), an ensemble method that utilizes label information to create an order among class predictions by adjusting class logits iteratively. PILE addresses the challenge of predicting probabilities from uncalibrated models and we demonstrate its effectiveness on multiple datasets, including CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, in combination with ResNet-50, showing improvements of 0.8% and 0.6% in top-1 accuracy respectively. Notably, PILE outperforms temperature scaling with minimal computational resources. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/alecjp/PILE. 

In our analysis, we reveal that PILE's performance gains stem from its ability to leverage label information effectively, while its lightweight design makes it suitable for deployment on mobile devices. We also show that PILE's convergence is relatively fast, with most of its improvement occurring within the initial 10 iterations. 

We believe PILE presents an attractive solution for enhancing the reliability of vision models that balance computational complexity and accuracy concerns evenly.

We anticipate that the placement of these sensors around the Earth can significantly reduce uncertainty associated with the fluctuations within the Earth's gravitational field, thereby providing clearer evidence of dark matter. We estimate that the necessary sensor sensitivity can be achieved with technology available within the next 5-year timeframe, making this proposal a viable option for the near future. To facilitate this analysis, we introduce a family of random matrices whose row spaces exhibit distinct eigenvalue distributions, and derive conditions under which these matrices yield sparse solutions with high probability. Notably, our findings apply to matrices with columns that have independent, uniformly distributed angles with respect to the matrix rows, a condition commonly met. Moreover, our work demonstrates that the desired sparsity properties can be achieved even when the number of non-zero coefficients in the solution vector exceeds the expected count, a phenomenon we attribute to the presence of over-complete dictionaries composed of linearly independent columns. To illustrate the validity of our model, we perform experiments using basis pursuit deconvolution and obtain results consistent with the patterns predicted by our theoretical analysis. Ultimately, our study highlights the significance of the eigenvalue spectrum in the row space of a matrix for obtaining sparse solutions, a crucial insight with potential applications in signal processing and related fields. hinders many aspects of this research. Existing works often rely on using drivers
for the target platforms, but this comes with limitations, such as restricted
access to hardware resources and limited knowledge of switch patterns.
Additionally, understanding the specificity of each platform requires in-depth
knowledge and can be very time-consuming.  We propose OpenSwitch, a user-friendly
library providing a common API for developing novel programmable switch
architectures, such as data switches, computation switches, and combined
switches. OpenSwitch offers a range of features, including different memory
management systems, diverse input processing mechanisms, and support for
customized memory handlers.  To evaluate the performance and versatility of our
library, we utilized a combination of compiler-based approaches and manual code
insertions to develop multiple examples of programmable switches, such as a memory
block that could operate independently on GPUs without the need for CPU

a demonstration of using OpenSwitch on an FPGA. OpenSwitch is currently
available online at https://cfs.rice.edu/oswitch.  We are seeking feedback from

Addressing fairness, fluency, and federated learning with differential privacy are key to addressing machine learning's long-standing ethical concerns. However, combining these techniques is complex due to their incompatible nature - fairness metrics require access to central dataset statistics, federated learning operates on decentralized data, and differential privacy introduces noise that renders metrics inaccurate. Our novel FairFedDP framework addresses this challenge by designing a combination of utilitarian and Kantian fairness approaches, compatible with differential privacy and adapted for federated learning settings. Our framework consists of two modules: adapter and aggregator. The adapter modifies local models by adding a fairness-enhancing mechanism, while the aggregator uses a combination of utilitarian and Kantian metrics, leveraged from a global dataset with permission, and applies differential privacy to conceal sensitive information. Our framework is implemented with state-of-the-art fairness metrics such as Maximum Norm Utilitarian Fairness and Kantian Fairness, and our experiments using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of FairFedDP in achieving both utilitarian and Kantian fairness under a differential privacy setting. Our results show the superiority of FairFedDP over existing approaches such as FedAvg and Meta-Fair FedAvg, and our contribution represents a pioneering effort in combining fairness, privacy, and federated learning. We explore how continuous-stage Runge-Kutta theory can be applied to Hamiltonian systems, leveraging neural networks as analytical solutions. By adopting neural networks as vector fields, we can generalize traditional Runge-Kutta schemes, ultimately constructing explicit numerical solutions to Hamiltonian problems. Our approach allows for the generation of efficient numerical integrators for polynomial Hamiltonian systems, surpassing traditional methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, even when starting with precise initial conditions and relatively few stages. Furthermore, our neural network-based solution can be paired with conventional Runge-Kutta schemes, blending traditional and modern integrator methods. Moreover, we examine the implications of our findings on symplectic integrators, exploring potential avenues for improvement. Our research demonstrates the immense potential of continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods, particularly those developed using neural networks. Moreover, our theoretical findings are reinforced by additional numerical tests, found in the accompanying appendix. Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent Neural Networks are commonly used in various machine learning applications. Due to their inherent efficiency in processing data with spatial or temporal relationships, they are frequently employed in image recognition, video analysis, natural language processing, and other domains. The success of these networks, particularly in tasks like object recognition, where a fully connected layer is often the final component, can be attributed to their ability to effectively learn features from data. In this research, we introduce an innovative technique called Local Critic Training (LCT), a two-phase training method. First, a pre-trained network, equipped with a local critic module, is trained in a self-supervised manner by optimizing a contrastive loss function that promotes discrimination between genuine and fake data samples. This process enhances the network's ability to extract robust, transferable features from the input data. In the second phase, the pre-trained network is fine-tuned using a conventional task-specific loss function, a process facilitated by the elevated feature quality produced by LCT. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of LCT when applied to Convolutional and Recurrent Neural Networks, as evidenced by enhanced performance on the CIFAR-10 and RNN-based language modeling on the Penn Treebank dataset. Notably, the improved accuracy achieved through LCT counterbalances a 30% reduction in model parameters, underscoring its efficiency and versatility. Moreover, the anticipated data from PRISM will enable the exploration of novel physics signatures, such as the appearance of long-range photon-muon jets or photon-photon jets accompanied by a muon, provided that the decay width remains narrow enough. Ultimately, the findings from PRISM are likely to yield significant insights into new physics theories. Human Action Recognition, a key problem in computer vision, requires precise identification of spatio-temporal atomic parts from video frames and their incorporation into a global model for classification. The Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) addresses this challenge by leveraging a hierarchical attention mechanism that reverses-gradients through multiple layers, enabling the exploration of relevant parts in video frames and their semantic features. This mechanism is comprised of three components: intermediate attention, pooling attention, and class attention. The intermediate attention focuses on extracting spatial features from single frames, pooling attention combines multiple frame features into a single representation, and class attention selects class-dependent video segments for classification. The HAN's reverse-gradients pathway enables learning of high-level features from supervisory signals. The HAN's ability to capture the intent behind multiple steps in time, along with its ability to reverse-gradients for pre-trained models, is key to its performance. The HAN achieves state-of-the-art performance on action recognition datasets such as Mini-Kinetics, Mini-Charades, and Breakfast, outperforming previous methods by significant margins. The process of star formation (SF) in molecular clouds holds significant potential to reveal the cosmos' abiogenic roots, i.e., how life arises from non-living materials. However,, star formation is a relatively rare event in galaxies, especially during the early stages of the universe, and it is difficult to observe and understand its detailed processes. To address this challenge, we conducted a comprehensive study of the formation of a massive galaxy named HD4-7170, based on extensive data collected from the CO, radio continuum, and stellar spectra. This data set allows us to examine the formation of SF in massive galaxies at a redshift of 4.7, and we are able to identify distinct components, including a central massive galaxy and numerous smaller systems surrounding it. Notably, we detected 13 clumps with enhanced CO emission, and found that most of these clumps are rotating in the same direction as the galaxy, and exhibit exponential dust distributions similar to disk systems. Analysis of stellar formation rates in these clumps reveals that they are comparable to those of similar objects at higher redshifts. Furthermore, we found a strong positive correlation between stellar formation rates and gas density, and propose a framework to describe the formation of galaxies through the continuous growth of SF clumps, and the absorption of smaller systems by the central galaxy. This research provides new insights into the formation of galaxies in the early universe, and the process of star formation in massive galaxies. Moreover, our findings offer a unique perspective on the development of life in the universe, and its potential origins from non-living materials. Based on this, we propose a cosmic scenario in which the formation of SF clumps, and the accumulation of mass in galaxies, are inextricably linked to the development of life and complexity in the universe. This celestial chemistry, driven by starlight and planetary illumination, gives rise to the diverse forms of life that populate the cosmos, and ultimately to the emergence of intelligence and civilization. This, in turn, sets the stage for the vast proliferation of life in the universe, and the increasing complexity of celestial communities throughout cosmic history. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the universe, and our place within it, in the ongoing quest for life's origins in the cosmos. To effectively protect Internet of Things devices from impending attacks, it is crucial to have a reliable attack classifier deployed directly on these devices. However, creating such a classifier poses a complex challenge due to limited device resources. In response to this, we developed the NBcoded tool, a lightweight, efficient, automatic classifier construction system tailored for IoT devices. NBcoded overcomes the limitations of existing solutions through its efficient construction of large code classifiers using a compressed neural network approach and a specialized encoding scheme, thereby allowing it to effectively run on resource-constrained devices. We thoroughly evaluated NBcoded and found that it surpasses existing solutions in terms of accuracy, model size, and inference speed, showcasing its potential as a pioneering solution for IoT security classification. Specifically, NBcoded outperformed the second-best classifier in reducing classification time by up to 7.3 times, model size by up to 6.04 times, and model compression time by up to 3.17 times, while maintaining superior classification accuracy compared to the Coded-NN and Coded-CNN methods, particularly in scenarios where memory was a limiting factor. For instance, NBcoded excelled on the TinyFog IoT Emulator in scenarios where 50% of the traffic was generated, achieving an average of 96.88% accuracy, compared to 96.23% for the Coded-NN method and 95.67% for the Coded-CNN method. Furthermore, NBcoded demonstrated adaptability across a variety of IoT devices by effectively classifying attacks on devices such as the Raspberry Pi 4 and Qualcomm Snapdragon 820, as well as in fog computing environments, showcasing its broad applicability and potential as a pioneering solution for IoT security classification. Efficient power network reconfiguration plays a significant role in maximizing power system efficiency. This research explores the application of hybrid quantum approaches to solve the generation unit capacity of reconfigured network problem. By utilizing mixed integer programming with electrical power flows, we evaluated the performance of both classical and hybrid quantum computers in solving large-scale partitioning problems. Our results indicate that under specific large-scale network conditions, hybrid quantum methods exhibit superior performance in comparison to classical techniques, specifically for larger numbers of electrical nodes. Furthermore, we analyze the potential future developments of hybrid quantum computing technology, anticipating improvements in performance and efficiency with advancing technology. It is anticipated that future hybrid systems featuring over 50 functional basic units will experience enhanced performance, ultimately making hybrid quantum computing an even more effective technology.

The origin of extreme damping observed in certain solid materials has been a subject of debate. A recent idea proposing that this is a result of the Peierls mechanism, where high-frequency optical modes mask the transmission of sound waves, needs to be reconsidered because this theory cannot account for the case of PbF1.17(Te0.83) where the damping of longitudinal sound waves increases at low frequencies, not high. This contradiction can be resolved by introducing a soft potential model, proposing that the long-wavelength displacement of atoms creates a gentle potential between them, causing the transmission of sound to be attenuated. This idea successfully explains the observed damping phenomena in PbF1.17(Te0.83) and PbTe, as well as the anisotropy in PbTe, without conflicting with existing data regarding thermal conductivity. Furthermore, this model can potentially be applied to other materials with naturally soft potential characteristics. Conversely, materials with a flat density-of-states curve, such as Si, have a hard potential and exhibit undampened sound waves, consistent with existing findings. Multi-objective optimization (MOO) aims to minimize or maximize multiple objective functions, while multimodal optimization (MMO) seeks to find multiple optimal solutions with similar function values. Despite these distinct definitions, most MMO algorithms can be transformed into TMOO methods that leverage local selection, reducing diversity's impact and often yielding fitter but fewer viable solutions. Our research introduces $\text{M$\mu$O}_{\text{LS}}$, an MMo algorithm that employs a delimiting strategy to prevent the over-suppression of diversity, allowing multiple near-optimal solutions to exist. We also present $\text{M$\mu$O}_{\text{LS}}$'s equivalence to an existing TMOO algorithm in the literature, along with empirical evidence of its effectiveness and efficiency. Interestingly, $\text{M$\mu$O}_{\text{LS}}$ produces a wide variety of diverse solutions while also achieving better fitness levels than its TMOO counterpart. We observed that $\text{M$\mu$O}_{\text{LS}}$'s unique characteristics facilitate the discovery of numerous candidate solutions in its population, leading to notable improvements in fitness and diversity. Our research indicates that even though most MMO algorithms can be classified as TMOO methods, our delimiting strategy allows $\text{M$\mu$O}_{\text{LS}}$ to excel in both diversity and fitness, making it a valuable addition to the MMO algorithm repertoire. We also present theoretical evidence to confirm that our delimiting strategy does not compromise the diversity-enhancing properties of $\text{M$\mu$O}_{\text{LS}}$. Based on our empirical results and theoretical analysis, we propose $\text{M$\mu$O}_{\text{LS}}$ as an effective and efficient MMo algorithm that outperforms its TMOO counterpart in diversity and fitness, along with a range of other promising MMO algorithms. Our research highlights the value of analyzing the underlying mathematical properties of optimization algorithms to ensure their correctness and efficiency. Ultimately, our research contributes five innovative MMo algorithms, along with six TMOO algorithms derived from existing MMO methods, providing a valuable resource for researchers in the field. Our research also provides a useful reference for researchers who aim to develop their own MMo algorithms, showcasing the potential benefits of combining diverse archiving strategies with local selection. Research on valley Hall effect transport is relatively underrepresented when compared to the extensive literature on the valley Hall effect itself. This underrepresentation is likely due to the fact that nonuniform strain significantly complicates the analysis. This complication can be overcome by employing Monte Carlo simulations that account for the random variations in strain. These simulations demonstrate that valley transport exhibiting valley Hall behavior is possible only when the strain's variability is weakly correlated with the electric field. Additionally, the valley Hall conductivity is found to be sensitive to the average strain rate, whereas the valley transconductance is sensitive to the root mean square of the strain rate. Furthermore, our findings suggest that valley transport can be optimized by adjusting the dopant distribution within the gate. Specifically, our results indicate that a uniform dopant distribution yields the optimal results. Finally, our work reveals that valley Hall transport is more robust in systems where the conduction band is parabolically shaped due to higher effective valley masses. On the other hand, the conductance is maximized in systems where the valence band is shaped parabolically due to higher effective valley masses. To efficiently correct errors in quantum computing, various decoding strategies can be employed depending on the specific method used. For low error rates, a basic approach suffices, but as the error rate increases, more advanced techniques become necessary. However, developing these techniques requires significant time and effort. We propose using reinforcement learning to automate the development of effective decoding strategies for various error rates. By employing a agent-based approach, the reinforcement learning system searches for an optimal decoding strategy given a specific error pattern and rate. Our results show that this method can achieve better performance, especially at higher error rates, and requires significantly less time to train than traditional methods. Due to the diversity of possible error patterns during runtime, the reinforcement learning system was designed to adapt quickly to new scenarios. We observe that the strategies learned through reinforcement learning often correspond to known methods used in standard decoding processes. This approach offers promising prospects for applying reinforcement learning to other challenging problems. Furthermore, the quantum information contained in the decoding strategies poses a significant challenge and reduces the overall success rate. We anticipate that future advancements in quantum computing will substantially improve these outcomes. To achieve this goal, we suggest developing enhanced training programs that leverage multiple error patterns and implement a waiting period to gather more information before making decisions. Our research indicates that the potential for applying reinforcement learning to other challenging tasks is substantial. The E97000 collaboration conducted a $189$ to $217~\text{GeV}/\text{nucleon}$ Au$+$Au experiment at RHIC using a $3~\text{cm}$ thin gold target, backward lead target, and various detector sets. The study employed a geometrically defined region of interest to identify the full range of on-going events, focusing on how the momentum fraction of quarks influences hadron yields in Au$+$Au collisions. The investigation revealed an increased yield of non-triggering hadrons with lower momentum and a significant production of hadrons below $1~\text{GeV}/c$ in Au$+$Au collisions, especially for quarks with a momentum fraction less than $0.1~\text{GeV}/c$. The study also discovered an increased total number of non-triggering charged particles by a factor of $2.3\pm0.2$ and $1.7\pm0.2$ for $200~\text{GeV}/\text{nucleon}$ and $292~\text{GeV}/\text{nucleon}$ respectively, in Au$+$Au collisions, while observing no such enhancement in $p+$$p$ collisions. The observed increase in hadron yields is consistent with quark re-scattering and does not contradict the notion of quark liberation in Au$+$Au collisions. The study further revealed that $200~\text{GeV}/\text{nucleon}$ and $292~\text{GeV}/\text{nucleon}$ $p+$$p$ collisions yield similar hadron production. Additionally, the investigation explored the relationship between quark and hadron momentum fractions and found that the hadron $p/Q$ is generally $5$ to $10$ times greater than the quark $p/Q$, while also observing that hadron $p/Q$ depends on event multiplicity. The study also examined the transverse momentum distribution of non-triggering hadrons in Au$+$Au and $p+$$p$ collisions, revealing a geometrically defined relationship between quark and hadron transverse momentum and demonstrating that hadron $p_T$ depends on event multiplicity. Ultimately, the investigation provides novel insights into the interplay between quark and hadron physics in Au$+$Au, $p+$$p$, and $p+$Au collisions. In this paper, we propose a digital-analog quantum computing method to simulate the Fermi-Hubbard model using quantum computers with qubits and measurements from a standard quantum circuit. By utilizing a complex quantum state that changes over time, we map the model's many-body Schr\"{o}dinger equation onto a quantum circuit design. The solution to the Schr\"{o}dinger equation is achieved through two circuit operations: a unitary evolution of the state and a projective measurement that truncates the quantum state to retain only its lowest energy components. The circuit design requires no knowledge of the initial quantum state and can be constructed based on the model's Hamiltonian, and it works for an arbitrary number of qubits and sites without scaling issues. We demonstrate the feasibility of our method for simulating the Fermi-Hubbard model up to 9 sites, and the highest energy level that can be truncated depends on the temperature of the quantum state, allowing our method to be a potential solution for simulating complex many-body physics with quantum computers. Furthermore, we show that our method can also be used to find the ground state of the Fermi-Hubbard model by utilizing a search algorithm that explores the close energy levels above the ground state energy. As a result, our method can potentially be used to find the ground state of complex many-body systems, and the close energy levels can be used for other applications such as quantum metrology. Finally, we show that our method can be used to find the dynamics of the Fermi-Hubbard model under measurement back-action by utilizing a Markov process that simulates how the quantum state changes under continuous measurements, and the results agree well with previous theories such as the spin-boson model, and the difference comes from how the continuous measurements affect the quantum state, and our method provides a potential solution for simulating complex measurement-induced dynamics with quantum computers. Therefore, our method can be used for simulating complex many-body physics, finding the ground state, exploring close energy levels, simulating complex measurement-induced dynamics, and potentially be used in future quantum applications. Deep learning models often excel in various applications by extracting relevant features from datasets, but the complexity of their architecture and data processing can be challenging to comprehend. Investigating the characteristics of distilled features is difficult due to the difficulty of relating the features produced by each layer. Our research introduces Bonsai, an efficient method that utilizes dimensionality reduction techniques to identify key features extracted by each layer in a neural network and maps their inputs to those features. Bonsai significantly simplifies the complexity of analyzing deep learning models, enabling feature visualization and highlighting the importance of each layer in extracting distinctive features. Experimental results demonstrate Bonsai's effectiveness in accurately predicting the features produced by subsequent layers in a range of datasets, including image classification, semantic segmentation, and generative modeling. Additionally, Bonsai's analysis correlated with manual inspections confirmed its ability to detect intricate patterns and the role of each layer in processing data. Notably, Bonsai's capabilities can be applied beyond understanding models during training and extend to analyzing pre-trained models, fine-tuned models, and even encoder-decoder models used in cross-modal learning. Our research showcases the potential of Bonsai in uncovering the inner workings of neural networks, and we anticipate its applications to expand into various domains in the future. This study presents an innovative approach to enhancing the clarity and detail of images that have passed through complex, scattered media using an advanced genetic algorithm. The effectiveness of our weight-mutation strategy is evaluated through a comparison with traditional mutation methods. The results demonstrate that this technique improves image clarity and the level of detail by approximately 25%, and also accelerates the convergence of the algorithm. The efficacy of our approach is confirmed by successfully recovering high-resolution images from various complex media, and the algorithm's parameters are minimized to achieve optimal convergence. Furthermore, the feasibility of our method is verified by achieving excellent results using the commonly-used Ball Refraction Model and a more realistic, light-scattering simulator. The output images obtained through our deconvolution process are remarkably similar to the ground-truth images, showcasing the robustness of our weight-mutation assisted genetic algorithm. The successful application of our method to image recovery from complex media paves the way for potential use in medical imaging, and the code is freely accessible online.

Our research centers around efficient policy learning techniques that leverage 
a pre-collected dataset, eliminating the need for online testing once 
training begins. Prior studies have established that value function estimates 
using uniform sampling can be overly optimistic due to biased generalization. 
In an effort to improve this, we investigate the potential of drawing tests 
from the target distribution defined by the current policy, rather than the 
optimal distribution. This leads to the development of two efficient value 
function estimates, along with analysis proving their convergence under 
sublinear regret bounds in both theoretical and practical scenarios. Our results 
further reveal that our method converges at least as quickly as upper confidence 
bound (UCB1) for the multi-armed bandit problem, in terms of sample complexity. 
Additionally, we demonstrate that our efficient estimates are just as accurate 
as those obtained through uniform testing, for a wide range of functions. 
Empirical evaluations confirm our theoretical findings, showcasing the benefits 
of our approach over existing methods. Notably, we observe a substantial 
performance gap in two challenging policy evaluation scenarios – a continuous 
ground truth approximation and the classic Atari games. Ultimately, our 
research highlights the potential for efficient policy learning based on 
efficient value function estimates derived from targeted testing.

This paper provides a detailed analysis of a monolithic small collection-electrode CMOS sensor built using a 180 nm CMOS process, specifically designed for the detection of minimum ionizing particles. The focus is on the properties of a prototype device featuring a 25 x-27 um sensor, coupled with an 10 x 10 um p+ conversion layer above the substrate. We examine the p+ implant's influence on charge collection through simulation and experimental results, revealing the distinct characteristics of pulse shapes, pulse heights, and associated signal recovery times for different conversion-layer thicknesses. Our findings also address the challenges posed by the finite thickness of the p+ implant and underlying N-well regions. Additionally, we investigate the pulse shape modifications resulting from biased N-well and p+ regions. This work aims to offer designers crucial insights to optimize the performance and overall thickness of such CMOS sensors. We also explore the full potential of a 25 x 27 um sensor, highlighting its suitability for the detection of minimum ionizing particles and/or X-ray photons at a low enough energy threshold. Specifically, our calculations indicate an optimal energy resolution of approximately 0.80 keV and a maximum signal charge yield of about 14.8 relative units for 27 um thick sensors. We further discuss two possible design variations to minimize the thickness and leakage current of these sensors, ultimately facilitating the use of such devices in medical and industrial applications where radiation sensitivity is undesirable. With a reduced overall thickness of approximately 0.7 um, our proposed designs retain a high degree of particle detection efficiency and maintain a low enough energy threshold to ensure efficient X-ray photon detection well below 1 keV. We also successfully assessed the efficacy of these designs in reducing the leakage current and achieving a high signal-to-noise ratio in charge signals. Prototypes featuring these two design variants have been successfully tested using X-ray sources and we are currently preparing to test them against 55 Fe sources in order to verify our theoretical predictions. We anticipate that such small CMOS sensors will find numerous applications in medical and industrial settings due to their exceptional radiation hardness, low power consumption, and minimal overall thickness. We envision their potential use as single-photon sensors in medical applications or as light sensors in CMOS-based gamma-ray spectrometers. Moreover, their exceptional properties make them an ideal choice for the detection of individual Cherenkov light signals in particle physics experiments. We have introduced a new approach using a deep neural network specifically designed for this purpose. Utilizing the current generation of 8 meter class ground-based telescopes for training and testing, our model has demonstrated improved performance in detecting exoplanets compared to a conventional reference image subtraction method. This innovative deep learning technique holds great promise for achieving the desired detection requirements outlined in the 10 meter class planet-level exoplanet detection concept. We have found that our model can successfully identify exoplanets even in scenarios where the point spread function and noise patterns differ from those used in the training process. Furthermore, our model has shown adaptability by effectively integrating data from multiple telescopes for improved exoplanet detection. We have evaluated various network architectures and found that a compact yet efficient architecture consisting of 15 layers and 3.3 million parameters offers an optimal balance between performance, flexibility, and computational efficiency for this application. We have also analyzed the potential benefits and limitations of our model for real-world ground-based exoplanet detection, which holds great promise for its practical implementation. This research introduces enhanced cluster-robust estimators that refine existing methods, addressing their limitations in small sample sizes and poor performance with certain data distributions. Our new estimators are direct modifications of the standard cluster-robust least squares and instrumental variables estimators, respectively. We propose to replace the typical within-cluster sum-of-squares denominator with a minimum variance estimator based on the unbiased estimators of the within-cluster variance. This approach ensures the revised estimators remain unbiased and with the same asymptotic properties as their original counterparts. We evaluate the performance of these estimators through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, considering different data configurations and sample sizes. The results demonstrate that the revised estimators offer improved performance even in large sample sizes, outperforming the original methods in this context. Furthermore, numerical investigations highlight the potential biases of the standard estimators, particularly in small sample sizes and specific data scenarios. In contrast, the proposed estimators demonstrate a significant reduction in bias, alongside better performance in terms of mean absolute error and coverage probability for confidence intervals. The research showcases the utility of the modified estimators, advising practitioners to use these alternatives to the classic cluster-robust estimators. Additionally, the accompanying code is available online for replication purposes. Specifically, the repository can be accessed at https://github.com/albertoquaranta/Cluster-Robust-Estimators. Both packages aim to enhance practical statistical analysis and research in the field of cluster-correlated data. We developed a novel, multi-time-step integration algorithm (MTSA) to speed up computational simulations of complex flows that interact with particles. The traditional approach used in particle-laden flow simulations separates the solution into different sub-problems: a fluid flow equation and particle position and velocity update equations. We combined these sub-problems using the finite element method (FEM) and introduced multiple time steps to optimize the solution, resulting in improved computational efficiency. We tested MTSA and compared it to traditional methods in a range of simulations, including a single particle interacting with a flow and multiple particles scattered throughout a flow field. The results show that MTSA reduces computational time by up to five times without compromising accuracy. This innovative algorithm is an essential step towards simulating larger-scale particle-laden flow phenomena. Additionally, MTSA provides a viable approach for extending the reach of existing particle-laden flow simulators and potentially influencing the development of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) software and fluid mechanics applications. Furthermore, MTSA has the potential to facilitate simulations of complex, large-scale phenomena such as dust transport, fluid-driven particle sedimentation, and astro-particle interactions. Due to its broad potential, the MTSA could contribute to significant discoveries in various fields. We plan to apply and refine MTSA in various applications in the future. To facilitate replication and further research, the source code and additional information can be accessed at https://git.io/MTSA. We examine the definition of particle number in cases of intense fields, focusing on weakly coupled situations such as those involving Yang-Mills and axion fields. Our analysis shows that the concept of particle number, as defined by the Bogoliubov method, varies over time due to interactions and particle production. This temporal fluctuation poses a question about the utility of the Bogoliubov definition, especially in situations where the number of particles is greatly exceeding the black hole mass. It is shown that the horizon definition of the number of particles is not dependent on the coupling or the details of the particle state and is applicable for any number of particles. Furthermore, the horizon definition yields a result that the number of particles in a black hole is not a conserved quantity in the classical sense but rather it is a gauge invariant one. We also investigate the process of black hole evaporation while strictly adhering to the gauge invariance by utilizing the horizon definition and find that the information paradox is resolved as the information is stored in the Planck density states of the Hawking radiation and that the number of these Planck density states is vast. We examine the resolution of the information paradox in detail. Lastly, various methods for determining the number of particles in intense field situations are reviewed and compared. We also examine the quantum properties of thermodynamic quantities such as temperature, entropy, and pressure, while strictly adhering to the principle of gauge invariance. Our findings indicate that these quantities arise from the gauge invariant states near the horizon and that they exhibit quantum properties even in the semi-classical regime. It is observed that the quantum properties of these thermodynamic quantities are closely related to the complex nature of the gauge invariant states near the horizon. The fact that these states contain massive numbers of particles in comparison to the mass of the black hole indicates a need to re-evaluate the concept of particle number in such situations. Our analysis shows that these gauge invariant states near the horizon could potentially be used as a source of entanglement leading to the emergence of thermodynamic properties in the near horizon region. We also explore the concept of entanglement in the context of the gauge invariant states and find that it may play a significant role in the generation of quantum properties in the black hole atmosphere. Consequently, it may influence the emission spectrum leading to the emergence of quantum regression and memory effects. Ultimately, it is discovered that the same entanglement that gives rise to the quantum regression and memory effects could possibly be responsible for the information encoding in the gauge invariant states near the horizon.

This research examines the behavior of a liquid jet flowing alongside its counterpart in a parallel channel, primarily focusing on how it responds to changes in fluid flow rates. In this study, we utilized three-dimensional numerical simulations to analyze the complex consequences of viscous forces, surface tension, and gravitational pull on the interplay between liquid and air. Our findings reveal the significance of accurately modeling air entrainment and the resulting changes in jet geometry, which in turn influence the flow rates observed in various regimes ranging from low to high contrast ratios of air to liquid flow rates. In certain situations, the air that becomes trapped between the two jets can significantly affect the behavior of the jets themselves, highlighting the intricate relationship between liquid and air dynamics. Ultimately, our results align with existing experimental data, while also providing potential avenues for future experimental investigation. Additionally, we discuss how the two-jets system might be applied to drop formation, which shares similarities with jet behavior in certain parameter ranges. In this context, we identify key factors that affect drop formation, which could be explored using the same numerical approach. Furthermore, we investigated the possibility of generating complex particles through a novel manufacturing technique known as "jet break-up," which involves manipulating jet behavior through airflow to produce intricate structures. This approach could be used to create a wide range of complex particle designs by adjusting manufacturing conditions, including surface modifications and multi-material production, by combining it with existing techniques such as 3D printing and photopolymerization. As a proof-of-concept, we demonstrated its applicability in producing a particle with a symmetrical, five-part structure. In conclusion, our study not only sheds light on the underlying physics governing the two-jets system but also offers a valuable tool for designing novel complex particles through controlled jet break-up. This manufacturing technique shares similarities with other processes such as co-flow, capillary break-up, and break-up in narrow channels, while also presenting opportunities for further investigation into particle design. In this context, we discuss potential future research directions, including the application of our numerical approach to drop formation and the exploration of new manufacturing techniques such as the use of laser light and heat to manipulate jet behavior. This could potentially be combined with existing techniques such as photopolymerization and 3D printing to produce complex structures. As data management systems shift to main memory, ensuring consistency in data across multiple processes becomes a primary concern, particularly when using algorithmic approaches that take advantage of algorithmic properties to prevent unnecessary data copies and maintain consistency. We have developed a general framework called KVTrees, which combines algorithmic knowledge to maintain various key-value traits, such as order-preserving, sameness, and monotonic increase/decrease, utilizing only a single pointer per node. This framework leverages efficient self-directing trees like B+ trees, which can adapt to different algorithmic objectives, effectively providing a fundamental building block for algorithmic consistency in data management systems. We have further specialized KVTrees to create efficient data structures, including interval trees, that demonstrate significant improvements over existing interval trees, particularly in queries related to range minimum/maxima. Our experimental results validate the performance benefits of KVTrees. Next, we have explored the application of algorithmic consistency in a broader context and introduced the concept of extended monotonicity, which consists of multiple consistency parameters that can be adjusted according to specific requirements. Finally, we have integrated our approach to create first-in-first-out queues with exponential capacity, thereby illustrating the potential of algorithmic consistency in more complex data management problems. HDTM significantly expands upon the widely used Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) model, enabling incorporation of additional variables such as author and document characteristics, dates, and geographic locations. This expansion enables the capture of multi-scale temporal and structural patterns within networks, outperforming traditional statistical methods with comprehensive testing. Notably, HDTM outperformed LDA in detecting hidden structures within Twitter posts related to the COVID-19 pandemic, revealing intricate patterns unnoticed by LDA. The suppression patterns of prompt $\psi(2S)$ and J/$\psi$ mesons were investigated in peripheral and mid-y range collisions of Pb-Pb, p-Pb, and pp at 5.02 TeV. The observed suppression of $\psi(2S)$ relative to J/$\psi$ increased with higher particle transverse momentum, particularly in high-energy p-Pb collisions and peripheral p-Pb collisions. When considering medium-induced lifetime effects, the ratio of $\psi(2S)$ to J/$\psi$ suppression still exhibited a significant increase with transverse momentum, indicating that additional factors influence this increase. Additionally, the ratio of $\psi(2S)$ to J/$\psi$ nuclear modification factors in p-Pb and Pb-Pb collisions displayed a notable dependence on transverse momentum, surpassing the dependence seen in pp collisions. Nuclear modification factors were further compared with theoretical models that account for the influence of cold nuclear matter in transport models. The models generally agreed that excess $\psi(2S)$ suppression relative to J/$\psi$ arises from the differing masses of the two mesons when interacting with the cold nuclear matter. However, the cold nuclear matter effect was insufficient to explain the entire $\psi(2S)$ suppression observed in the highest transverse momentum range. The LHCb collaboration presented these findings in the context of a 2015 theoretical prediction that states the cold nuclear matter effect should primarily account for the excess $\psi(2S)$ suppression. The findings reported here represent a crucial verification of that theoretical expectation. The collaboration further noted that the excess $\psi(2S)$ suppression might be attributed to a combination of cold nuclear matter effects and the differing charmonium formation time variations between $\psi(2S)$ and J/$\psi$. The collaboration also explored the possibility of addressing the systematic uncertainties in the measurement of nuclear modification factors by incorporating the direction-dependent tracking of charm quarks in the detector. The use of the forward pure sample of beauty quarks allowed the collaboration to achieve notable improvements in the precision of the forward rapidity modification factors and nuclear dependence measurements at rapidities greater than one. The findings reported here represent a crucial advancement towards the precise evaluation of charm quark interaction with the dense medium in the forward rapidity region. Lastly, the collaboration conducted a comparative evaluation of the dependence on rapidity and transverse momentum of prompt D$^0$, D$^+$, and $\bar{D}^+$ mesons in the forward and mid-rapidity regions.

In continuous logic, equivalence relations within a metric space are shown to have a connection with ultrafilters on the space's domain, resulting in a novel characterization that links these relations to complete metric spaces. This characterization yields a distinct set of axioms for equivalence relations, offering an alternative framework for the relations. The equivalence of these two approaches is demonstrated through a proof of category-theoretic duality between the category of metric spaces and that of equivalence relations, providing a unified perspective on complete metric spaces within this context. The construction of projective limits of metric spaces is explored, revealing that the spaces can be represented as equivalence relations with an added metric structure, quantifying the relationship between these two structures. The investigation also delves into the representation of complete metric spaces as projective limits of metric spaces, uncovering non-trivial instances of such representations. The research focuses on one-dimensional spaces, demonstrating that the spaces can be equivalent to projective limits of one-dimensional spaces containing a standard copy of the real line, adorned with additional metric structure specified by ultrafilters. A set of conditions, referred to as the 'completion axioms,' is defined for one-dimensional metric frames, providing a framework that characterizes those frames that are compatible with the real line's metric structure. The axioms are shown to be equivalent to a set of conditions derived from the ultrafineness of ultrafilters, highlighting their connection to a fundamental aspect of ultrafilters in continuous logic. The study culminates in the characterization of metric frames that are complete according to a lexicographic metric, providing conditions for such frames to be projectively equivalent to the real line, along with a characterization of metric frames that are complete with respect to a gamma-metric. In particular, it is found that any one-dimensional metric frame that is complete with respect to a gamma-metric is projectively equivalent to a complete metric space in the classical sense. The research also explores the uniqueness of representations for projective limits of metric spaces, demonstrating the uniqueness of certain categories within a broader category of metric spaces, encompassing ultrafilters on the spaces' domains. In particular, it is found that the category of metric spaces is equivalent to a category of equivalence relations with a metric structure, whose projective limits correspond to equivalence relations representing complete metric spaces. The research concludes in continuous logic by characterizing equivalence relations within a metric space that correspond to complete metric spaces, offering an alternative framework for the relations through a novel characterization that links these relations to complete metric spaces. Over time, software evolution brings about modifications that can decay the performance of a system or its adapted versions. Various approaches have been proposed to monitor changes using mathematical concepts like singular value decomposition (SVD), but they have generally focused on specific issues or tools. To enhance flexibility in managing software evolution, we propose an open framework that integrates SVD to efficiently detect and analyze changes across diverse systems. This approach is evaluated using eight widely-used software platforms from three categories (database management, search engines, and operating systems), which validates its broad applicability and practical utility in understanding and predicting software evolution. Furthermore, we have made our experimental data publicly accessible. To facilitate widespread adoption of this technique, we have established a public repository containing step-by-step guidelines and the necessary tools. This enables software engineers to apply the proposed method to their own projects, regardless of the specific software framework used. Existing tools can be leveraged to implement our concept, as demonstrated by our source code examples available at https://github.com/manas22/SVDEval. Specifically, we utilized the following widely-used libraries: Caliper for performance evaluation (https://github.com/caliper-io/caliper), Google Test for unit testing (https://github.com/google/test/tree/main/google-test), and Valgrind for memory and performance analysis (https://github.com/vladimirvivien/valgrind). This research was inspired by prior studies, including those using latent semantic analysis (LSA) on software documentation (https://github.com/jeanamarques/LSEval) and matrix singular value decomposition on configuration files (https://github.com/jeanamarques/SVDEvalDB). Notably, our current framework has been adapted from a previous iteration that integrated SVD with database schema changes (https://github.com/jeanamarques/SVDEvalDB), as well as a version that analyzed search engine configurations (https://github.com/jeanamarques/SVDEvalSE). Existing research has not been replicated but rather expanded upon to develop the presented framework. This approach provides a general solution for monitoring software evolution, as demonstrated by our comprehensive empirical analysis, which is detailed in the following sections. Deep sequential models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various applications involving time-series data. However, these models often struggle with retaining context from distant areas, a limitation exacerbated in cases of extended data sequences. To overcome this challenge, attention mechanisms were introduced, enabling the selection of significant information at each step regardless of its origin in the sequence history. This paper delves into the development and implementation of attention-based deep sequential models, exploring how different designs influence their performance. It also offers a comprehensive benchmark comparison of these models, incorporating commonly used pooling layers in convolutional neural networks to further refine context representation. Notably, the proposed models have achieved exceptional performance in real-time, long-range activity detection, specifically on the activity net dataset, outperforming previous benchmarks and matching state-of-the-art performance. Notably, our best models were simple yet effective, incorporating only minimal additional computational complexity compared to their baseline counterparts. These results strongly indicate the value of attention mechanisms and limited context focusing for deep sequential models in retaining context from distant areas. This research investigates the minimum size of the smallest subset of a random binary string, whose subset sums are all unique, when taken to various powers. Previous studies by Peres and Zrimmer demonstrated that a certain minimum size exists, but left finding the exact value as an open question. Our investigation focuses on situations where subsets can be of a size equal to or less than a fraction of the total string length, and reveal exact values in such cases. Unlike Peres and Zrimmer's approach, our proof centers on identifying extremal instances, particularly those consisting of equal parts ones and zeros, where calculations are simplified by using finite field characteristics. We have derived both upper and lower limits for the minimum size of these extremal cases, where our lower limits are directly applicable to random binary strings. Our analysis further demonstrates that achieving distinct subset sums requires a lower bound of n/2 for subsets of size n/2 and up to n/2, but allows a lower bound of n/2.05 for subsets of size n/2.05 and above. Our results show near-optimal performance when subsets are at least n/2 in size, but may fall short by a factor of two or more for smaller subsets. Our research provides exact answers to open questions in the field, while offering insights into the problems at hand. Our findings also highlight connections to finite field characteristics, particularly through the use of finite field polynomials, which transition into a discussion on the infinite Ramsey theory. Our investigation is further expanded to explore variations on the distinct subset sum problem, particularly where subsets may consist of a variable number of elements, but are always full in their dimension. Our analysis in this area is largely straightforward, but does reveal an interesting connection to the one-dimensional binomial model, particularly through the calculation of tail probabilities. In this research, we explore the relationship between two distinct phase transitions - deconfinement and superconductivity - that occur within quark stars. The deconfinement phase transition is analyzed using a bag model that accounts for strong interactions among quarks, while the superconductivity phase transition is analyzed through a framework that incorporates both strong and electromagnetic interactions. The presence of strong interactions causes quark matter to undergo a transition from a normal state to a 2SC state, and further research reveals that this transition can occur either within a single flavor or a three-flavor regime, depending on the value of the strange quark mass. When the strange quark mass is less than 100 MeV, both the normal and 2SC phases are characterized by a phase transition that is both first-order and influence quark star radius, while a third-order phase transition does not impact quark star properties. However, if the strange quark mass is greater than 100 MeV, the deconfinement phase transition becomes the leading order transition, and the 2SC transition characterizing quark star behavior within the dense star interior transitions to a second-order phase transition. The presence of a deconfinement phase transition influences quark star properties, with maximum masses ranging from 1.26 to 2.16 solar masses, depending on the value of the bag constant. Consequently, if the mass of a quark star candidate lies between 1.26 and 2.16 solar masses, it is plausible to infer the occurrence of a deconfinement phase transition. Finally, our research predicts that a quark star candidate with a mass greater than 2.16 solar masses will not exhibit a first-order deconfinement phase transition. However, a quark star with a mass less than 1.36 solar masses will always display a second-order transition, regardless of the value of the strange quark mass. As a result, it is not feasible to use quark star mass to infer the nature of the deconfinement phase transition. Instead, the occurrence of a deconfinement phase transition should be inferred from quark star radius, which it is possible to infer the occurrence of a deconfinement phase transition if the quark star radius lies between approximately 10.37 and 13.9 km, depending on the value of the bag constant. Conversely, if the quark star radius lies outside of this range, it is not feasible to infer the occurrence of a deconfinement phase

This noise can be used to calculate the damping constants of the mirror's motion using the methods of both power spectral analysis and variance calculation. As a result, the compass technique offers a reliable method for measuring mechanical damping, with potential applications including the detection of dark matter and the identification of gravitational waves in microgravity environments. With its ability to monitor continuous motion, the compass may significantly improve fundamental physics experiments, at an equivalent or improved sensitivity, with the added benefit of simplified design and reduced complexity. Notably, the compass-based method enables the monitoring of a single object, as opposed to previous techniques that required tracking two coupled systems. We explored the statistical properties of the compass, finding that even minimal variance in the compass reading can accurately determine the damping parameters. Additionally, the compass's accuracy can be further enhanced by incorporating advanced signal processing techniques, such as the Kalman filter method. We investigated the effectiveness of the compass in measuring the damping of both small and larger objects, specifically in the cases of a 1-micron test mass and a 1-kg mass in free fall, with the latter representing a realistic option for microgravity experiments. We estimated that with each compass measurement, the variance can be reduced to less than $10^{-16}$ rad$^2$, with approximately 15 minutes to 1 week required to achieve this level of precision in a 1-micron test mass measurement. Conversely, a single compass measurement can achieve a precision of less than $10^{-14}$ rad$^2$ in a 1-kg mass measurement.
