We start by defining a more extensive class of palindromic numbers, known as $R_\mathcal{M}$ numbers, with the property that their reverse reflections, $\mathcal{M}$, can't be expressed as a sum of squares of positive integers. Our investigation into the density of unduplicable integers within this class reveals a significant decrease compared to the broader palindromic integers, particularly those defined by a fixed set of smaller, positive integer square roots. Specifically, the density of unduplicable $R_\mathcal{M}$ numbers is shown to be less than or equal to $O(\sqrt{\log N}/\log\log N)$ times smaller than the density of unduplicable palindromes. Moreover, our proof employs novel strategies, such as the simultaneous application of Weyl's criterion and Erdős's measure, providing a more precise estimate of their ratio. Additionally, our work highlights a striking analogy between this problem and the comparison of unduplicable integers within the class of "almost palindromes." It's also noteworthy that our approach allows for the extension of several powerful methods from number theory, such as the complex embedding of finite algebraic varieties and the application of Diophantine properties of certain polynomial systems, to the broader examination of $R_\mathcal{M}$ numbers. As a result, our work contributes to the understanding of the representability of integers as sums of perfect squares, a problem that has received significant attention in the field of number theory. Lastly, our work formally incorporates numerous observations, providing a clear and organized argument that draws from multiple insights and resources. Ultimately, our investigation into $R_\mathcal{M}$ numbers offers a fresh perspective and expanded toolkit for future work in this area, as well as related problems involving the representability of integers as sums of squares. As a related note, our findings are more expansively documented in the papers "A Comparative Study of Unduplicable Palindromes" and "The Complexity of Diophantine Properties in Almost Palindromes." Conversely, this current report focuses exclusively on the density of unduplicable $R_\mathcal{M}$ numbers, a topic initially explored in our initial publication. Finally, our work is part of our larger project on the palindromic representation of integers, a topic more comprehensively covered in our most recent publication. A new low-dose CT image reconstruction technique uses a transparent convolutional neural network to tackle noise in CT scans. The model addresses the issue of over-reliance on prior information in existing non-local mean filtering and weighted least squares optimization methods. It achieves this by employing a convolutional neural network framework that is adapted to resist changes when its parameters are modified. The effectiveness of our model was tested on the National Institute of Health's CatScan450 dataset and the results demonstrate its ability to produce high-quality, low-dose images that are comparable to those obtained using prior information. The images reconstructed by our model also exhibit lower noise levels than those produced by other deep learning-based methods. Additionally, the transparent CNN's resistance to parameter changes enables the reconstruction of images from various dose regimes without requiring re-training, thus enhancing its practicality. The proposed method successfully reconstructs high-quality, low-dose CT images from scans as low as 2.0 mGy without relying on prior information, thereby expanding the range of acceptable radiation levels. Furthermore, our results show that the transparent CNN outperforms other deep learning-based methods in terms of noise reduction capabilities. Given its enhanced robustness and versatility, the proposed method offers a promising solution for automated noise reduction in low-dose CT imaging. We developed Bayesian Program Learning, a machine learning approach that
infuses Bayesian inference techniques into probabilistic program development
to generate precise, high-fidelity simulations of complex systems from minimal
data. As its initial real-world application, BPL was used to create an
automatic handwriting system that produces realistic, human-like writing
samples. The method involves establishing a probabilistic relationship between
pen movements and handwritten images, using basic strokes to represent key
variables. The resulting BPL model was trained on just ten samples of
handwriting, following which it produced a vast array of unique, naturally
distributing writing samples. Notably, the model's outputs exhibit the same
level of spatial coherence as its training samples, and its generated images
accurately reflect the pen movements that produced them. When used to create
samples of size 2560, the BPL model produced drawings that were indistinguishable
from those created by professional human calligraphers, and the model's
coherence and consistency improved significantly over time through the
reapplication of Bayesian inference. The model's ability to capture subtle,
high-level features of handwriting, as well as its capacity for rapid output
generation, make it an invaluable tool for tasks such as generating custom,
historical-style signages or decorative artwork. Moreover, the model's unique
properties suggest its potential application in the fields of computer graphics
and animation. The code for the BPL model is publicly available at https://github.com/alex2102/bpl. A video showcasing the model's capabilities can be found at https://youtu.be/6sD1dK7KmQY. such as entanglement offered by von-Neumann and correlator methods. 
Next, it delves into recent advancements in quantum electronic devices, 
including transistors, amplifiers, generators and switches. 
The impact of quantum electronics on national security and medicine is also touched upon. 
Finally, it examines the future prospects of this field and how quantum electronics can be used to understand and control nature, 
while also enabling innovative technologies. 
The ultimate goal is to create a pathway for quick advancements in this field, 
either in parallel with or driven by advancements in quantum computing. 
Such an approach can accelerate the development of quantum electronics by 10-50 times. 
The scope of this work is broader than previous reviews in this area, 
with additional applications including rectifiers, oscillators and logic gates, 
along with devices based on coherent states and anti-bunching phenomena, 
particularly tunnel junctions and micro-masers. 
Finally, it covers the latest developments in the use of coherent photon-tronics, 
coherent junctions and coherently-driven tunnel junctions. 
The primary objective of this work is to facilitate quick advancements in this field, 
either in parallel with or driven by advancements in quantum computing.

The duration required to achieve this outcome is expected to be in the triple digit years.

This paper examines two-loop anomalies in the renormalization group for four-twist operators in Wilson Fisher modules derived from AdS/CFT. We calculated the anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators at the next-to-leading order in the large-N limit. Our results show that in the conformal limit, the growth of anomalous dimensions is linearly scaled. Furthermore, we derived a non-linear relation governing the anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators and found that their ratio converges in the large-N limit, representing a non-trivial consistency constraint. We provided all necessary two-loop vertex and three-loop mixed corrections to twist-four operators as subsidiary results. Notably, our findings hold both at and away from the conformal limit. Additionally, we examined the one-loop corrections with mixed-twist quantum numbers and derived a crucial relation for their interactions. We also determined the one-loop and two-loop corrections to the mixed-correction vertex. Our analysis focuses on the SU(N) color group with restrictions on the color trajectories to avoid infrared divergence. These results are crucial for further analysis involving finite-size effects in string theory and the growth of anomalous dimensions in the Penrose-Fitchall limit. Moreover, our results have implications for the study of finite-size effects in the 1/2-spin strings of the ferromagnetic state in the sector of NS2. Our analysis also reveals that the growth of anomalous dimensions in the Penrose-Fitchall limit is similar to the scenario where the spin is much larger than the twist, with the difference being linearly scaled. Conversely, our results show that the growth of anomalous dimensions in the limit of high spin is generally greater than in the limit of high twist. Furthermore, our results indicate the possibility of speedier growth of anomalous dimensions in the limit of high spin and low twist as compared to the scenario of high spin and twist. We have further explored the implications of these findings and discussed their relevance in the context of string theory. The long-standing problem of memory management on GPUs persists as a major obstacle.
Despite significant progress, developers still struggle with unpredictable memory allocation,
leakage, and synchronization issues under CUDA. Our previous research led to the creation of
DynaSOAr, a memory allocator capable of adapting to various workloads while minimizing overhead
and synchronization barriers. By combining a hierarchical approach with efficient locking mechanisms,
DynaSOAr efficiently manages memory across multiple CUDA streams. In this enhanced version,
we refine the allocator's structure to simplify implementation and improve performance, resulting in
substantial improvements for both small and large memory allocation scenarios. By streamlining
internal processes, we increased the throughput of a single allocator by 30% and enhanced
scalability when using multiple allocators. These advancements allow DynaSOAr to surpass
standard CUDA allocators in both raw performance and throughput. When compared to the
highly optimized PMbench benchmark suite, DynaSOAr's throughput stands at approximately
90%. Our experiments with real-world applications, including STB and VoltaTensorCore,
demonstrated a 2-4 times increase in performance using DynaSOAr over standard allocators. 
Notably, DynaSOAr's benefits extend to a wide range of CUDA versions, including support for
CUDAToolkit 11.8 and CUDA Toolkit 12.0. Furthermore, our solution is compatible with
high-performance computing clusters utilizing the Slurm workload manager. As an example of its
success, DynaSOAr's performance with the deep learning framework TensorRT 7.2.3 resulted in a
substantial 2-4 times increase in frame rates when running on a GeForce GTX 1660 Ti GPU. 
In addition to its performance gains, DynaSOAr's memory efficiency allows it to achieve a 2-4 times
reduction in peak memory usage during allocation. As a result of these improvements, developers
can create applications with a 2-4 times cap on peak memory consumption by DynaSOAr. 
Consequently, the maximum amount of memory that can be safely allocated on a GPU is limited to
3-4 Gigabytes. Ultimately, the dynamic nature of DynaSOAr's allocators enables a wide range of
scale factors from 10^2 to 10^5 while maintaining a consistent level of performance. As a byproduct of
this capability, DynaSOAr's throughput remains relatively insensitive to memory fragmentation.

The primary goal of this research is to establish an analytical formula to calculate the minimum pre-tension required in straw tubes designed for particle detection, taking into account their dimensional and mechanical characteristics. This formula can be useful for manufacturers and designers to set appropriate pre-tension levels during the production and design phases. In particular, the research focuses on determining the minimum pre-tension necessary to withstand an internal pressure of 10 Pa in straw tubes made from 1 mm diameter, 10 mm radius of curvature materials. In simulations, the team explored a straw tube with properties similar to a Tubal-R (T-R) profile, specifically with a 1.5 mm wall thickness, made from an aluminum alloy. This analysis found that a pre-tension of approximately 60 N per meter of straw length would be sufficient to withstand an internal pressure of 10 Pa. This result aligns with the pre-tension levels currently used in straw tube applications at the Brookhaven National Laboratory. In addition to establishing the minimum pre-tension required, the research also identified the pre-tension range that allows the straw tube to maintain its original dimensional and mechanical characteristics. This work further involves comparing the mechanical properties of straw tubes designed using 1 mm and 1.5 mm diameter profiles under both external pressure and pre-tension. In simulations, the team found that both straw tube designs exhibited similar ability to withstand internal pressures, while the pre-tension levels used in the 1 mm diameter straw were approximately 2 times higher than those used in the 1.5 mm diameter straw. This work ultimately involves studying the effects of imperfections in straw dimensions on their ability to withstand internal pressures and pre-tension, showing that imperfections can significantly reduce the pre-tension levels required to prevent the straw from collapsing under internal pressures. In simulations, the team found that a straw with a 10% imperfection factor could potentially collapse under an internal pressure of 10 Pa even with a pre-tension level of 120 N per meter, while a straw with a 1% imperfection factor could withstand an internal pressure of 10 Pa even with a pre-tension level of 20 N per meter. This research concludes that straw tubes designed for particle detection should be constructed using materials and dimensional profiles that can withstand internal pressures, maintained within a range of 10^-3 to 10^-2 Torr, through a pre-tension level of 60 N per meter of straw length. The framework consists of two main components:  Firstly, we define a metric that measures the stability of a decision function, reflecting changes in its behavior under varying parameter conditions. Secondly, we propose an approach to approximate the optimal decision function by ensuring it excises a bounded neighborhood around its parameters, while still aligning with our original preference for risk-averse decision-making. This robust version of the decision function emerges from a optimization problem involving a multi-faceted trade-off of preference, risk aversion, and stability. Our study focuses on scenarios with uncertain independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) parameters, applying a Monte Carlo approximation to optimize the decision function, and evaluating its performance through both theoretical analysis and numerical experiments. Additionally, we explore the potential drawbacks and advantages of this approach, suggesting possible enhancements for future research. Researchers impregnated a glass of rubidium-87 with approximately 10,000 highly cooled and extremely tightly packed bosonic atoms, creating a nearly perfect crystalline structure with a tiny impurity that vibrates oscillatory. This impurity, when present, induces new phonon modes called "crystalline melting phonons" that produce an unusual "crystalline melting mode" resonance when scanned with a highly sensitive detector. Interestingly, these oscillations cause other phonon modes to shift in frequency and harden the roton minimum, ultimately preventing the system from solidifying into a more stable structure, thus highlighting an intriguing connection between this "crystalline melting mode" and the formation of supersolidity. This phenomenon of "crystalline melting phonons" offers an innovative approach to studying the intersection of sound and vibration in highly cooled atomic gases. Moreover, this method of detecting "crystalline melting mode" resonance may enable the creation of a novel and highly sensitive detector of vibrational modes in highly cooled atomic gases. This research was inspired by a similar discovery made by Anderson's theory of "crystalline melting" in 1984, where he proposed the presence of a "crystalline melting mode" resonance. This theory was later validated by simulations and experimental research in 2013, and this current research is the experimental proof of that validity. This research is also the first to show that this "crystallity melting mode" can be present in a highly cooled rubidium-87 atomic gas, and that its frequency of vibration can be calculated by using a complex mathematical formula that takes into account its distance from the impurity and the strength of the impurity's vibration, as well as other factors such as the gas's temperature and concentration of atoms. Moreover, this "crystalline melting mode" can be used as a highly sensitive detector of impurities and vibrational modes in a highly cooled atomic gas, and that it can be present even when the system is in a highly stable structure, and that its resonance can be scanned and studied when the impurity's vibration is changed in frequency and strength. Moreover, this "crystalline melting mode" can be used as a highly sensitive detector of a highly cooled atomic gas's transition from a liquid to a solid structure, and that it can be present even when the system is in a highly stable structure, and that its resonance can be scanned and studied when the impurity's vibration is changed in frequency and strength

Our analysis explores the spatial pattern of molecular gas within the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) of the Galaxy using a comprehensive dataset. This includes data at 1.3 mm from the ATLASGAL, GLIMPs, and HOBYS projects, as well as radio recombination line observations from the Hi-GAL survey. We combined the information into a 30' x 30' map at a 20" pixel size and calculated the second-order multipole moments of the density distribution on various spatial scales. Our research indicates that the CMZ exhibits density anisotropy, displaying more pronounced effects at smaller scales. We observed a shift from anisotropy-dominated behavior at scales of 270", to a more nearly isotropic distribution at scales of 1.5 arcminutes and larger. Our findings show that the CMZ's kinetic energy, associated with anisotropy, significantly exceeds its potential energy. We suggest that the CMZ's evolution involves interactions between molecular gas and the Torus, a large molecular disk surrounding the Galaxy's central parsec. Analysis of the CMZ's hierarchical structure reveals a major filament that splits into two in the north-south direction. We propose a hierarchical modeling approach, incorporating theoretical predictions of Larson's law for the CMZ's sub-regional structure. Our model indicates that the CMZ's primary division is located approximately 1 degree (or about 90 parsecs) north of the Galaxy's center. Hierarchical modeling also reveals that the CMZ's mass is primarily composed of two massive filaments, each weighing in at approximately 10^6 solar masses. Our research further suggests that these filaments are engaged in a disk-jet interaction system involving massive outflows and relativistic jets. Based on our findings, we speculate on the potential for the CMZ to give rise to a new generation of compact radio sources, including very high energy gamma-ray emitters. Our research offers novel insights into the structure, mass distribution, and dynamics of the CMZ, suggesting a new understanding of this region as a dynamically active, hierarchical molecular gas structure. Our conclusions emphasize the significance of continued observation and analysis of the CMZ, highlighting the potential for future studies to shed light on the region's further development.

electronic excitation, and electron redistribution are underrepresented in these

theory with the local spin density functional approximation and the constrained
density functional theory to investigate the ultra-short pulse length and high
fluences effects on metal nickel.  Our computational model incorporates rapid
electron redistribution into an initial independent electron model through
constrained exchange-correlation potential calculations.  Our results indicate that
electron redistribution plays a crucial role in determining non-linear absorption
changes at high fluences levels.  The maximum change in absorption is found to rise
significantly from 10% to about 50%-60% when considering 100 fs pulse lengths in
contrast to 1 fs pulse lengths.  A strong correlation exists between the maximum
change in absorption and the energy absorbed per nickel atom, and the existence
of a two-phonon state at 2.5 eV energy level is also observed.  Our research shows
that electron redistribution can lead to a vast non-linear absorption variation at
high fluences levels, and the maximum change in absorption is found to be directly
proportional to the energy absorbed per nickel atom.  Moreover, our research reveals
the presence of a 2.5 eV peak feature originating from a two-phonon state, and our
computational approach based on TD-DFT+CDFT is capable of accurately modeling the
ultra-short pulse length and high fluences effects in metal nickel.  Our research
model can be extended to other d-band metals like aluminum, titanium, and lithium.

The rise of IoT devices demands efficient identification to ensure their security, 
yet, current device classification typically relies on suspicious behavior patterns, 
leading to false positives when innocent devices are flagged. To prevent and compensate 
for these misclassifications, we introduce a risk-based cost-aware classification approach, 
where the cost of misclassification is factored in alongside accurate device classification. 
Our contribution is two-fold: first, we define a general framework for risk-based cost-aware 
classification in IoT contexts, incorporating specific risks such as device and user privacy breaches. 
Second, we develop a detailed mathematical programming model for IoT risk-based cost-aware classification, 
considering trade-offs between classification accuracy and risk minimization. Our proposed approach is flexible and 
can accommodate various IoT scenarios and industry requirements, as illustrated through a security-sensitive IoT environment. 
Our method for solving the mathematical programming model involves iterative Benders decomposition and subgradient methods. 
Our results show that accounting for the risk of misclassification often yields a compromise between higher risk and lower error, 
highlighting the need for our risk-based cost-aware classification approach. Our approach also achieves optimal solutions efficiently, 
especially when the optimal solution involves no mixed-integer variables, thanks to our decomposition strategy. 
Finally, our approach is resilient to irregularities in IoT data and can adapt to varying IoT configurations and environments. 
Our study on IoT risk-based cost-aware classification paves the way for more efficient IoT device classification, 
as our method demonstrates in our experiments with real-world IoT data, showing the potential for a 30% reduction in misclassification. 
Our research on IoT risk-based cost-aware classification approaches offers promising avenues for future research in this area. 
Our code for solving the mathematical programming model is freely available at https://github.com/iot-risk-based-classification/tree/main/code.

We demonstrate how asynchronous block-iterative decomposition, a scalar extension of the standard iterative decomposition algorithm, can be derived using Hahn's diagrammatic approach, providing a universal methodology applicable to diverse decomposition methods, including recursive factorization, distributed computation, and incremental algorithms. Additionally, we examine the relationship between Hahn's diagrammatic and oriented graph representations, as well as the connection between net theory and the directed path cover problem. Notably, we explore a novel generalization of the directed path cover problem, namely the multi-digraph cover problem, and discuss its implications and challenges. The distribution of bubble sizes in a liquid foam follows a distinct power law, regardless of the roughness of the container walls. This universality led to a new variable of of interest, the "roughness factor," which characterizes the impact of container surface conditions. By simulating liquid foam formation using the front approximation, researchers found that the roughness factor is directly related to the distribution of plateaus in bubble sizes. Furthermore, the study found that the typical exponent of 2.0 for the distribution of these sizes regions is generally accepted, although the study found evidence supporting the use of a different exponent. Additionally, the and research found that the magnitude of the roughness factor is typically relatively low, reaching a maximum value of approximately 1.1. This finding suggests a limited impact of container wall conditions on the characteristic "broad" distribution of larger bubbles in a liquid foam. Conversely, a smaller exponent for the distribution of smaller bubbles was observed, resulting in a more pronounced effect of surface conditions on the distribution of these smaller bubbles. The study's results support the use of a Weibull distribution to model the distribution of bubble sizes, given the non-uniform nature of Weibull exponents when considering different regions of the distribution. This model was shown to provide a precise fit to the second central moment, offering a useful tool for characterizing liquid foam dynamics. Lastly, the study found that the surface tension and viscosity of the liquid in a foam have a minimal effect on the distribution of bubble sizes, given the prevalence of viscous effects within the foam itself. Instead, the surface conditions are primarily influential on the distribution of smaller bubbles, while the overall shape of the distribution is largely determined by the protein aggregation behavior of surfactants. As a result, adjustments to surface tension or protein properties can effectively modify the characteristic exponents of a bubble size distribution in a liquid foam. Furthermore, the study found that the protein dynamics, specifically the time it takes for a protein to bind with a bubble, is largely independent of the bubble size. Consequently, increasing the time for protein binding to occur leads to a more extreme power law distribution of bubble sizes, characterized by a larger value for the resulting homogeneity parameter. Conversely, decreasing the time for protein binding results in a distribution of bubble sizes that more closely resembles a normal distribution, characterized by a smaller value for the resulting homogeneity parameter. High-performance image classification has long been a convolutional neural network (CNN) hallmark, with numerous architectures like VGG, ResNet, and Inception exemplifying its efficacy. Recently, combining multiple ensemble classifiers has further accelerated the learning process and enhanced overall accuracy. This research takes a innovative ensemble approach by initially training distinct CNN architectures on a given dataset, and then selecting a subset of them based on pre-defined performance criteria. Subsequently, we utilize another dataset to train classifiers for the selected base classifiers, thereby creating an sophisticated multi-level ensemble. Our methodology demonstrates exceptional outcomes on multiple benchmarks, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNIST, noticeably surpassing the performance of individual component networks and numerous state-of-the-art configurations. Given its remarkable generalization capabilities and transportability, this deep ensemble method serves as a durable and transferable solution for image classification tasks. Our code is openly accessible at the repository address https://github.com/asharkhwan/Deep-Ensemble. Moreover, all experimental data has been uploaded to https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/17Q4gQoQYRl6Q4xgT4xgT4xgT4xgT4xgT4x. Kubernetes was utilized for accelerating computation in simultaneous training of 50 networks. Our findings suggest that deep ensemble methods represent a promising avenue for pursuing robust and long-lasting performance in the ever-evolving deep learning landscape. Following the conference, our work has been accepted for publication in the PR pattern recognition journal in April 2021. The accordion graph class A[n,k] consists of graphs that consist of a collection of convex blocks in a linearly ordered set, combined with a finite number of crossings that occur at the same level. We examine the circulant nature of these graph classes, and find that A[n,k] is not circulant for specific values of n and k. Our results imply that there are two distinct methods of describing the structure of these graphs, and the technique used provides consequences in the study of monotone metacirculant combinatorial objects. We also explore properties of convex blocks and establish a lower limit on the number of blocks in minimal convex graphs. Additionally, we identify a new infinite graph class, which contains non-circulant graphs of various orders, and find that it encompasses the generalized Kockoff graph and the dipyramid graph J2[n]. We conclude by discussing open problems and potential areas for further research. Since many of these results can be confirmed using basic observations, we have included numerous examples to illustrate the non-circulant nature of specific graph classes, thereby providing short and accessible proofs for these assertions. These findings highlight that graph theory offers an expansive and varied range of examples that can contribute to the understanding of circulant graphs. To date, the known examples of non-circulant graph classes primarily consist of direct products and twisted double covers. In contrast, the accordion graph class A[n,k] offers the first known instance of a meta-circulant graph class that is not circulant. As a result, our research provides evidence that investigating higher-order structural properties can provide valuable insights into the circulant nature of graph classes. By extending this reasoning, we propose that there may exist even more intricate graph classes that are not circulant, awaiting discovery. Moreover, we propose the development of methods to identify necessary and sufficient conditions for graph class circulancy, and present an instance of a well-defined property that satisfies these criteria for the class of direct products but fails for the class A[n,k]. This raises questions about the potential applicability of these methods in determining the circulant nature of more intricate graph classes. We have investigated the persistent current in a two-dimensional quantum walk within the context of a flat, smooth-walled circular arena. The model we studied is based on a classical Ising model description, where the Doplicher-Horn scenario, characterized by a divergence in wave patterns, affects trapping angles. The detrapping angle was calculated using theoretical predictions and numerical simulations across various temperatures. At the detrapping angle, the participation ratio displayed a distinct anomaly in both numerical and analytical results. The time-dependent momentum spread was also examined, showing that the detrapping angle can be pinpointed based on a sudden change in this phenomenon. The research was extended to a 3D scenario, resulting in an interesting finding where the detrapping angle can be approached from both the interior and exterior perspectives. The momentum spread in the 3D case revealed distinct patterns in terms of internal and external trajectories. Additionally, the participation ratio was found to be sensitive to the detrapping angle in all examined scenarios. The research was further expanded to a 2.5D scenario, characterized by a Gaussian distribution of quantum states. The results showed that the participation ratio can be utilized as an effective tool for identifying the detrapping angle, both theoretically and numerically. The momentum spreads in this scenario demonstrated distinct patterns, while the 3D case revealed an effective method for pinpointing the detrapping angle based on the radius and wavelength of the wave function. The research was finally applied to a 1D tight-binding Walker Aharonov model, resulting in the participation ratio's failure to accurately predict the detrapping angle due to the model's discrete nature. Our analysis indicates that the model can be characterized by two distinct phases: an early phase where the viscosity coefficient dominates, leading to early deceleration, and a late phase where dark energy dominates, resulting in late-time acceleration. Additionally, we evaluated the model's consistency with observational data from the Cosmic Microwave Background and Hubble Snapshot experiments, finding that it aligns reasonably well with these expectations. We examine the ill-posedness of the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations in higher-dimensional spaces. Specifically, the adverse differential effects of velocity gradient matrices indicate that the solution becomes increasingly unstable with higher dimensions, and in dimensions of at least three, the adverse effects prevail, resulting in ill-posedness. Consequently, the solution cannot be approximated using the fixed-point method. Moreover, the adverse effects intensify with higher spatial smoothness, and the example we provide cannot be approximated even when using Fourier series expansions up to infinite orders. Notably, in two-dimensional spaces, the fixed-point method can be utilized for approximating the solution, and the resulting Taylor series expansions converge converges infinitely, exhibiting logarithmic growth. The examples we present also demonstrate that in three-dimensional spaces, the adverse effects cannot be overcome by choosing arbitrarily small initial perturbations. Additionally, the examples reveal the inherent instability of the adverse effects, and the non-uniform nature of the approximations, particularly in the case of non-zero initial perturbations in two-dimensional spaces. Lastly, the examples highlight the distinct behavior of the adverse effects compared to the well-posedness of the compressible Euler equations. Furthermore, the adverse effects in the three-dimensional space can be distinguished from the instability exhibited by the Pelczer example through a change in scale, and the examples also illustrate the non-uniqueness of the approximations using Fourier series expansions up to finite orders. To summarize, our study shows that the adverse effects are inherent in the three-dimensional space, and the examples provide concrete evidence of the ill-posedness in this space; moreover, the distinction between the adverse effects and the instability in the Pelczer example has been elucidated, and the non-uniqueness of the approximations using Fourier series expansions up to finite orders in two-dimensional spaces has been illustrated. Quantifying the uncertainty of predictions is crucial in various applications, 
but the standard Gaussian process and its surrogate approximations are often 
limited by their simplicity and inability to adapt to complex data. By applying 
a Bayesian perspective, we aim to address this issue. Our approach involves 
reinterpreting the standard loss function as a probabilistic objective and 
minimizing the expected loss subject to constraints on the model's accuracy. 
This methodology is known as robust Bayesian optimization and can be applied to 
machine learning tasks such as regression, classification, and feature ranking, 
especially in high-dimensional datasets. We develop efficient algorithms for 
approximating the robust posterior and propose a stochastic gradient descent 
method that outperforms existing approaches by several orders of magnitude, 
demonstrating superior performance on real-world classification and regression 
challenges. Furthermore, our method provides a practical solution for 
hyperparameter tuning in deep learning, yielding impressive results in 
residual networks and the evolution of Latin square cross-validation designs. 
Notably, our approach offers a general framework for optimizing any objective 
function and can be adapted to various loss functions, including those that are 
not differentiable. This research opens up new possibilities for 
posterior-optimization and point-estimate Bayes methods to leverage the robust 
prior, presenting promising avenues for future exploration. Our work may 
eventually replace surrogate models in applications such as computer vision, 
as our methods exhibit superior performance over the current state-of-the-art 
models in various tasks. Ultimately, our approach provides a practical solution 
for practical Bayes methods, paving the way for a revival of the Bayes rule 
in the era of deep learning. This research is supported by the ANR project 
Exploring Uncertainty in Deep Learning (EUDL).

Short videos demonstrating human movement and related expressions can effectively illustrate multiple aspects of human behavior, such as emotional states and body language, thereby facilitating research into human vision and recognition. These videos serve as training data for open-world facial expression recognition models and allow the exploration of how certain facial movements are constructed through time. Additionally, they aid in understanding complex human actions and how they can be used in human-robot interaction. Creating such videos, however, is labor-intensive due to the need for high-quality actors and sophisticated editing software. We propose MinuteVideo, a tool for designing and producing short videos, reducing the production time and costs associated with it. With MinuteVideo, you can create versatile videos in any size, showcasing the dynamics of both individual human body parts and composite movements. The software combines a video generator module, utilizing a subject's 3D mesh and animation, with a rendering module that applies real-world textures and lighting to the generated video. Performance tests demonstrate that MinuteVideo can produce high-quality 360-degree videos in a short period. For instance, it can create a 360-degree video of a single human movement in a taxling action in under 10 seconds. We envision MinuteVideo as a valuable platform for researchers to develop new theories and ideas regarding human movement, recognition, and vision, thereby expanding the existing knowledge on human body behavior. The software will soon be made available for public use at <https://github.com/ChenXuUI/MinuteVideo>. A video showcasing its capabilities can be found on YouTube at <https://youtu.be/6Q9vG6f4V7g>. The monopole's ground state displays unique properties unaffected by an external magnetic field, yet it exhibits a gap when coupled with an "anyon" matter in the same way a lattice gapped confining phase does, and this gap closes at the monopole's mass. The monopole's susceptibility in a Dirac spinor theory is solely determined by its mass in a way that doesn't rely on the details of the confining phase, and this susceptibility is likely absent in the continuum theory. The monopole's mass can be viewed as the energy required to break a confining string, and it's influenced by both the monopole charge and the string's Luscher charge. The monopole's interaction with charge-invariant defects also exhibits the characteristics of a gap, and it's likely that these defects are related to the monopole's confinement. The monopole's properties may also be relevant to the nonperturbative spectrum of QED$_3$ with massless fermions. To evaluate the performance of weather forecasting models, we utilize extendable datasets that can be enlarged by incorporating more data. We normalize these datasets to facilitate comparison with established benchmark models. Our investigation focuses on a standardized weather forecasting dataset from the Google DeepMind Challenge Award winner, DeepMind's Weather Network, which we expand with double the original size. We normalize this enlarged dataset using the minimum-maximum method and employ established metrics to assess model performance, including mean absolute error, symmetric mean absolute percent error, and clipping error. To evaluate the effect of normalization, we train and tested models with and without normalized data. Our findings indicate that normalizing datasets for training and testing purposes results in better evaluation and increased chances of surpassing the benchmark models. Nonetheless, normalizing data for benchmarking purposes yields underestimation of the benchmark scores. Moreover, normalizing data improves the chances of achieving benchmark performance when comparing individual model results to established benchmarks. Ultimately, our research underscores the significance of normalizing data for both training and testing, as well as scaling the datasets when employing extension mechanisms to maintain fair model comparisons. Our findings contribute to the advancement of the field by highlighting potential pitfalls in evaluating and comparing weather forecasting models, along with proposing effective evaluation methodologies. The PPT conjecture proposes that PPT states remain positive semi-definite when viewed from the perspective of local operators. Historically, this hypothesis has been confirmed in finite dimensional spaces by the Yang-Mills theory. Notably, in infinite dimensional spaces, distinct mechanisms underpin PPT states' positivity. 

This research focuses on exploring the underlying mathematical structures common to all PPT states within the domain of Gaussian states, irrespective of the dimensionality. It highlights key results, such as the commonality shared by Gaussian PPT entanglement measures, the connection between certain non-Smith normal form matrices and PPT states, and the existence of distinct PPT-preserving maps in infinite dimensional spaces. 

In conclusion, this research demonstrates that, unlike the case in finite dimensional spaces where the PPT conjecture's validity is certain, in the realm of Gaussian states the PPT conjecture remains an open question. 

In addition to this, this thesis delves into linear optico-electronic networks comprised of passive components like beams splitters and phase modulators, used for processing Gaussian states. It establishes a clear distinction between the domains of input states that are classical and those that are non-degenerate. Ultimately, this thesis derives various transformations that maintain positivity in the PPT sense. 

Finally, this thesis investigates the relationship between non-degenerate free states and their entanglement structure. Specifically, this involves exploring SDP relaxations for non-degenerate free states, analyzing their convergence, calculating entanglement structure for specific non-degenerate states, and formulating non-degenerate free states with specific entanglement structures. 

As a whole, this thesis addresses multiple open questions in the field of PPT states and Gaussian entanglement structures, providing concrete answers and methodologies. It contributes new ideas to the field of PPT states, builds connections between PPT states and Gaussian entanglement structures, and extends known results in the field of linear optico-electronic networks. Additionally, this thesis provides novel insights into free states and their entanglement structures.

The unique transport mechanisms in neurons are integral to various cellular processes, including the transportation of vital materials from the base to the tip of neurons. The intricate networks within neurons, consisting of microtubules that make up the cytoskeleton, play a crucial role in this transportation system. The transport system in neurons relies on long, thin structures such as astrocyte processes that extend deep into the brain, allowing them to interact with neurons through specialized structures called synapses. As the most abundant cells in the brain, astrocytes interact with neurons by providing them with essential nutrients and energy, helping to maintain the complex transport systems in neurons. However, the relationship between astrocytes and neurons is still not fully understood, particularly how materials are transported and exchanged between them. We developed a new, three-dimensional model of the brain that includes the interactions between neurons and astrocytes, allowing us to study how materials are transported and exchanged between them. Our model reveals the intricate transport mechanisms in the brain, including the role of microtubules in neurons, how transport systems are regulated, and how materials are exchanged between neurons and astrocytes, providing new insights into the complex processes in the brain. Our model also highlights the importance of understanding the structure of the brain at different scales to reveal the underlying transport mechanisms in the brain. Ultimately, we hope that our model will contribute to the development of new treatments for neurodegenerative diseases, such as those caused by defects in the transport of materials in the brain. Our model is available at https://github.com/Neurophysics/BrainTransport. Any modifications to the model can be reported at https://neurophysics.github.io/BrainTransport. Our model provides a new approach to studying the complex processes in the brain, and ultimately understanding how materials are transported and exchanged between neurons and astrocytes in the brain. Banks employ complex systems that integrate various operations with different rules and constraints. Graph representation learning offers an effective approach to understanding bank processes, enabling the use of node embeddings and edges to model real bank transactions. However, existing methods lack a comprehensive framework for generating valid bank transaction graphs, leading to low accuracy in learning node embeddings. To address this issue, we introduce the exploration of bank-inspired graph generation, a novel neural architecture called CGGNAP, consisting of a conditional graph generative neural network with a Markov chain that ensures the validity of generated graphs. Our research includes the creation of a dataset consisting of 21 bank transaction graphs and the implementation of a dataset called BankGraphs with 21 types of bank transactions. Our experiments show that the proposed architecture outperforms state-of-the-art methods in learning valid node embeddings, particularly on the dataset of bank transactions. Moreover, we conduct an ablation study on a large dataset and find that the Markov chain in our architecture contributes significantly to the validity of the generated graphs. Our work on bank-inspired graph generation enables the development of fraud detection models that learn from real bank transactions, offering an improvement over previous methods that may predict false negatives due to the generation of invalid transactions. With the increasing importance of graph representation learning in various domains, our research on bank-inspired graph generation offers insights into the challenges of learning valid node embeddings in complex domains. In binary systems consisting of a white dwarf and a neutron star, the lighter star's mass drives the formation of an accretion disc around the heavier star. For systems where the masses are close to equal, the lighter white dwarf resists being engulfed by the heavier neutron star, and instead, the mass transferred during the initial merger process forms a disc around the black hole that may eventually appear as a bright precursor to the merger event. The formation of an accretion disc via mass loss from either the white dwarf or the neutron star has been largely overlooked in studies of equal-mass binary mergers. In this work, we employ three-dimensional simulations to investigate the behavior of non-rotating, equal-mass binary systems consisting of a white dwarf or a neutron star, and find that mass loss from both stars contributes to the formation of an accretion disc around the black hole. The resulting discs, however, significantly differ in mass depending on the original companion star, and could potentially impact the dynamics of the post-merger disc and its observational characteristics. The discovery of pre-merger accretion discs may also shed light on the origin of ultraluminous X-ray binaries. Further research is needed to explore the broader implications of this finding, and to investigate its connection to other binary systems consisting of a white dwarf and a neutron star. The development of efficient algorithms to handle mass loss from both stars without interfering with each other may also be a useful area of exploration. The mass loss from both stars could be a common occurrence in nature, and as such, should be a key consideration in the study of equal-mass binary mergers involving neutron stars and white dwarfs. We investigate a family of metric models that is based on the symmetric Tversky ratio, which is popular in data fusion applications, particularly k-nearest neighbor searches. The structure of its metric space is not fully understood, so we provide a characterization of the extreme points within this space for any fixed k, establishing that the set of optimized centroids is a convex polygon with at most k vertices. Our approach to identifying convex extremes involves a novel reduction of the optimization problem in question to a simpler convex optimization problem within the space of positive definite symmetric matrices, which we solve explicitly. Our findings are based on a comprehensive characterization of the metric's positive definiteness properties, as well as the existence of a dual geometric interpretation to the optimization problem at hand, which offers insights into the underpinned data fusion applications, particularly from the perspective of optimizing binary classification problems. Our proposed algorithm for computing the optimized centroids is based on an iterative reweighting method that converges to the optimal solution, achieving a computational complexity of O(N log k). For the specific case where k equals 1, our results imply an optimal solution that can be computed in O(sqrt N) time. Our findings are further reinforced through the analysis of a few illustrative datasets. To the best of our knowledge, our work represents the first algorithm that can efficiently solve this optimization problem for large datasets, particularly when k equals 1. Our research also opens up new avenues for data fusion applications, particularly binary classification, where the proposed algorithm can be used to efficiently compute the conditional most similar k-nearest neighbor given the class label. Our findings are further strengthened by two such examples. Our findings represent an initial exploration of the geometric properties of this metric space, particularly its effective rigidity properties, at a finite value of k. Our research is further strengthened by the analysis of two distinct datasets, each for the values k equal 1 and k equal 2. Our outcomes imply that this metric space possesses non-trivial effective rigidity properties, particularly in the cases k equal 1 and k equal 2. A widely recognized issue in vision, deblurring, aims to recover sharp images from blurry ones, often resulting from camera shake or other factors.
Recent studies have focused on addressing this problem using two combined modules: a deblurring network and a reblurring module, aiming to counteract the effects of the former with the latter.
However, incorporating both modules can lead to unsatisfactory outcomes, given that the deblurring network may occasionally fail to fully restore the blurriness and the reblurring module cannot compensate for this failure in some cases.
In this study, we introduce an innovative and simplified approach that surpasses the existing state-of-the-art methods, incorporating an adaptive reblurring module that selects whether or not to reblurr an image based on the quality of the deblurred image.
Additionally, we upgrade the traditional image and feature guide loss used in deblurring with a novel data-driven constraint, resulting in superior deblurring results.
Our approach not only yields outstanding results but also demonstrates the importance of accurately assessing the quality of deblurred images, further expanding the applicability of this method to a range of low-quality and real-world deblurring scenarios. In recent years, AI model benchmarking has gained significant attention in the data-driven and machine learning communities to compare the performance of different architectures. However, traditional benchmarking methods require the execution of AI models on remote cloud or supercomputer infrastructure, which often results in inaccurate or unreliable benchmarking outcomes due to differences in hardware environments. Additionally, the large size of AI models poses another challenge, making remote benchmarking less efficient and unreliable. This paper introduces a novel approach to remote benchmarking that leverages the power of lightweight model execution. By developing a lightweight version of the target AI model, typically consisting of only a few weights, BenchmarkNet executes the remote benchmarking workflow in an end-to-end manner. This execution is facilitated through a collaborative and distributed computing platform, where a controller node orchestrates the benchmarking process and a worker node executes the lightweight model. The proposed system allows for remote benchmarking of complex AI models on various hardware devices, such as GPUs, TPUs, FPGAs, and custom hardware, without the need for model replication. Experimental results demonstrate the accuracy and effectiveness of BenchmarkNet in remote benchmarking of AI models, exemplified by a 94% match between benchmarking and actual application inference latencies. The proposed system has been successfully applied to remote benchmarking of various computer vision tasks on Google Cloud infrastructure, equipped with GPUs, TPUs, and custom Cloud TFPs. To address the issue of limited data in tree parsing, researchers have been employing self-training techniques for a long time. Currently, the most widely used approach is self-enhancement, which iteratively refines a parser by training on its own predictions. However, this method has reached a plateau due to its limitations, primarily caused by the biased capture of easy sentences in each iteration, leaving the remaining hard sentences unaddressed. In an attempt to overcome these limitations, we propose Deep Contextualized Self-training, an innovative approach that leverages pre-trained tree transformers to incorporate context-dependent representations for sentences, thereby enabling the model to better capture the inherent relationships in sentences, especially for hard samples. By combining the strengths of self-enhancement and leveraging pre-trained tree transformers, DCST achieves superior performance compared to the existing state-of-the-art systems on the WSJ and AllenIQL datasets for parsing tasks. Notably, DCST shows notable improvements of 0.37 and 0.15 F-factor on the out-of-domain and in-domain tests of the WSJ dataset, respectively. Furthermore, DCST demonstrates the capability to correct its own previous errors through analysis of sentence contexts. We believe DCST to be a vital addition to the tree parsing toolkit. In the future, we aim to explore the applicability of DCST on other data-hungry parsing techniques. Additionally, we plan to investigate the potential uses of self-supervised pre-training on sequential data for tree-structured sequential data. Last but not least, we aim to delve into the underlying theoretical aspects of self-supervised pre-training on trees. In conclusion, we hope DCST will inspire more research in this domain and contribute to the advancement of tree parsing technology. We investigate the complexity of recognizing and counting solutions to linear equations of the form a1.x1 + … + am.xm = c over a finite field GF(q), where coefficients x1 through xm are variables taking on values from the set {0, 1, …, q-1}. This problem is parameterized by variables and field size. We demonstrate that a broad class of equation instances have a computable solution, and establish that the general solution-counting problem is coNP-complete under any non-trivial field operations. Furthermore, we prove that the existence of solutions to specific unordered linear equation systems is definable within the CPT logic framework, and explore analogous results for ordered equations. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of first-order queries over finite fields under the Compressing Path Trailing Zeros semantics. Additionally, we identify a previously unknown coNP-hardness instance for the field GF(8) that contrasts with the numerous known NP-hard instances over the same field. Our analysis also delves into the complexity classification of first-order definability and counting logic for general linear arithmetic formulas. This research is further illustrated through numerous open questions and intriguing discrepancies between NP-hard and coNP-hard instances. The study is based on prior work by Ghadati, Kozlov, and Nurmonen, and extends their findings in the context of finite fields. We also discuss connections to related problems, including the factorial prime search and the bilinear form decoding problem. A key technical contribution involves the development of a novel polynomial-time algorithm for solving equation systems with unique integer solutions modulo a prime. We conducted an in-depth examination of the electronic and magnetic properties in the (Eu1-xBix)2Ir2O7 series, which was created by substituting various amounts of Bi into Eu2Ir2O7, a material known for its unique magnetic monopole properties. Our research used a combination of synchrotron-based x-ray photoemission spectroscopy, transport measurements, and direct current magnetometry to understand the impact of Bi doping. As the amount of Bi being doped increases, we observe a gradual disappearance of the magnetic monopoles in our transport and magnetometry measurements, along with a significant change in the valence band x-ray photoemission spectra. For high levels of Bi doping, our data suggests the emergence of a metallic state, features a Curie temperature of approximately 10 K, and exhibits a strong similarity to 115-based heavy fermion compounds, a comparison that we plan to further investigate in future studies. Notably, even at high Bi doping levels, our x-ray photoemission spectra display a clear distinction between the Bi 6s and Eu 4f peaks, indicating that the Bi atoms are fully doped and present in the material. However, the magnitude of Bi doping required for this effect to occur is substantially higher than what was previously thought. Our research provides clear evidence that Bi doping can be used to engineer the magnetic and electronic properties of this material class, a discovery with significant and far-reaching implications for the field of quantum magnetism. Moreover, the observed behavior may also be related to the recently proposed Bi four-fold spin and associated quantum magnetism that was initially proposed for the Bi-ordered variant of this material class. We would like to note that further research is required to fully understand the nature of this effect, as well as its potential to be observed in other material classes within the 214 family. The aim of this research is to reduce the size of a software system's binary by eliminating features that are not utilized during execution. Our proposed method identifies the source code files that are not deployed to the target system's configuration and removes the corresponding compiled components. This approach specifically targets systems with optional components that can be enabled or disabled at runtime via command-line flags or other mechanisms, and assumes that the system's developer provides comments indicating whether a feature requires additional code beyond the basic system. Furthermore, our method enables the reconfiguration of systems without requiring manual intervention, and supports adding new features that rely on the source code without affecting existing binaries built from different configurations. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by creating a tool that applies these techniques to the Linux kernel, reducing the size of its binaries by 19% and requiring only a small overhead in terms of source code changes. Our tool also supports online reconfiguration actions that can be performed while the system is running, and identifies a group of related commands that can be removed without impacting performance. Additionally, our method allows the optimization of system performance by disabling unused hardware support and removing corresponding drivers from the binary. Our research reveals that the Linux kernel is often shipping more than it needs, with approximately 37% of its configurations containing unused code on average, and more than half of its projects evaluated having projects with unused code in more than one configuration. These findings suggest that our method can significantly improve the situation, reducing the size of the binary by up to 43% and eliminating more than half of its build-time dependencies. Furthermore, our research indicates that the source code can often be reduced using techniques such as code merging and feature-enabled code detection, resulting in a reduction of more than 50% in its compiled size with no additional overhead in terms of source code changes. Our tool has been designed to support these detection techniques, allowing the replacement of macro expansions with optimized versions and the efficient detection of compile-time options. We also propose an information structure called the compile-time dependency tree that can be used to efficiently identify the source code files without deploying the target configuration, and demonstrates its effectiveness by showing that the tree can be constructed in less than one second for systems with tens of thousands of configuration options. Overall, our research indicates that our method can significantly improve the situation by reducing the size of the binary, eliminating unnecessary build-time dependencies, and efficiently identifying the source code files without deploying the target configuration. We expect these results to motivate further research in these areas and encourage the development of new techniques to optimize the compilation process.

A fundamental concept known as active force is a basic ingredient in theories of active matter that can be realized through different mechanisms, including the use of uneven potentials to create stable equilibrium points that give rise to thermal fluctuations exhibiting harmonic and anharmonic behavior. In this study, we examine fluctuations in one-dimensional systems driven by a single type of active force and demonstrate how their analysis depends on the characteristics of the potential. When the potential behaves like a harmonic, the fluctuations conform to the predictions of the Lorentz gas model, resulting in normal diffusion. Conversely, when the potential deviates from harmonic behavior, the fluctuations conform to a nonlinear force that gives rise to anomalous diffusion, specifically characterized by power-law relationships between the mean squared displacement and time. Our research provides a connection between this phenomenon and the theories of diffusion involving fractional derivatives, offering distinct views of the same physical phenomenon. In systems influenced by two types of active forces, we find that fluctuations can exhibit characteristics from both types of driving mechanisms, giving rise to unique behaviors in the system's dynamics. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how different mechanisms of active force impact the system's ability to move over long distances. Additionally, we have extended our research to systems where the active force is not uniformly distributed, finding that this can give rise to directional differences in a particle's ability to move. In extreme cases where the non-uniformity is pronounced, we observe an extreme variation in a particle's ability to move in one direction versus another, leading to the possibility of a particle moving a certain distance in one direction but a significantly larger distance in the opposite direction. This research explores the fundamental principles of a fundamental concept known as active force and its impact on a particle's ability to move, using mathematical models that can be tested through experiments to refine our understanding of how these forces work. Adapter-FineTuning is particularly suited to handling multilingual inputs of varying lengths, enabling it to handle tasks like translation, summarization, and language detection, across multiple language pairs. Key innovations of our framework include the application of multilingual pre-training adapters to enhance linguistic understanding and a novel fine-tuning strategy, dubbed the 'Sample-Based Adaptive Mean', which calculates the adapter weights distribution efficiently. Our adapter-based approach allows for efficient distribution of adapter weights among multilingual Longformer models. Notably, our adapter-based approach allows the models to achieve efficient performance across all tasks by allowing the adapter weights distribution to be learned from task-specific data without pre-existing labels. Experimental outcomes reveal that our adapter-based approach results in efficient length-efficient multilingual Longformer models capable of performing effectively across a range of tasks without requiring task-labeling. We investigate the effects of multi-objective optimization in reinforcement learning, particularly in the context of learning dynamics models from raw, high-dimensional inputs. It is hypothesized that learning a universal dynamics model across multiple tasks can facilitate transfer, but our research reveals a potential drawback: utilizing a single model may introduce task interference, causing it to learn unfavorable characteristics in one task due to its common structure with another task. To test this hypothesis, we employed a suite of synthetic lockers, carefully designed to vary their characteristics based on multiple underlying features. Initially, a policy optimized for one task occasionally learns a conflicting structure in its parameterization, causing significant suboptimal performance on a second, concurrently optimized task. Notably, this interference can be minimized by employing a dynamics model with a task-dependent architecture, thereby preventing the sharing of features and subsequent task interference. Our empirical findings align with theoretical justifications, offering insights into the critical design considerations for multi-objective optimization and transfer learning in the future. The code for our experiments can be found at https://github.com/alexrame/multi-objective-rl.

Time-frequency attention mechanisms have shown exceptional performance in speech recognition tasks by capturing and analyzing the distinct properties of speech at various frequency intervals. Nevertheless, the basic feed-forward network architecture may not be sufficiently expressive to capture the intricate, internally correlated patterns within speech, particularly the periodic patterns that arise from a much deeper root cause - the vibration of the vocal folds. Inspired by the hierarchical structure of the natural environment that gives rise to these periodic patterns, we propose a novel solution called CASCade network (CASCADe-NET), where a primary network detects the underlying vocal fold vibration frequency, and subsequent cascaded networks utilize this frequency to enhance the resolution and accuracy in analyzing the associated periodic patterns within the speech signal. The CASCADe-NET has been successfully applied to the Residual Memory Network (RMN) to form CASCADe-RMN (C$^2$RMIN), which has achieved a 2.0% relative reduction in the error rate compared to RMN on the VOICE BANK dataset. Furthermore, C$^2$RMIN has exhibited better robustness in noise conditions and a 14.0% reduction in the error rate when confronted with the deepfake speech attack Voice-2-2. We anticipate that C$^2$RMIN will serve as an influential model in the field of deepfake speech detection. Additionally, our research has highlighted the significant advantages of CASCADe-NET, and we anticipate it to be a versatile and effective tool for various computer vision and signal processing applications in the future. The success of Collaborative Filtering (CF) in Recommender Systems stems from its ability to produce accurate user and item embeddings through multi-way data interaction modeling. Biclustering-Based Collaborative Filtering methods have gained popularity due to their ability to model complex interactions between users and items in two-dimensional subspaces. These methods, however, often struggle with biclusters of unequal size, resulting in poor performance. To address this limitation, we propose the Unified Biclustering-based Filtering and Clustering framework (USBFC), an innovative approach that enhances existing CF methods by standardizing and optimizing filtering and clustering processes. First, we standardize biclustering sizes to facilitate accurate feature extraction from user and item perspectives. Next, we optimize the clustering of user and item groups to extract fine-grained filtering requirements from both perspectives, thereby producing higher accuracy recommendations. To achieve this, we apply the optimal clustering algorithm for user and item clustering based on our proposed bicontact measure. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets showcase USBFC's superior performance over state-of-the-art CF methods. Notably, our proposed model outperforms the second-best method by up to 10.3% in terms of accuracy performance. The common X-ray stars in the Milky Way are found in close binary systems, consisting of a neutron star orbiting a normal star.  Identifying similar active stars, especially those that are not yet known to emit X-rays, is a key goal of the MESS survey.  Operating on board the SOFI telescope at the La Silla Observatory in Chile, the MESS survey employs a special filter that highlights $\beta$-Messier objects while blocking X-ray emissions, allowing researchers to study their properties more accurately.  In particular, studying the variation in the H-alpha line, which is a well-established indicator of magnetic activity on the surface of stars, is a key focus of the MESS survey's analysis.  In this article, we discuss how these stellar observations support the MESS project's goals.  In particular, we have found that observing the H-alpha line at the most sensitive point of the emission curve provides the most reliable information about the surface magnetic activity of stars. The occurrence of a zero-energy peak in subgap conductance spectra from hybrid FeSe/InSe devices has been previously attributed to non-Majorana effects. Our research reveals that the peak's intensity and directional asymmetry can be manipulated through a magnetic field, lasting as long as it lasts. Upon increasing temperature to 2 K, the peak's intensity diminishes while its asymmetry enhances, before disappearing at 4.2 K. Conductance spectra recorded at finite temperatures show the peak's asymmetry grows as temperature rises. The observation of this phenomenon suggests the presence of a dynamic mechanism. The intensity of the peak is believed to decline due to the contamination of a nearby conductive channel, caused by a temperature-driven increase in tunneling rate. This explanation is supported by the notable occurrence of the peak at 4.2 K. The asymmetry of the peak, however, is thought to stem from a conductive channel with directional selectivity influenced by a magnetic field. The dynamic mechanism responsible for the peak's occurrence involves the interaction between this quasiparticle state and a nearby conductive pathway. Our research further reveals that the peak can be modified through the application of a magnetic field. Our theory suggests that the peak's occurrence is a manifestation of a long-standing issue in studying unconventional superconductors using tunneling spectroscopy: the presence of charge inhomogeneity leading to a non-uniform asymptotic gap. Many cutting-edge video analysis methods rely on individual frames being connected to represent multiple temporal moments. The effective mapping of a single frame to represent a sequence is, however, a highly challenging task. To address this, we introduce the context ground module (CGM), an innovative attention mechanism that guides a transformer encoder in selecting essential frame features for a given sequence. The CGM module discovers the essential characteristics of each sequence, enabling a frame to be more effectively mapped to represent the sequence. The CGM module outperforms existing attention mechanisms in video analysis tasks, such as action recognition, as demonstrated by our results. The CGM module can also be applied to other video-based applications without modification. The proposed method significantly improves the accuracy of our frame encoding approach, resulting in state-of-the-art performance in multiple video recognition benchmarks. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning for modeling continuous data are marked by the success of Variational Autoencoders and similar approaches, which have led to deeper understanding of unsupervised learning techniques. Building upon this progress, a novel approach has been developed by integrating stochastic networks trained with expected lower bound optimization in a hierarchical framework. The initial module compresses high-dimensional data into a compact latent space, while a secondary module leverages prior distributions from the compressed data to generate remote samples in the latent space, thereby enhancing the flexibility of the model. The proposed method was successfully applied to multiple synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating improved sample quality and diversity over prior methods. Furthermore, the method has shown potential in generating data in the presence of noisy or limited observations, as evidenced by its performance on a partial face recovery task. Our proposal for the Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE) challenges the conventional belief that data compression and decomposition must be two symmetric operations. By introducing a 'bicephalous' head for each task, the BCAE enables simultaneous data compression and decomposition through its respective encoding and decoding networks. We have adapted the BCAE into a domain adaptation framework, utilizing two heads to change the network's output layer accordingly. The compression head reduces the dimensionality of the input data from one domain to the other, while the decomposition head increases the dimensionality. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in domain adaptation, with the benefit of reduced parameters and computational requirements. Additionally, the compressed data serves as a useful representation for future applications. Notably, the improved quality of the compressed domain adaptation output compares favorably to existing methods using more complex networks. Given its numerous advantages, the BCAE has potential applications beyond domain adaptation, including efficient data storage and transmission, as well as enhanced robustness to adversarial attacks. We plan to explore these avenues in future research. Our proposed framework has been implemented using PyTorch, and the code along with the datasets used in our experiments can be accessed at the mentioned repository. Our proposal's theoretical contribution resides in its combination with the domain adaptation technique known as second-order adaptation, presented in the accompanying manuscript. Both papers may be jointly read as we describe our proposed framework, followed by its application to second-order adaptation. To achieve this, we apply a mathematical framework known as the epsilon-expansion, commonly used in field theory to study critical behavior, to our fundamental description of matter, and similarly for gravity. This survey article focuses on the current research regarding convex geometric hypergraphs, specifically presenting challenges of saturation problems along with the known saturation numbers for certain geometric configurations. It also introduces a new result concerning the existence of certain geometric n-k-2-structures, alongside an associated lower bound for the number of full layers in such structures, especially when n is significantly large. Furthermore, we take a closer look at the properties of a specific geometric 3-hypergraph and examine its relationship to the long-standing Fano problem. Additionally, we present an alternative approach to the Fano problem by focusing on a more general concept of flag structures. This survey also explores a range of open questions within the field of convex geometric hypergraph theory. Due to the diverse nature of these questions, we do not attempt to provide comprehensive lower and upper bounds for them, but rather aim to stimulate further research and encourage the exchange of ideas within the field.

Trident, a climbing robot inspired by the Pacific Lamprey, has been developed at the University of California, Berkeley with the goal of navigating unstructured, indoor environments. Unlike other robots, Trident employs a unique sealing mechanism allowed by its air-filled body to facilitate smooth movement over soft surfaces. As a result, it can move along smooth surfaces with speeds of up to 0.85 meters per second, while also withstanding external pressures of up to 200 Newtons per square meter when navigating through more textured environments. With its innovative design, Trident has demonstrated the ability to climb over a variety of soft materials and has successfully completed a series of challenging tasks in unstructured indoor environments near its factory, marking a significant milestone in its development. Furthermore, we have conducted a thorough comparison of Trident's capabilities to those of the Pacific Lamprey, identifying key areas where the robot can be improved in the future. Our research highlights the potential for soft robots like Trident to facilitate exploration and analysis of unexplored environments. With its unique features and the potential applications it may yield, we believe Trident can contribute to a broader understanding of the world around us.
