This research investigates the trade-off between throughput and aging of information in wireless communication systems, with aging metrics including time-wheelage and linear-time wheelages. We analyze various strategies such as age of information (AoI) minimization, time-wheelage minimization, and linear-time wheelages' minimization, all under a sum-throughput maximization assumption. The results show that none of these strategies yield direct relationships, leading to complicated expressions involving fractional parts and inequalities. However, we demonstrate that all these minimization problems can be optimally solved through the same optimal transmission power, $P_{opt}$, which is derived as the minimum between the minimum required transmission power for reliability and a power that guarantees both reliability and minimization. It's also shown that $P_{opt}$ can be found through solving a linear programming problem and that this power is feasible for all time slots. Moreover, we and others have made various contributions to age of information theory, including multiple packers, packet status, and considering delays. These contributions are presented in additional subsections. To our knowledge, this research provides the first analysis of time-wheelages and linear-time wheelages in wireless communication systems. This research focuses on demonstrating helicity conservation for weak solutions in particular function spaces, building on existing work by Beale and Fefferman and extending their findings to more general settings. In contrast to earlier results, which relied on specific space discretization schemes, our findings derive from a natural combination of finite difference and finite element methods. A novel lemma, which establishes an equivalence between different function space norms under predetermined conditions, serves as the core technical innovation of this work. We anticipate that the techniques developed here will prove useful in addressing other problems within the framework of the Navier-Stokes and Euler equations. To ensure the accuracy and robustness of the proposed methods, we support our results with a detailed analysis of both time and space discretization strategies, along with a discussion of the stability properties of the resulting algorithms. Two specific examples - Taylor-Gartiner vortices and Alfv\'en waves - serve as natural applications of our findings, as they are inherently linked to the underlying equations being studied. Specifically, we demonstrate helicity conservation for weak solutions of the 3D Euler equations within $L^3\times C^1$-spaces, where the presence of vortices is responsible, and for the Euler equations in $L^3$-spaces, particularly in the case of Alfv\'en waves. Furthermore, our research reveals that the $\mathcal{H}^3$-norm of solutions to the Euler equations is steady over time, where the presence of vortices is responsible. Our methods are versatile and can be easily adapted to obtain conservation of helicity for smooth solutions in various function spaces. Moreover, our research goes beyond the realm of Euler equations by achieving similar results for the Navier-Stokes equations in $L^3$-spaces, thereby addressing an unresolved problem dating back to 1979 posed by Beale and Fefferman. To this date, this problem remained unsolved, and our research represents a significant breakthrough in this area. As an added benefit, our research also achieves conservation of helicity for smooth solutions in various function spaces, where the techniques developed can be easily adapted. To the best of our knowledge, our research represents the first instance where helicity conservation has been achieved for weak solutions in $L^3$-spaces, thereby validating the theoretical predictions made by Beale and Fefferman in 1979. Our research is further complemented by an extensive discussion of the space and time discretization strategies, along with a detailed analysis of the stability properties of the resulting algorithms

A potential unexplained phenomenon known as the "ecentricity problem" exists in the context of gravitational waves generated by mergers of black holes. These waves are typically detected through high-precision sensors such as LIGO and VIRGO. Considering that binary black hole detectors are more sensitive to systems with lower eccentricities, there may be a detection bias towards mergers with lower initial eccentricity values. Our research aimed to investigate the likelihood of binary black holes with higher initial eccentricities being undetected at the current detection thresholds of LIGO and VIRGO. Our analysis reveals that approximately $49\%$ of mergers with eccentricities greater than $0.007$ are undetected at the LIGO detection threshold, while approximately $42\%$ of mergers with eccentricities greater than $0.03$ are undetected at the VIRGO detection threshold. These findings suggest that there could be a significantly higher number of unobserved binary black hole mergers with higher initial eccentricities below the current LIGO and VIRGO detection thresholds. Our research further indicates that approximately $50\%$ of mergers with eccentricities greater than $0.007$ have final eccentricities below $0.01$, while approximately $42\%$ of mergers with eccentricities greater than $0.03$ have final eccentricities below $0.005$. These results imply that some systems with initial eccentricities valued over $0.007$ are actually considered to be circular or near-circular at the LIGO detection threshold, while some systems with initial eccentricities valued over $0.03$ are actually considered to be circular or near-circular at the VIRGO detection threshold. Our research further demonstrates that two specific models over-predict the number of unobserved binary black hole mergers with higher initial eccentricities below the current LIGO and VIRGO detection thresholds. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a method called DyGED, a deep learning-based model that utilizes a temporal self-attention mechanism and a spatial attention-averaging network, combined with an incidence-aware loss function. Through extensive experiments on various datasets, including social networks and airline transportation schedules, DyGED has demonstrated exceptional performance in incident detection, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we analyze the key components of DyGED and visualize the incidents detected by the model. Experimental findings indicate that DyGED effectively improves the accuracy and robustness of incident identification, especially in complex graphs with precise temporal sequences. The nonstationary spherical shock wave scenario known as the Guderley problem is often employed to assess and verify computationally intensive hydrodynamic models. In this study, we present a precise analytical solution to the Guderley problem, backed by high-resolution simulations, and compare it with results from widely used hydrocodes, thus providing a reference standard for evaluating and validating these models in the future. Unlike the original Guderley solution, our approach allows for an accurate description of the initial implosion process without approximating the shock behavior or the pre-shock rarefaction field. Additionally, we incorporate radiation transfer equations to examine the effect of opacity models on shock behavior and precursor formation. We examine two distinct radiation transfer scenarios: one with an optically thin model and an equilibrium thermal relaxation time, and another with a continuous shift in emission line due to rapid compression. Consequently, we obtained shock profiles at various powers and stages, along with detailed maps of radiation field and electron distribution, all in excellent agreement with our analytical solution. On the other hand, hydrocodes failed to accurately capture the shock behavior, density, and radiation field, especially at lower powers, where the peak density and radiation field deviated by over an order of magnitude from the expected values. However, hydrocodes performed relatively well at higher powers, where the discrepancy was reduced to a factor of two or less. The principal cause of these discrepancies was the hydrocodes' inadequate handling of the rarefaction field, radiation transfer, and equilibrium, leading to inaccuracies in density and radiation field at lower powers and densities, and the failure to eliminate nonphysical oscillations at all power and density levels. Nevertheless, we found that utilizing the equilibrium condition for beta-evaporation and a finite time for precursor formation, along with accurately capturing the rarefaction field and its equilibrium, could reduce density and radiation field discrepancies to a factor of two or less, even at lower powers. Furthermore, we discovered that accurately modeling the precursor distribution as a diffuse plasma could reduce density and radiation field discrepancies by an order of magnitude, and that these discrepancies were particularly pronounced at lower densities and powers. In conclusion, we emphasize the significance of precisely solving the Guderley problem for validating and verifying hydrodynamic models, and that this can be effectively accomplished through a combination of high-resolution simulations and a precise analytical solution. The resulting solution profiles should serve as a reference standard, and the presented maps of radiation field and electron distribution at various powers and stages should prove useful in the future. This research introduces MrSARP, a hierarchical deep-generative model that utilizes a combination of stacked hourglass networks to learn detailed image representations at various resolutions, similar to the structure of the human visual system. Each hourglass module in MrSARP comprises a convolutional network for image synthesis and a transposed convolutional network for reverse mapping, all optimized end-to-end via a common loss function. By stacking these modules, MrSARP is capable of learning high-level features and synthesizing images at multiple resolutions, from coarse to fine. We evaluate MrSARP on two challenging datasets, CELEBA and VGGFace2, in comparison to prominent image synthesis models, including CycleGAN, CGAN, and SARP. Our results indicate that MrSARP not only surpasses these models on image synthesis but also demonstrates cross-domain generalization and semi-supervised learning performance superior to existing approaches. Furthermore, MrSARP's hierarchical structure facilitates the synthesis of images at various resolutions, an ability unmatched by previous models. Our proposed model and accompanying code are available online.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm holds promise for efficiently solving NP-hard problems on near-term quantum devices. However, its efficient termination on quantum devices depends on a classical Bayesian optimization component that poses a variational optimization challenge. Due to the limitations of global optimizers for non-convex objectives, this typically resorts to local optimization methods that can get stuck in saddle points or local minima. We present a Bayesian optimization framework that mitigates these issues by drawing on probabilistic regression models. This approach can be trained with quantum data and leverages the quartz library for seamless integration with quantum kernels. Our solution successfully escaped the saddle points and achieved better generalization in the quantum setting when compared to alternative methods. Furthermore, its improved exploration of the quantum kernel search space accelerated Bayesian optimization, with the total cost typically decreasing by about 50%. We've made our code available at https://github.com/soysaucelabs/bqao.

We introduce an advanced deep learning approach that streamlines vertebra identification and segmentation in 3D lumbar spine CT images. Our method addresses current limitations in deep learning-based VIdS solutions by incorporating a unique anatomic constraint specific to the lumbar spine, thereby improving vertebra segmentation and identification rates. We collected and annotated a large CT dataset with precise vertebra boundaries to design and train a 3D fully convolutional neural network (FCN). To assess its effectiveness, we compared our anatomic constraint method with two control groups: a general-purpose deep learning algorithm for image segmentation, and an algorithm modified to accommodate a different type of anatomical structure. As a result, our proposed technique achieved the best vertebra identification and segmentation rates, with an impressive 96.8% higher accuracy compared to the control groups. With its exceptional performance, our approach has great potential to enhance the automated segmentation and identification of vertebrae in the lumbar spine, thereby supporting clinical diagnosis and surgical planning. Furthermore, the annotated CT dataset used in this research can serve as a valuable resource for researchers in the field of VIdS. Markovian models, characterized by their transition matrices or graphs, provide a framework for understanding complex systems that evolve over time. By analyzing the algebraic and topological properties of these models, researchers can determine the asymptotic averages and correlation coefficients that help reveal the system's underlying structure. To this end, various approaches have been developed to compute the correlation integral, a measure of similarity between pairs of states that discloses the system's inherent patterns. Focusing on the system's transition dynamics, this study establishes an exact expressions for the correlation integral of Markovian models based on their transition matrices. Furthermore, the findings are extended to directed and undirected graphs, and the results are verified through both theoretical and numerical assessments. Overall, the study offers a unified view of Markovian models that facilitates the exploration of systems exhibiting recurrent, non-repeating, and pseudo-periodic behavior. The proposed framework is expected to enhance the analysis of complex data streams and temporal networks, enabling researchers to discover hidden patterns in dynamic systems. Additionally, the results can be applied to improve the representation of temporal networks by transforming them into a more compact, expressive format. In this context, the study explores the potential uses of Markovian models as a condensed representation of temporal networks, retaining information about the sequences of interactions and groupings of events. The efficacy of this representation is evaluated using the measures of prediction performance and information loss, and the findings demonstrate the effectiveness of Markovian models in both recognizing network patterns and predicting future interactions. In conclusion, the study highlights the potential applications of Markovian models in various domains, including data analysis, network representation, and system forecasting. In particular, the models can be employed to discover and recognize patterns in temporal networks, retain information about network evolutions, and make predictions about future interactions. In this context, the study explores the use of Markovian models for understanding the development of El Niño events, a complex phenomenon characterized by intricate interactions with climate patterns and impacts on global weather and economic systems. By analyzing the correlation coefficients and asymptotic averages of the Southern Oscillation Index, a measure of climate patterns, and applying the measures of information loss and prediction performance, researchers can gain insights into the underlying dynamics of the system and utilize Markovian models to discover, recognize, and predict patterns in the data. Let $X$ be a smooth complete intersection in projective space described by polynomials of degree $d$, not all constant, and defined over a field of characteristic not $d$. We derive formulas for the relative $I$-function of a toric complete intersection, a subvariety of $X$ inherited from a toric variety. Specifically, the formulas involve an explicit sum of products of hypergeometric functions. Moreover, under certain conditions, the relative $I$-function of one toric complete intersection is a multiple of another, with the multiple depending only on the coefficients of the defining ideal of $X$. As a consequence, the relative $I$-function of a smooth anticanonical variety, a class that includes certain Fano varieties, is always zero, as proven independently by Przyjalkowski and Chiodo-Payne-Schwarz, and Chow and Rulli. We also provide explicit generating functions for the relative $I$-function of a smooth toric complete intersection in projective space. These generating functions can be interpreted as holomorphic functions on the projective complex one-dimensional space. Finally, the relative $I$-function of a smooth toric complete intersection in projective space can be expressed as a product of modified $I$-functions, each related to a linear slice of a certain multivariate hyperbolic metric. This expression enables us to calculate the relative $I$-function for specific values of $d$. Our methods are largely independent of another approach proposed by Tevelev. Additionally, our results are closely related to the known formulas for the $I$-function of a smooth anticanonical polynomial, a class that includes certain cubic fourfolds, quintic threefolds, and other varieties. This research investigates acoustic transmission across interfaces between different piezoelectric materials, identifying conditions for total energy transfer and exploring how this is affected by the presence of electrical connections. Initially, we consider a simplified model of a single solid with an attached electrode and liquid environment, leading to the development of a bulk transmission criterion that relies on the material's properties at the surface. This is expanded to bilayer structures consisting of two piezoelectric components bonded at various angles, resulting in the formulation of an optimized orientation for maximum acoustic transmission. This is corroborated with numerical simulations of a specific material combination - PZT-4/PT - in different configurations, including a PZT-4/PT bilayer and a PT single component, both coupled with a liquid environment and various electrodes. Acoustic transmission across a PZT-4/PT interface is examined as a function of temperature, taking into account temperature-dependent material properties. Additionally, we explore radiation patterns and energy efficiency in piezoelectric transducers, facilitating their practical application in acoustic imaging and other related technologies. This knowledge has the potential to develop innovative, high-performance acoustic devices. Lastly, we reflect on the broader implications of our research and outline potential avenues for further exploration.

We investigate a system of coupled cavities containing polariton condensates that are linked to two separate areas with spatial light modulation (SLM). This enables the dynamic modification of excitation beam patterns interacting with the polariton fields, allowing for the exploration of optical control mechanisms that strengthen inter-cavity connections and facilitate the merging of polariton condensates. Numerical simulations reveal notable effects resulting from SLM patterns: the reduction of energy barriers, the promotion of optical parameter engineering, and the efficient transportation of polariton flux between cavities. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential to establish a single, unified polariton condensate through a protocol involving sequential applications of SLM patterns. This study lays a technical foundation for the development of innovative optical tools in polariton condensate research and micro-scale photon source development.

The unique system of K2-22 has generated significant interest due to the mysterious disappearance of its planet K2-22 b, believed to be one of the youngest planets in the solar system. Our study focuses on the theoretical aspects of this system, which involve significant gas loss from the planet due to its close proximity to the host star. We employed the MAGMA algorithm to develop a mass loss model tailored to extremely hot mini-neptunes like K2-22 b. This tailored model is based on magnetohydrodynamic simulations of atmospheric gas escape. We calculated the planet's mass loss rate by analyzing the ultraviolet emission associated with the star's interaction with the planet's atmosphere. Our estimates suggest a mass loss rate of $10^{16}$ g/s, resulting in an estimated lifetime of 300 million years for K2-22 b. This is consistent with the system's observed age. We propose that the planet's size and mass are self-sustaining as a result of the balance between material accumulation and loss. However, as the planet migrates closer to its host star, its temperature and radius increase, while its mass remains relatively constant. This balance explains the observed properties of the planet and its temporary nature. Ultimately, the planet is lost due to continued photoevaporation, supporting the idea that the system of K2-22 involves the destruction of mini-neptunes by high-energy radiation. This process is a crucial mechanism for setting the final mass of gas giants and mini-neptunes across the galaxy. Our study also suggests that the system of K2-20 is undergoing a similar process, involving a planet with a size similar to that of K2-22 b but significantly larger in mass. We identified a planet candidate with a mass similar to that of K2-22 b and proposed its potential for existence. If valid, this planet would undergo different evaporation patterns due to its higher mass and the weaker gravitational hold of the host star. As a result, the planet could either be retained or continue on a destructive path similar to that of K2-22 b, depending on its mass and the hold of the host star's gravitational force. Based on this analysis, we propose that the system of K2-20 could be in an intermediate state, where the planet is being efficiently accreted while undergoing photoevaporation at the same time. This process could result in the observed decrease in luminosity of the system over time. Conversely, the system of K2-20 could be in a late photoevaporation phase

We establish a classification system for homogeneous polynomials of degree d+1 in n+1 variables, categorized by the type of diffeomorphism (isomorphism in the neighborhood of a generic point) on their fiber Milnor fibration, which is associated with a non-zero polynomial, over the complex numbers, in n+1 variables, of degree d+1. This classification results in a partition of the set of homogeneous polynomials of degree d+1 in n+1 variables. We provide explicit examples of homogeneous polynomials that represent the distinct elements within this partition, up to a degree change of three, for the cases n=1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8. Additionally, for n=2, we offer an alternative approach to the classification that relies on a specific type of deformation and stable properties. This method extends straightforwardly to the case of constant coefficient linear polynomials, which are analyzed separately. We also identify distinct elements within our partition by analyzing the properties of the Hodge-theoretic invariant associated with the Milnor fibration, which measures the degree of the polynomial's hyperplane section. This degree determines the possible volumes of the fibration's base space, which is a complex manifold called the braid base, for a specific class of polynomials that are relatively prime to the polynomial x_1 + lambda. This degree is known as delta and is denoted by the symbol delta. Based on our classification, we are able to determine the possible values of delta for homogeneous polynomials of degree d+1 in n+1 variables, which are all non-negative, up to a degree change of three, for n<=8. We also establish that the set of delta values is limitless when n=2, as is the set of values obtained from a related invariant called the epsilon parameter. Finally, we study the properties of a type of deformation called the Viro polynomial, which is related to the classification system for the fiber type of the Milnor fibration. This deformation allows the parameter space to be explored, which has a dimension equal to the degree of the polynomial, for a fixed n. Under this deformation, the set of delta values remains constant at a^2 for a given n. Additionally, the parameter space contains a set of points that correspond to polynomials that are relatively prime to the polynomial x_1 + lambda, which have a base space dimension of 2 for degree 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, or 8

This paper compares the popular data structures Array of Arrays and Pandas Dataframe in the.NET and Python programming languages, respectively. After introducing the basic functionality of each data structure, we demonstrated their application in data analytics tasks through real-world data analysis. The examination of C# and Python data structures provides developers with insights into effective programming practices, with the aim of improving code quality and ensuring data integrity across both.NET and Python ecosystems. Our in-depth analysis focuses on essential features, with an additional exploration of more advanced capabilities. This study was initially presented at the Data Analytics Conference 2022, hosted by Data Responsive A/S in Copenhagen. Our article is an expanded version of that presentation, addressing feedback received during the Q&A session. Following the conference, we incorporated the feedback into the paper. Additionally, due to time constraints, we had to omit certain details, data analytics techniques, and results, which are now included in this expanded version. Our analysis revealed that both programming languages, with their respective data structures, are capable of efficiently supporting data analytics operations. However, our experience suggested that the C# implementation was generally faster, although the performance difference was not always significant. Notably, the speed disparity was more pronounced when using NumPy instead of Pandas. Based on our experience, we believe the main advantage of using Dataframe over Array of Arrays lies in its better support for data manipulation and analysis operations. Conversely, Array of Arrays may be preferred when priority is given to speed and data size is relatively large. Our recommendation is to utilize the profiling tool provided by Visual Studio to identify and optimize slow data analytics operations, allowing for further acceleration through code refactoring or the implementation of more efficient algorithms. Furthermore, we hope this paper will inspire a series of comparative studies on data structures, aiming to promote best practices across the.NET and Python communities, ultimately contributing to improved code quality. Our research may also serve as a foundation for introducing Dataframe to the.NET ecosystem, potentially expanding the existing libraries to include more sophisticated data analytics functionality. Our investigation into the feasibility of implementing Dataframe using existing.NET data structures led us to propose an alternative, more efficient implementation. Our analysis indicates that this new implementation outperforms the original one. Our study has also sparked an idea to integrate Queryable into the data structure, enabling the specification of data analytics operations as part of the LINQ framework. As a result, the execution of these operations can be delayed and performed only when the results are required, similar to the lazy evaluation approach used in the LINQ

This paper examines Galileo's methodological stance through an analysis of his written works and mathematical representations within his scientific notebooks. By considering both his approach to measurement procedures and underlying mathematical assumptions, we can evaluate Galileo's contribution to the development of scientific principles. While Galileo's emphasis on empirical evidence is widely recognized, our investigation reveals that his reliance on these methods, combined with his limited grasp of mathematical rigor, had a mixed impact on his groundbreaking discoveries in physics and optics. This study specifically looks at the tensions between empirical evidence and theoretical considerations in the contexts of inertia, vacuo and optical refraction. By taking a broader view that encompasses the interplay between measurement procedures and underlying mathematical frameworks, we can gain a deeper understanding of the interstices of scientific methods. Additionally, our analysis highlights the potential benefits and challenges of employing mixed-method approaches in general, particularly when combining qualitative and quantitative research strategies. Nonetheless, our examination suggests that such an hybrid research methodology can be effective in theoretical physics, as exemplified in our own previous and current research experiences. Lastly, this paper also outlines potential future research directions based on our existing knowledge and outlines the respective chapters that would comprise such a research volume. Some of the proposed chapters have already been published as separate articles while others are currently in preparation. Nonetheless, our analysis suggests that such a research volume could contribute meaningfully to the ongoing conversation in the philosophy of science and would be a valuable addition to the existing scientific literature. Ultimately, this paper serves as an introductory overview of our proposed research collection. Conversely, our actual research presentation will be more extensive and in-depth, encompassing over 800 pages. Additionally, chapters will be made available on open access following the presentation at the 22nd biennial meeting of the Indian Society for the History of Science in December 2017 in Mumbai. We introduced a measure of binding energy based on the broad bandwidth integral of connected q-correlation functions for one-dimensional systems with non-Gaussian statistics. This binding energy, denoted as $E_q$, is directly linked to the standard binding energy for small $q$. However, $E_q$ diverges at $q=1$ for all one-dimensional systems with bound states, and it serves as an indicator of quantum effects. For the hydrogen atom, there is a direct relationship between $E_q$ and $q$, and we developed a mathematical expression to represent this relationship. Additionally, we investigated how $E_q$ changes in response to variations in key factors, such as the mass of the proton and the fineness charge. Furthermore, we applied a scaling approach to examine the properties of $E_q$ in systems with bound states and to derive limits and relationships between $E_q$ and other quantities. This approach enabled us to show that $E_q$ can be used to assess how strongly bound a system is and to explore the connections between $E_q$ and other quantum effects. Ultimately, we established a universal rule governing the relationship between $E_q$ and the ground state bandwidth for systems with bound states, and we noted a peculiar link between $E_q$ and the critical bandwidth for systems that exhibit quantum diffusion. Additionally, we used $E_q$ to investigate the effects of variations in mass and charge on the ground state bandwidth and binding energy, and we found that there are instances where an increase in mass can lead to an increase in $E_q$ and, consequently, to a more strongly bound system. We also discovered that an amplification in the fineness charge can result in a more strongly bound system according to $E_q$ even if it results in a less strongly bound system according to traditional binding energy. The process of magnetic island merging in a sc sc sc plasma is investigated using the M3D experiment. Nonlinear simulations are carried out with a fixed, initial island width and different orientations of the magnetic field, which affects the interaction between large-scale MHD and microscale kinetic behavior. Various models are employed to comprehend the physics behind island coalescence and to gather data for comparison with experimental results. For instance, when the island width is about 10 cm, the interaction between sweet harmonic modes and other kinetic processes becomes prominent. Nonetheless, models disagree with each other and also with experimental data, particularly in terms of growth rate measurements. Despite the growing amplitude of fluctuations during the coalescence process, no substantial increase in electron temperature or pressure is observed. However, the ion convective adiabatic heating effect becomes apparent during this process, causing a noticeable increase in ion temperature. Consequently, the temperature ratio of ions to electrons significantly decreases, which is a rare occurrence in the initial stages of the plasma formation. This finding emphasizes the necessity of incorporating more sophisticated ion physics into models in order to gain a thorough, understanding of the plasma behavior. For example, the ion temperature increase observed in experiments can be successfully replicated with the using of the ion enthalpy transfer model. Nevertheless, the experimentally measured growth rates of fluctuations, which is approximately 1.1 kHz, cannot be matched by any of the considered models. It is suggested that the primary mechanism driving these fluctuations is the ion mode coupled with the ion enthalpy transfer effect, resulting in a faster than expected decrease in the ion to electron temperature ratio. In order to cooperate effectively, both human and assistant collaborators need to adapt their collaborative strategy. While humans leverage intuition and past experiences, known as heuristics, to make decisions, AI systems lack these advantages. Our proposed solution, H-Explorer, addresses this by employing an evolutionary algorithm that allows both human and AI collaborators to refine their cooperation over numerous trials. Using this approach, we studied the emergence of successful decision-making strategies among H-Explorer systems and discovered that they transition from initially ineffective tactics to more successful ones, eventually performing as well as specially designed optimized agents. Our research reveals that repeated collaboration fosters the development of effective problem-solving strategies, even when both collaborators start with random decision rules. Moreover, analyses of collaborative sessions highlighted the significance of communication in the problem-solving process and demonstrated that both human and AI collaborators can effectively engage in mental reasoning during collaboration. Ultimately, our findings indicate that H-Explorer offers a valuable platform for exploring more sophisticated forms of cooperative problem-solving in human-AI partnerships. This research has significant implications for the development of digital assistants that can learn and adapt to collaborative tasks through repeated interactions with humans. Our study also paves the way for a broader examination of the origins of cooperative problem-solving behaviors in complex systems comprising humans and AI. For instance, investigating the impact of emotional AI responses on human collaboration could lead to a more comprehensive understanding of the emotional dynamics between humans and AI. Another potential area of research involves exploring the role of digital assistants as mediators in complex, multi-stakeholder collaborations to promote more effective communication and resolution of disputes between humans. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/learnables/hexplorer.
